item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman and Kiké Hernández continue to add to their postseason résumés.
An inning after Freeman was denied an opposite-field home run over the left field wall at Truist Park by Mauricio Dubón, he thought he might try hitting one right.
But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first.
The two got the Dodgers on the board, to give them a 3-0 lead in the fourth inning of the NLDS, by hitting home runs over the walls in left and right field.
Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Braves starting pitcher Chris Sale and sent it 406 feet out of the park for a two-run homer. One batter later, Freeman obliterated a 96 MPH sinker and sent it screaming off the bat at 103 MPH for 399 feet.
Sale managed to get out of the inning in the following at-bat, but at first glance, it looked he was going to gve up another homer.
Teoscar Hernández just came short of Sale’s slider out of the park, after hard-hitting Sale at 108 MPH.
Both Freeman and Hernandez, continue to show why they are dominant in October, as both of them have had playoff heroics.
Freeman has a career batting average of .268 with 82 hits, 17 home runs, and 40 RBI through 81 postseason games.
Kiké Hernández has a career average of .272 with 80 hits and 16 home runs, with 42 RBIs in the postseason.
The combination of Hernández and Freeman came on the same day; manager Dave Roberts made a surprising decision to bump four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani down to the fifth hole in the Dodgers lineup and have Freeman hitting second, behind Mookie Betts, while Hernández was hitting ninth.
So far, his decision is paying off as Los Angeles holds a 3-1 lead against the Braves.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Freddie Freeman not adding to narrative of facing Braves in postseason
item.dc:creator: Matt Borelli
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers and Atlanta Braves are facing off for the sixth time in MLB postseason history, but their latest meeting comes with an interesting twist. It’s the first time Freddie Freeman is playing his former team in October since signing with the Dodgers prior to the 2022 season. Freeman enjoyed a decorated 12-year career with the Braves, earning five All-Star Game selections, winning the 2020 NL MVP and leading them to a World Series title in 2021. It was widely expected that Freema
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and Atlanta Braves are facing off for the sixth time in MLB postseason history, but their latest meeting comes with an interesting twist.
It’s the first time Freddie Freeman is playing his former team in October since signing with the Dodgers prior to the 2022 season.
Freeman enjoyed a decorated 12-year career with the Braves, earning five All-Star Game selections, winning the 2020 NL MVP and leading them to a World Series title in 2021. It was widely expected that Freeman and the Braves would work out a new contract in free agency, but that never came to fruition due to a reported disagreement over the inclusion of a sixth year.
Freeman understands the significance of playing the Braves in the postseason but doesn’t want to make a big deal out of it, via Bob Nightengale of USA Today.
“I’m going to try and not treat it any differently, and nor should anybody else treat anything differently,’’ Freeman told USA TODAY Sports and MLB.com outside the Dodgers’ clubhouse. “I understand it will be a storyline. I get it, but it is five years later. But I’m not going to try and look at it any differently. It’s another team that I’m trying to get through to win another championship, and I know they’re thinking the same thing.
“It’s not the Los Angeles Freddies, you know? But I understand. I get the storyline. And it’s an easy storyline. So, I try not to think about it like that. Come game time, I don’t think anybody’s going to be worrying about it. We could talk about it now, but by (Saturday), I don’t think anybody’s going to be worrying about who played for what team.”
Freeman will always have a special place in his heart for the Braves, but he is rightfully choosing to treat the NLDS like any other playoff series as a way to not let his personal history become a distraction.
It took Freeman a while to completely move on from the Braves, but he has since become a huge part of the Dodgers’ identity and is responsible for some of the biggest moments in franchise playoff history.
Braves appreciate Freddie Freeman’s replacement
When it became clear that they wouldn’t resolve their contract dispute with Freeman, the Braves moved on by acquiring All-Star first baseman Matt Olson. The Atlanta native has done an exceptional job replacing Freeman and earned praise from manager Walt Weiss.
“Matt had a lot on his plate when he first got here. He was replacing an icon,” Weiss began. “I think we got the only guy that could do it, the only guy that could step in that role at that time, and Matt’s been a superstar for us.
“Freddie, obviously, he’s a Hall of Famer. I still stay in touch with Freddie quite often. It’s always good to see him, but tough facing him when he’s on the other side because he’s such a good player. Like I said, I think Matt’s the only guy that could have pulled this off to replace that guy. He’s done it very well.”

On Tuesday night, the two teams will meet for Game 3 at Truist Park in Atlanta, with the Braves sending out left-handed ace Chris Sale while L.A. will start right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in what should be one of the best pitching matchups we’ve seen so far this postseason. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are tied with the Atlanta Braves at one game apiece in their best-of-five series in the NLDS.
On Tuesday night, the two teams will meet for Game 3 at Truist Park in Atlanta, with the Braves sending out left-handed ace Chris Sale while L.A. will start right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in what should be one of the best pitching matchups we’ve seen so far this postseason.
Ahead of the game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made some major lineup changes, including one involving veteran slugger Freddie Freeman.
Dodgers Announce Freeman Move
With Shohei Ohtani struggling at the plate recently, Roberts decided to move him down to the No. 5 spot in the lineup Tuesday night.
As a result, Freeman will move up from the cleanup spot to the No. 2 spot, while Mookie Betts remains in the leadoff spot.
Teoscar Hernandez and Will Smith will fill the No. 3 and No. 4 spots, while the back end of the order will remain fairly close to what the Dodgers have used recently, despite bringing Andy Pages back into the lineup.
Here’s the full Dodgers lineup:

K. Tucker RF
E. Hernández 3B
Y. Yamamoto SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) October 6, 2026
Freeman’s 2026 Postseason
While it’s only been two games, Freeman has been one of the most consistent bats in the Dodgers’ lineup against his former team.
He’s recorded three hits across seven at-bats, including two on Sunday, one of which was a home run.
Freeman spent the first 12 years of his MLB career with the Braves and became one of the greatest players in franchise history. Now, he’ll play the next two games in a ballpark he called home for more than a decade.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Shohei Ohtani dropped to fifth in Dodgers' batting order for Game 3 of NLDS vs. Braves
item.dc:creator: Chris Cwik
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are pushing two-way star Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the batting order following a tepid start to the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves. After hitting second in the first two games of the series, Ohtani was dropped to fifth ahead of Game 3 on Tuesday. Per The Athletic's Fabi
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are pushing two-way star Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the batting order following a tepid start to the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
After hitting second in the first two games of the series, Ohtani was dropped to fifth ahead of Game 3 on Tuesday. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernández and Will Smith will hit ahead of Ohtani in Game 3.
In the two previous games in the series, Betts led off and Ohtani hit second.
Per The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya, Dodgers managers Dave Roberts told reporters that the move to fifth would be just for Tuesday's game against Braves ace Chris Sale. A lefty, Sale has been notoriously tough against left-handed batters over his career.
Roberts added that when he approached Ohtani about moving down in the order on Monday, Ohtani responded that he'd considered suggesting doing so in September as he struggled through injuries.
Hitting fifth is unusual for Ohtani, who hasn't hit that low since 2020, when he was a member of the Los Angeles Angels.
Ohtani hasn't been terrible in the first two games of the series, going 2-for-8 with two strikeouts. But other members of the team have outperformed the slugger in the NLDS. Freeman and Hernández, in particular, have ignited the Dodgers' offense. Smith, however, is hitless in eight at-bats thus far.
At the plate, Ohtani has been worse against lefties over his career, though he still has an excellent .853 OPS against them. That's actually higher than Smith's career OPS against left-handers.
Ohtani, however, came into the playoffs battling multiple injuries. On Friday, he acknowledged that left knee and right biceps issues will impact him throughout the postseason. Those same issues seemed to affect Ohtani in the second half, as he hit .241/.322/.472 in August before collapsing with a .200/.300/.233 line in eight games in September. At that point, the team put Ohtani on the injured list to give him time to recover for the playoffs.
Now that the playoffs are here, the Dodgers will try to ease Ohtani into a bigger role. While he hit second in the order early in the NLDS, a combination of his performance and Sale's presence on the mound will drop Ohtani much lower than he has hit in recent seasons.

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers land two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal in blockbuster deadline deal, sources say

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- For as much as they might have downplayed the possibility behind closed doors, the Los Angeles Dodgers were long seen by rival executives as overwhelming favorites to land generational ace Tarik Skubal. Their farm system was too good, their goals were too lofty, their rotation had become too uncertain.
On Saturday night, a day and a half before the trade deadline, they pulled it off.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal, the reigning back-to-back American League Cy Young Award winner, from the Detroit Tigers for a package of three prospects: outfielder Zhyir Hope, and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith, sources told ESPN's Jeff Passan.
Skubal, a 29-year-old pending free agent, will now headline what was arguably already the best rotation in the sport. Alongside him will be Yoshinobu Yamamoto, making a strong case for a Cy Young of his own, followed by Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani and Tyler Glasnow, all of whom are in varying stages of returning from injury.
The Dodgers had long touted their depth as a reason they didn't necessarily need Skubal. Snell, who has made one start all year, is expected to rejoin the rotation after his next rehab outing. Glasnow, out since May 6 with back spasms, will begin a minor league rehab assignment next week. And though Ohtani is still troubled by a sore left knee that only seems to bother him on the mound, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said earlier this week he fully expects him to pitch in October.
The Game 1 starter, though, will be Skubal, who might be the best pitcher in the world.
Skubal boasts a 2.79 ERA in 16 starts this year, striking out 116 batters and issuing 14 walks in 96 innings. The only thing that could stop him were bone chips that began to cause irritation in his left elbow in late April. Skubal underwent a less-invasive, revolutionary NanoScope procedure and returned in about six weeks. His ERA in July is 2.03. And as he addressed the media in the visiting clubhouse at Sutter Health Park in Sacramento late Saturday night, moments after being informed of the trade, Skubal at one point got choked up.
"Going into the season, this isn't what I planned on doing," Skubal said before getting on the verge of tears while reflecting on his time in Detroit. "But circumstances change, situations change. I'm very appreciative of everything that the Tigers have done for me."
A late bloomer who lasted until the ninth round of the 2018 draft, Skubal began to emerge as one of the game's most talented pitchers in 2022 and 2023 and took it to another level thereafter. From 2024 to 2025, Skubal went 31-10 with a 2.30 ERA and a whopping 469 strikeouts in 387 innings. His 12.6 FanGraphs wins above replacement led all major league pitchers.
When Skubal and members of the Tigers' front office exchanged arbitration figures in the ensuing offseason, the two sides were $13 million apart. An independent arbitrator ruled in favor of Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, rewarding him a $32 million salary as he headed into his free-agent year.
Rumors had swirled throughout the offseason that the Tigers would trade him then. Instead, they doubled down, signing fellow starter Framber Valdez to a three-year, $115 million contract with the hope of winning the AL Central. Instead, the Tigers flopped. By the end of May, they were tied with the Colorado Rockies for the worst record in the majors, prompting executives throughout the industry to assume Skubal would be traded.
The Tigers proceeded to win 28 of their next 46 games, and suddenly it seemed as if Skubal might stay. But their momentum ran out. The Tigers lost back-to-back games to the last-place Kansas City Royals over the weekend and dropped two of three to the Baltimore Orioles thereafter. The last of those losses, on Wednesday night, saw Skubal take the mound and record his 1,000th career strikeout, then sit in the dugout while his team blew a 7-0 lead.
After it was over, the Tigers were seven games below .500, six games out of first place and three games out of a wild-card spot.
To many observing Skubal's availability, it was a death knell to his time in Detroit.
The Atlanta Braves, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, New York Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays were all in on Skubal to some extent, with the Brewers, deep in prospects, the favorites among that group. But the Dodgers were the clear frontrunners all along. And now they'll add Skubal to a laundry list of talent they've acquired from the outside over the years, following Ohtani, Snell, Yamamoto, Glasnow, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and, this offseason, Edwin Diaz and Kyle Tucker.
The vast majority of those players came via free agency. The Dodgers loathe the high asking prices at midseason. But in getting Skubal, they parted from an outfield group that is stocked with talent -- one that is still headlined by Josue DePaula, a consensus top-25 prospect, along with Eduardo Quintero, ranked 45th on Kiley McDaniel's latest ESPN rankings. They also maintain all of their young major league starting pitching, namely Justin Wrobleski, Emmet Sheehan and Roki Sasaki.
In Hope and Ryan, though, the Tigers came away with two top-50 prospects.
Hope, 21, was slashing .293/.369/.530 with 23 home runs and 18 stolen bases for the Dodgers' Double-A affiliate and brings explosive power from the left side, top-tier speed and an ability to handle center field.
Ryan, 27, made a brief stint in the major leagues in 2024, putting up a 1.33 ERA in four starts. He then underwent a prolonged rehab from Tommy John surgery and has made eight starts in Triple-A, putting up a 4.46 ERA. He has been out since the middle of June with a hamstring injury, but McDaniel ranked him 49th in his midseason top 50 in May.
Smith, 21, was a third-round pick out of high school in 2023 who has put up a 3.88 ERA in 19 starts at the Class A level this season.
In three months, Skubal will head into the open market with the chance of signing the most lucrative deal ever rewarded to a starting pitcher. Before then, he will join a Dodgers club that boasts the highest run-differential and second-best record in the major leagues -- and help them try to become the first team in NL history to win three consecutive championships.
Asked his thoughts about joining the Dodgers, Skubal took about 15 seconds to compose himself before saying: "Yeah, it's exciting. I'm excited. They've got a good group."

item.title: [roundtable.io] Freeman Wants Dodgers to Find Ways to Score Without Home Runs
item.dc:creator: Anthony Arroyo
item.description: Freddie Freeman believes the Los Angeles Dodgers need to find more ways to manufacture offense after falling to the Atlanta Braves 3-2. Both teams have received strong pitching through the opening two games of the series, making consistent offense difficult to produce. Freeman believes the Dodgers need to create more opportunities, get runners on base and deliver the timely hit when those chances arise. The Dodgers have already demonstrated an ability to produce runs through the home run, but Fr
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman believes the Los Angeles Dodgers need to find more ways to manufacture offense after falling to the Atlanta Braves 3-2.
Both teams have received strong pitching through the opening two games of the series, making consistent offense difficult to produce. Freeman believes the Dodgers need to create more opportunities, get runners on base and deliver the timely hit when those chances arise.
The Dodgers have already demonstrated an ability to produce runs through the home run, but Freeman sees manufacturing offense as an important part of their approach moving forward.
Atlanta's bullpen creates challenges
Atlanta used multiple pitchers throughout Game 2, creating a difficult matchup for the Dodgers' lineup.
Freeman acknowledged how challenging it can be to face a different arm repeatedly throughout a game. Each pitcher can bring a different combination of velocity, movement and release point, forcing hitters to adjust from one at-bat to the next.
That approach helped the Braves escape several important situations and keep the Dodgers from building a larger offensive threat. Ultimately, the Dodgers would finish 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position, leaving seven runners on base.
Atlanta's pitching staff has been able to limit Los Angeles through the first two games, contributing to two closely contested games. Freeman expects that challenge to continue as the series moves forward.
Dodgers need to capitalize on opportunities
While the Dodgers struggled to produce consistently, Freeman noted that the team did have opportunities during Game 2.
The difficulty comes from stringing together enough hits to turn those opportunities into multiple runs. In the postseason, where the quality of pitching is often at its highest, putting together several consecutive hits can be especially difficult.
That makes timely hitting even more important.
The Dodgers do not necessarily need to radically change their offensive approach. Instead, Freeman believes the lineup needs to continue controlling the strike zone and trusting its individual plans at the plate.
Freeman feeling good at the plate
Freeman also enters the next stage of the series feeling positive about his swing.
After a productive stretch leading into the postseason, the veteran first baseman believes he has been seeing the ball well through the opening games. He hopes to carry that consistency into the upcoming road portion of the series.
For Freeman, the key is maintaining the same approach rather than becoming overly aggressive in an attempt to create more offense.
The Dodgers' hitters will have to balance that patience with the need to capitalize when opportunities arise.
With the series now tied 1-1, Los Angeles heads into its next game needing to find additional ways to score. Freeman believes the answer is not abandoning the team's approach, but executing it better when the biggest opportunities arrive.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Ponders Dodger Lineup Tweaks Ahead of Game 3
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta. The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2. With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly. Díaz Could Close “I think that we’ve buil
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have faced two bullpen games to kick off their National League Division Series battle with the Atlanta Braves.
On Tuesday, things will get much more difficult.
The Dodgers are going up against 10-time All-Star and former Cy Young award winner Chris Sale. The left-hander is coming off a regular season in which he had a 2.16 ERA and 200 strikeouts over 162.2 innings. He then allowed three runs over 6.1 innings in his wild-card Game 1 start, and pitched 1.1 scoreless innings to close out Game 3.
The Dodgers know what they're up against with Sale, one of baseball's best pitchers.
"Chris is going to be tough," Roberts said. "We know we're going to be in for a dogfight."
The difficult lefty matchup also has manager Dave Roberts considering some lineup changes.
“I think so," Roberts said. "I am considering it. I think that’s a very fair question. I think that I have to be mindful of — it’s two games, and then with the two games, what have I seen?”
Roberts mentioned Enrique Hernandez and Miguel Rojas as potential options to be in the lineup. The only Dodgers with any semblance of success against Sale in their careers are Mookie Betts (7-for-18) and Freddie Freeman (5-for-16).
The Dodgers have been especially reliant on the home run this series, with all seven of their runs coming via the long ball.
In Sunday's Game 2, they went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position.
Sale faced the Dodgers on Aug. 27, firing a complete-game shutout with 11 strikeouts and just five hits allowed.
Dave Roberts Considering Moving Shohei Ohtani Down in the Lineup
The Dodgers have plenty of players struggling in the lineup, including Will Smith (0-for-8), Andy Pages (0-for-7) and Tommy Edman (0-for-5).
At the top of the lineup, however, is Shohei Ohtani, who is 2-for-8 with two singles and two strikeouts. He's looked far from his usual self.
"I think there's, like we've talked about, he's not 100%," Roberts said on Monday. "But at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone. ... I think that's something that — it's hard to have success when you're out of the zone. ... And Shohei understands, any hitter understands that. So I think that's the thing is — then the question is how do we get him into it? I think there's a little bit of trying to do too much. I think that's a piece."
Roberts said he's open to moving Ohtani down in the lineup, especially with the tough left-hander on the mound.
However, he wouldn't commit to anything on Monday.
"Going further than [No. 2]? I'm open to it," Roberts said. "It's something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day, every conversation I've had with him is, whatever is best for the team, he's all in on.”
For what it's worth, Ohtani is 3-for-15 against Sale in his career with five strikeouts.
"At the end of the day, our guys are our guys," Roberts said. "And, yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats."

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk.
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz.
"A loss is a loss, but to get walked off never feels good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "We didn't play a clean game, a great game, on either side of the baseball, but we did enough to put ourselves in position to win a game.
"Unfortunately, we couldn't finish it."
It was another rough outing for Diaz, who has an 11.00 ERA over 11 outings this season. The 32-year-old is a three-time All-Star, but he hasn't helped the Dodgers much after signing a three-year, $69 million deal during the offseason.
Waldschmidt connected on Diaz's hanging slider, hitting it into the left-center field seats for his second career homer and first big league walk-off.
"It's the slider," Diaz said. "The fastball was great today, but I missed the slider right in the middle. I think I was trying to be perfect with the pitch, and I'm missing right in the middle. I've got to be better. I'm a big league pitcher, so I've got to make pitches."
The Dodgers were swept by the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs coming into Friday night's game. They still have a comfortable lead in the National League West -- 7 games in front of the Diamondbacks -- despite a 10-16 record since July 5.
Roberts acknowledged that Diaz has been struggling since his return from the injured list on July 29, but the manager wasn't necessarily ready to try a new closer. His reasoning was simple: There's no clear-cut alternative.
"Honestly, you've got to look at the options," Roberts said. "The way some of these guys are throwing, they're not throwing great either."
The Dodgers still look like a formidable team, particularly after adding ace left-hander Tarik Skubal in a trade-deadline deal with the Detroit Tigers last week. Two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell is slated to return Tuesday after missing most of the season because of injuries.
And the lineup still has plenty of star power with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker.
Roberts said before Friday's game that the remedy for the recent troubles was simple.
"We've just got to play better," Roberts said. "I don't think the standings -- I mean they're important, they matter -- but I just feel like with the talent we have, we've just got to play good baseball and it'll take care of itself. It always does."br/]

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Offense Feels the Urgency After Night of Missed Chances
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have hit enough home runs to stay alive in this series. What they have not done yet is build innings. That was the theme running through the clubhouse after Sunday’s 3-2 loss to Atlanta. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Miguel Rojas all came back to the same point in slightly different ways. The Dodgers are getting runners on base. They are giving themselves chances. Now they need somebody to come through with the hit that keeps an inning moving. Freeman put it mos
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have hit enough home runs to stay alive in this series. What they have not done yet is build innings.
That was the theme running through the clubhouse after Sunday’s 3-2 loss to Atlanta. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Miguel Rojas all came back to the same point in slightly different ways. The Dodgers are getting runners on base. They are giving themselves chances. Now they need somebody to come through with the hit that keeps an inning moving.
Freeman put it most plainly.
“We’ve got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” he said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now. Get guys on base, get that big hit, and hopefully our pitching keeps doing what they’re doing.”
The Dodgers Are Getting Traffic
The Dodgers had chances throughout Game 2 and could not turn them into runs. Freeman said that is where the frustration lies.
“It’s really hard to do,” he said. “You see what’s being thrown at us on their side and our side. It’s hard to get hits in the big leagues, especially in the playoffs. Stringing hits together is very hard, but we’ve had a couple opportunities. Hopefully we can cash them in on Tuesday.”
Betts saw it much the same way.
“I don’t know what’s going on right now,” he said. “We need to get going offensively. It’s not going to be easy, but we knew that from the beginning.
“We had some moments today, but we didn’t come through, but that’s part of the game. We just have to keep giving ourselves moments, and eventually something will happen.”
Rojas pointed to the same missed chances.
“We just missed the big hit,” he said. “We created a lot of traffic, which is good. I think when you’re playing playoff baseball, you’re not facing any easy arms out there. They have really good stuff.
“We’ve got to continue to see what we can do to put together better at-bats when we have runners in scoring position.”
That is the heart of the issue. The Dodgers have found ways to reach base. They simply have not turned enough of those chances into runs.
Bullpen Games Make It Harder
Freeman also talked about the challenge of facing a different look almost every time through the order.
“Bullpen games are hard,” he said. “It’s hard to win those games. It’s also hard to hit those games. We were able to do good in one of them, and they pitched really well tonight.
“It’s tough because you’re facing a different arm every single time you’re going up there. Different angles, different velocities, different things.”
Rojas gave Atlanta credit as well, especially for the work of Didier Fuentes and Robert Suarez.
“They’re throwing the ball really well,” he said. “They’ve got guys with big arms and they know how to use them. Fuentes was really good, and obviously Suarez coming out of the bullpen in that inning with a couple guys on, he was able to get the out.
“Sometimes you’ve got to tip your cap and move on.”
Betts echoed that.
“They’re a good team,” he said. “They did a pretty good job giving ourselves chances. We just didn’t come through.”
Stick With the Plan
The Dodgers also pushed back on the idea that the answer is to simply start swinging earlier or get more aggressive.
Freeman said each hitter has to stay with what works for him.
“Everyone has their own plan and approach going into each at-bat, and you just try to execute it,” he said. “I don’t think anybody’s going to go in and try and start swinging at every pitch. Usually when you do that, you start swinging at bad pitches.
“Just try to control the strike zone like we have been doing and get that big hit.”
Rojas said the same thing in his own way.
“We’ve got a game plan going into the game,” he said. “I don’t think we need to change anything and come on Tuesday swinging at every first pitch because that’s not how baseball works.
“We’ve just got to trust our plan, trust our discipline at the plate. We’re really good at that. I’m looking forward to getting better results.”
That might be the most important part of the whole discussion. The Dodgers know what they are trying to do. They also know forcing the issue can make things worse.
Freeman Feeling Good
One encouraging sign has been Freeman himself.
“I feel good,” he said. “I’ve had a good work week, and obviously the first couple games have been good. Hopefully I can carry it into the road series.”
His home run Sunday was one of the few big swings the Dodgers produced, and it tied the game at the time.
Still, Freeman came back to the broader problem.
“We just didn’t score enough runs tonight.”
Simple as that.
A Short Series Gets Shorter
Betts also put the moment in perspective as the Dodgers head to Atlanta tied 1-1.
“Nobody expected us to go 11-0,” he said. “We know it’s going to be a tough matchup no matter who’s on the mound.”
Chris Sale will be on the mound next, which raises the degree of difficulty even more.
“It’s the same challenges as today,” Betts said. “Nothing’s going to be easy. Obviously we know Chris Sale, so we’ll see how it goes.”
Rojas said the clubhouse understands what is at stake.
“We are not satisfied, to be honest with you, because we got the opportunity to win two games right here,” he said. “But at the same time, you’ve got to understand that the other team is trying to win too.”
He also stressed the need to keep moving after a missed chance.
“The next at-bat is the one that counts,” Rojas said. “A lot of guys in this clubhouse have been in situations where we’re struggling, and once you have an at-bat that can get you what you need to help the team win, that can change things.”
That is where the Dodgers stand now.
The home runs have kept them in the series. The pitching has kept games close. The chances have been there.
Now they need to start turning those chances into runs.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Mookie Betts Isn't Crowing about the Dodgers' 100-Win Season
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — The Dodgers finished the regular season with 100 victories, but Mookie Betts already has his attention firmly fixed on October. Speaking with reporters following Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants, Betts discussed how he plans to maintain his recent offensive surge during the Dodgers’ five-day break, the importance of team chemistry, and the change in intensity that comes with postseason baseball. While Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández expressed appreciation for reachi
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — The Dodgers finished the regular season with 100 victories, but Mookie Betts already has his attention firmly fixed on October.
Speaking with reporters following Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants, Betts discussed how he plans to maintain his recent offensive surge during the Dodgers’ five-day break, the importance of team chemistry, and the change in intensity that comes with postseason baseball.
While Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández expressed appreciation for reaching the 100-win milestone, Betts offered a characteristically understated assessment.
A Hundred Wins? That’s Nice.
Asked whether another 100-win season carried particular significance for him and the team, Betts wasn’t especially sentimental.
“No, I don’t think so. Unless it’s some type of record or something. Not that I’m aware of. So, it means we played pretty good.”
For Betts, the more immediate concern is preserving the rhythm he established during a terrific September. The Dodgers’ shortstop has been one of the club’s hottest hitters over the final month, but maintaining that feel without regular games presents a challenge.
“I’m not sure. I don’t know if you can, just because games are kind of how you develop the rhythm,” he explained.
“But we’ll have the intrasquad games, and I’ve been in the league, what, 13 years now? So I’ll figure it out.”
Coming Together for Another October Run
The Dodgers successfully navigated a similar five-day break in 2024, using that time to prepare for the postseason while strengthening the team’s connection away from the field.
Betts believes that experience contributed to their championship run and expects the club to follow a similar approach this year.
“Yeah, I would say so. And I think we’re going to do it again. You know, I think this is the time where you really have to come together.
“There’s going to be a lot of adversity and whatnot. But it’s something that we’ve all been doing together for a while, and we get an opportunity to do it again.”
Asked whether his businesslike approach helps establish the team’s attitude heading into October, Betts said the entire clubhouse understands what lies ahead.
“Yeah, I would say so. But I think everybody has the same attitude. I think everybody, once we get to this time, we’ll be ready to go.
“And we understand that there is a distinct difference between now and the regular season. But, I mean, you obviously got to play the regular season.
“So now, getting to the postseason, we’ll keep the same attitude, but probably add a little more intensity and whatnot because it’s a short amount of time.”
September Momentum Is No Guarantee
The Dodgers’ offense enjoyed an excellent September, with Betts among the players finding their stride at precisely the right time. But when asked whether that momentum can carry into the playoffs, he offered a refreshingly straightforward answer.
“No idea.”
Betts elaborated that the quality of pitching changes considerably once the postseason begins, making it difficult to predict whether a team’s offensive success will continue.
“Yeah, I mean, you’re facing all the best pitching. Momentum is a thing, obviously, and so you never know. You never know what’s going to happen, and you can’t predict it.
“So you just got to go be ready.”
For Betts and the Dodgers, that preparation begins now. They’ll spend the next five days working through intrasquad games, maintaining their timing, and preparing for the winner of the Phillies-Braves Wild Card Series.
And when Saturday arrives, Betts expects the Dodgers to bring the same collective approach that helped carry them to last year’s championship, with a little extra October intensity thrown in.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Blake Snell’s rocky outing leads to de facto bullpen game
item.dc:creator: Jacob Macofsky
item.description: The Dodgers needed one win to send the Atlanta Braves to the brink of elimination on Sunday. Instead, the Braves lineup forced an early exit from Blake Snell and scored two defining runs against the bullpen in a 3-2 win over the Dodgers, forcing the series back to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4. It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured lis
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers needed one win to send the Atlanta Braves to the brink of elimination on Sunday. Instead, the Braves lineup forced an early exit from Blake Snell and scored two defining runs against the bullpen in a 3-2 win over the Dodgers, forcing the series back to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4.
It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured list. The southpaw had looked like his usual dominant stretch once he returned in August, but the ultimate test was to see how he would perform against the lone team that roughed him up.
Snell made quick work of Drake Baldwin for the first out, but after allowing a one-out single to Ronald Acuña Jr., he walked both Matt Olson and Ozzie Albies to load the bases. Snell managed to get Michael Harris II to fly out in foul territory for a crucial second out, but Mauricio Dubón tacked on the game's first run with an infield single. Snell faced seven hitters in the first inning, needing 27 pitches to give the Dodgers a chance to hit.
Snell's biggest flaw on Sunday was his inability to get quick innings, unlike Tarik Skubal on Saturday. Snell needed four pitches to get two quick outs in the second inning, but allowed a six-pitch walk to Baldwin and needed another eight to strike out Acuña. Snell allowed another two-out baserunner in the third inning, this time a single from Harris, needing 19 pitches after tossing 18 the inning prior.
Snell's hopes at a clean inning were dashed in the fourth inning, as he walked a pair of hitters and tossed 26 pitches before the plug was pulled on his night. The Dodgers got him off the hook in the bottom of the fourth inning with a Freddie Freeman home run, but the Dodgers employed six relievers out of the bullpen over their final 5 1/3 innings on the mound.
Snell had a postseason to remember last year, as his defining moment came in Game 1 of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, facing the minimum over eight shutout innings. Sunday's outing was the first time he failed to log four innings in a postseason start since he began the 2022 Wild Card series against the New York Mets back when he was a San Diego Padre. Out of the 90 pitches he tossed against Atlanta, 47 of them went for strikes.
Snell's final start of the regular season was limited to just one inning after he dealt with left groin inflammation. Dave Roberts was quick to deny any concern over Snell's groin issue, noting that he was battling himself on the mound.
"No, it wasn't that. He was fighting himself in his delivery all game. Today, I just think the fastball was really good, the changeup was good at times, but I think, in total, didn't have fastball command, didn't have slider command, and the changeup wasn't there. He was pulling it. I think overall it wasn't the groin, and he wasn't sharp tonight."
Roberts felt optimistic about his chances of Snell on the mound while Atlanta went with their own bullpen game, beginning with left-hander Ray Kerr. The pieces just couldn't fall into place on Sunday.
"Felt great. Anytime I feel I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher felt good. Going to getting Kerr out of the game and then getting [Grant] Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did. We just couldn't execute as the game progressed."
Now the Dodgers will face the only pitcher to shut them out in the regular season, left-hander Chris Sale, in a crucial Game 3 at Truist Park on Tuesday. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the mound for the first time in the playoffs since his Herculean performance in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series.

item.content:encoded:
After the Atlanta Braves captured a 3-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS Game Two on Sunday afternoon, the series between the two World Series hopefuls is knotted at one apiece, with the series shifting to Atlanta for the next two games.
LA outhomered the Braves 2-0 in Game Two, and all of the Dodgers’ runs have come via the homer, which is a bit concerning. Dodgers’ infielder Freddie Freeman hit a solo shot on Sunday evening, but ultimately, LA came up short.
Following the game, Freeman spoke with the media and shared his reaction to the loss, as well as his thoughts on how the series is going thus far.
Freddie Freeman Shares Thoughts on Dodgers Loss to Braves
Via SportsNetLA, here is what Freddie Freeman had to say after the Dodgers’ loss on Sunday:
“Gotta find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run; that’s our biggest thing right now.”
“Two really good teams going at it,” Freeman also noted.
Freddie has emerged as a true leader on the Dodgers roster, and he makes a great point. LA was 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position on Sunday, so they had no issue tallying baserunners, but driving them in was the issue.
NLDS Between Dodgers and Braves Shifting to LA
The Dodgers got a solid outing from Blake Snell on Sunday, but walks were a huge issue; despite the Braves going to a bullpen game, Didier Fuentes shut down the Dodgers offense from the 6th inning on.
However, now both teams will have their ace starters going on Tuesday, with Atlanta opting to start Chris Sale, and LA going with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
Game Three is the biggest game of both teams’ respective seasons, and with both All-Star starters going, it should be another tense, low-scoring affair.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers heroes, zeros from NLDS Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani concerns grow

item.description: Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series: Zero Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single. Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but. Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off
Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series:
Zero
Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single.
Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but.
Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will Smith (0–for–8), Andy Pages (0–for–7, one walk) and Tommy Edman (0–for–5, one walk) are all vying for that honor.
But if there was any hope that the team’s playoff-opening bye week would fix the two-way amid his ongoing right arm and left knee injuries, these two games have been a reminder of just how far he is from his typical self.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine,” manager Dave Roberts said.
But…
“I don’t know if he’s trying to do too much because he doesn’t feel perfect,” the skipper added, in what felt more like a tacit acknowledgement.
A healthy Ohtani, after all, wouldn’t go 0–for–2 against plucky feel-good story Ray Kerr, striking out on an inside fastball in the first inning before popping out in a key spot with two aboard in the third.
A healthy Ohtani wouldn’t need to slap the ball the other way Ichiro-style just to get a base hit, as he did on his lone single in the fifth.
The most telling thing for the 32-year-old superstar the last two days?
The Braves haven’t been afraid to challenge him, throwing him nine fastballs in the middle-third of the strike zone so far. And he hasn’t been able to punish them for it, turning only one into a hit (that first-inning, Game 1 single) while also chasing more outside of the zone after failing to end his at-bats.
“He’ll be in there Game 3,” Roberts confirmed. “We’ve just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Hero
At least the Dodgers’ other pre-NLDS injury question mark has seemingly turned a corner.
In his final 66 games of the regular season (going back to July 5), Freddie Freeman had hit only one home run. In September, he slumped to a .184 average with only one extra-base hit while battling a right knee injury that threatened to linger into the playoffs.
However, the bye week seemingly did wonders for him, following up a one-hit, one-walk performance in Game 1 of the series with a two-hit night Sunday that included a solo homer to right field.
“I feel good, so I think we can be done with those questions,” he quipped when asked about his swing and knee injury. “Just more consistently getting myself in a good spot, being able to put good swings on it.”
Unsung hero
There were times this year when Edwin Díaz’s fastball velocity dipped as low as 92 mph.
During his scoreless appearance in the sixth inning on Sunday, the resurgent right-hander dialed it up to a season-high 100.8 mph.
That was just one impressive aspect of Díaz’s latest standout performance, in which he extended his scoreless streak to six innings (including 15 straight batters retired over his last five outings) since returning from his second injured list stint of the year on Sept. 18.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “I think if you look at tonight, try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
Key stat
Zero: As in 0 hits with runners in scoring position for the Dodgers on Sunday, and 0 runs scored via any method other than a home run so far in this NLDS.
Ironically, the club’s lack of power had been the bigger concern coming into the playoffs.
While they could be (extremely) up-and-down in the regular season in situational at-bats, they still rank seventh in batting average with runners in scoring position and third in OPS.
That, however, hasn’t translated to October yet.
“Got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” Freeman said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now.”
Quote of the night
“We’ve been in tougher spots than this one,” outfielder Teoscar Hernández said, when asked how crucial the team’s past October experience (especially in back-and-forth series like the 2024 NLDS and 2025 World Series) would be in the face of what is now a best-of-three showdown. “It’s a 1–1 series. We know they’re going to have the best pitcher that they have, starting pitcher, in [Game 3 with Chris] Sale. But we’re just gonna try to be ready and just go with the best plan and just try to execute it.”

item.title: [Infobae] El colombiano Didier Fuentes ponchó a Shohei Ohtani, el mejor beisbolista del mundo, con los Bravos de Atlanta
item.dc:creator: Camilo Zabaleta
item.description: El colombiano Didier Fuentes lanzó tres entradas y dos tercios desde el bullpen de los Bravos de Atlanta, ponchó a Shohei Ohtani y ayudó a la victoria por 3-2 sobre los Dodgers de Los Ángeles en el Dodger Stadium. item.content:encoded:
El colombiano Didier Fuentes lanzó tres entradas y dos tercios desde el bullpen de los Bravos de Atlanta, ponchó a Shohei Ohtani y ayudó a la victoria por 3-2 sobre los Dodgers de Los Ángeles en el Dodger Stadium. El resultado dejó igualada 1-1 la otra Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Fuentes ingresó en el sexto episodio y permitió un imparable y una carrera limpia, sin otorgar bases por bolas. Realizó 47 lanzamientos, de los cuales 30 fueron strikes, y logró tres ponches durante su primera actuación de postemporada.
El relevista colombiano enfrentó a Ohtani con cuenta completa. Luego de una recta a 162,4 km/h, que fue declarada bola, recurrió a una bola curva 137,3 km/h, para conseguir el tercer strike.
También retiró por la vía del ponche a Will Smith y Freddie Freeman. Fuentes dominó a los primeros 11 bateadores que enfrentó, hasta que Max Muncy conectó un cuadrangular con dos outs en el noveno inning.
Esa es la racha más larga de un relevista de 21 años o menos en un juego de postemporada en la historia de la MLB. Ningún relevista de 21 años o menos ha tenido una racha tan larga en un juego de temporada regular desde Tom Gordon el 12 de abril de 1989, según lo publicado por Opta Stats en su perfil de X.
El único punto negativo de la jornada para el joven beisbolista cafetero fue el jonrón de Muncy impulsó la entrada de Iglesias, quien retiró al único bateador al que se enfrentó para conseguir la victoria. Pero eso no arruinó lo que fue una noche memorable para Fuentes, quien lanzó cuatro rectas a más de 99 mph en la novena entrada.
“Fue muy emotivo y emocionante. Así que le doy gracias a Dios por la ayuda que me ha permitido mantenerme sano y poder competir”, dijo el nacido en Tolú, Sucre, tras su primera gran noche en la liga más importante de béisbol en el mundo.
“¿Tiene 21 o 22 años? Está haciendo eso a esa edad. Es increíble, sobre todo lanzar a 100 millas por hora. Se enfrenta a situaciones de alto nivel y las supera. Fue realmente impresionante” dijo Kerr, el lanzador principal de los Bravos de Atlanta, sobre Fuentes.
Mientras que Matt Olson, primera base de los Bravos, se refirió a la potencia en el brazo que tiene el colombiano: “No podía creer que volviera a lanzar en la novena entrada, pero lo hizo y seguía lanzando a 100 millas por hora. Eso fue impresionante.”
“Después de su tercera entrada, miré a nuestro entrenador de lanzadores y le dije: ‘Veamos cómo se siente’”, dijo Weiss. “Si se siente bien, quiero que vuelva a lanzar. No quería cambiar algo que funcionaba bien. Estaba lanzando muy bien”, declaró el manager del equipo.
Los Bravos habían abierto el marcador con un sencillo productor de Mauricio Dubón en el primer episodio. Freeman igualó para los Dodgers con un jonrón solitario en el cuarto, pero Atlanta volvió a tomar la ventaja en el quinto mediante una jugada que permitió anotar a Michael Harris II.
Harris amplió el marcador en el séptimo con un doblete productor que llevó a Matt Olson al plato. Fuentes se anotó su primer hold, la estadística asignada a un relevista que preserva una ventaja en una situación comprometida. La serie se trasladará a Atlanta para el tercer juego, programado para el martes a las 5:00 p. m., hora de Colombia.
En las Series Divisionales con el formato actual 2-2-1, los equipos que consiguen dividir victorias como visitantes antes de regresar a casa para los Juegos 3 y 4 han ganado la serie 30 de 49 veces (61%).

The Dodgers felt it was more rust than any lingering effects from the left groin discomfort that caused Snell to leave his start early on S
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers and Braves shift their National League Division Series to Atlanta, tied at one game apiece. On the off day Monday, let’s look back a little more at the disappointing Game 2 loss by Los Angeles.
Blake Snell got only 11 outs on 90 pitches, and though he only allowed one run, the Dodgers used six relievers to cover the final 5 1/3 innings on Sunday. The Dodgers felt it was more rust than any lingering effects from the left groin discomfort that caused Snell to leave his start early on September 16 in Cincinnati.
“He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game,” Roberts said. “I think, in total, didn’t have fastball command, didn’t have slider command and the changeup wasn’t there. … It wasn’t the groin. He just wasn’t sharp tonight.”
All five runs the Dodgers scored in Game 1 came on home runs — two-run shots by Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker, plus a solo shot by Mac Muncy. Then in Game 2 the Dodgers’ only two runs were on solo home runs from Freddie Freeman and Muncy. From Kevin Baxter of the Los Angeles Times:
“We’ve to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” added Freddie Freeman, who homered Sunday and has three hits in the series. “That’s our biggest thing right now. So keep getting guys on base and get that big hit.”
Freeman said the Braves have done a good job keeping the Dodger hitters off-balance by emptying their bullpen, sending in a fresh pitcher every couple of innings.
“It’s tough because you’re facing a different arm every single time you’re going up there,” Freeman said. “It’s different angles, different velocities, different things. So stringing hits together is very hard.
More from Roberts on Braves reliever Didier Fuentes, who retired 11 straight batters before Muncy homered in the ninth to pull the Dodgers within a run , from Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register:
“I think it was just the fastball,” Roberts said of Fuentes, who threw two scoreless innings against the Dodgers during the Braves’ three-game sweep in Atlanta in August. “Tonight you could see the fastball, it was 99, 100. There was a lot of balls we were just missing as far as lazy fly balls, and we just couldn’t hit the ball flat against him. Then he was mixing in his split once in a while.
“Tip my hat to him, two days off (since pitching in the Wild Card Series) and doing what he did was pretty impressive.”

item.title: [heavy.com] Dodgers’ Mookie Betts Makes Feelings Clear After Loss to Braves
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading to Atlanta with their home-field advantage gone. A 3-2 loss in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday night evened the series at one game apiece and handed the Braves exactly the split they were looking for. The Dodgers failed to deliver a single hit in eight chances with runners in scoring position over the two home games. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading to Atlanta with their home-field advantage gone. A 3-2 loss in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday night evened the series at one game apiece and handed the Braves exactly the split they were looking for.
The Dodgers failed to deliver a single hit in eight chances with runners in scoring position over the two home games. The offense that was supposed to carry them through October has yet to find a consistent rhythm.
After the loss, one of the team’s veteran leaders offered a straightforward assessment of where things stand.
Betts Sets the Tone for Atlanta
Mookie Betts did not sugarcoat the challenge but refused to frame the situation as a crisis.
“It’s just not gonna be easy,” Betts said. “But I mean we knew that from the beginning… We know it’s gonna be a tough matchup, no matter who’s on the mound.”
The comment reflected the mentality of a player who has been through deep October runs before. Betts helped the Dodgers win titles in 2024 and 2025. He knows what the grind looks like, and he knows that a tied series heading into a road game is far from a death sentence.
Still, there was no dodging what happened Sunday. The Dodgers had their best opportunity in the fifth inning with two runners on and nobody out but came away empty. Six different Braves relievers held the lineup in check for the majority of the night.
Betts’ Game 2 Showed the Problem
Betts finished 0-for-2 with a pair of walks in Game 2. He reached base, drew pitches, and did his part to set the table from the leadoff spot. The production behind him did not follow.
The Dodgers collected just four hits beyond Freddie Freeman‘s game-tying home run in the fourth. Max Muncy added a solo shot in the ninth to pull within a run, but by then the damage had been done.
Through two games, the pattern is clear. When the lineup cannot string hits together, it relies on the long ball. That approach has a ceiling, and the Dodgers hit it Sunday.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Mookie Betts #50 of the Los Angeles Dodgers throws to first base during the seventh inning against the Atlanta Braves in game one of the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
Final Word for the Dodgers
Chris Sale is waiting in Atlanta. The Braves ace held the Dodgers scoreless when the two teams met in the regular season and will have the benefit of additional rest heading into Game 3 on Tuesday.
Betts’ message was simple. This was never going to be easy. The series is tied, the road gets harder, and the Dodgers need their lineup to find a way beyond home runs.
Two games in, that is the one thing they have not figured out.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Atlanta Braves, 3-2, on Sunday as the National League Division Series evened out to one game apiece. With the best-of-five series now heading back to Atlanta, the two-time defending champions are in a much more troublesome spot than expected.
Left-hander Blake Snell was far from his best on Sunday as he struck out five across 3.2 innings of work (90 pitches) with an earned run and five walks. Snell, Kris Bubic and Edgardo Henriquez all allowed an earned run while the four remaining relievers were hitless in their respective outings.
Offensively, Freddie Freeman tied things up in the fourth inning with a solo home run, just his second since the All-Star break. When the Dodgers were down to their final out, Max Muncy slugged a solo home run — but it was too little too late for LA.
The Dodgers also officially announced that the starter for Game 3 of the NLDS will be the ace: Right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. The reigning World Series MVP had a 2.16 ERA in his last five regular season starts and will now make his 2026 postseason debut.
Yamamoto will face off against southpaw Chris Sale for the Braves, who is working with a 2.16 ERA across 27 starts this season. So far in the postseason, Sale struck out nine across 6.1 innings in Atlanta's first wild-card game, and on one day of rest, closed out Game 3 of the wild-card round with three strikeouts across the game's final four outs.
Finally, manager Dave Roberts made a bold prediction regarding right fielder Kyle Tucker following his abysmal regular season to kick off the Dodgers chapter of his career. Tucker was hitting just .228 with 11 home runs going into September before he appeared to start to turn things around
“It’s been fun to watch Kyle build some confidence," Roberts said before the NLDS. "You can see him just freed up a little bit. He’s been working hard this whole year, and he’s been in it. And I give him a lot of credit for continuing to persevere and [I] expect the best of him to be at the end of the season.”

item.title: [TSN] Dodgers' Ohtani admits he won't be fully healthy in playoffs
item.dc:creator: Alden Gonzalez
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Dodgers’ two-way star Shohei Ohtani called the past few days “very productive” and believes his swing is “in a better place” heading into a National League Division Series showdown against the Braves that begins Saturday. But Ohtani won’t be fully healthy then and perhaps at any point this postseason. The left knee and right biceps ailments that compromised him throughout the summer will linger into the fall, Ohtani and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts indicated Friday. “As of now, it
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Dodgers’ two-way star Shohei Ohtani called the past few days “very productive” and believes his swing is “in a better place” heading into a National League Division Series showdown against the Braves that begins Saturday.
But Ohtani won’t be fully healthy then and perhaps at any point this postseason. The left knee and right biceps ailments that compromised him throughout the summer will linger into the fall, Ohtani and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts indicated Friday.
“As of now, it’s something I’m just going to have to manage,” Ohtani said through an interpreter.
Knee and biceps injuries finally sent Ohtani to the injured list in early September after a 14-game stretch during which he compiled seven hits and 22 strikeouts. Ohtani returned with five regular-season games left and was inconsistent, putting together an encouraging stretch against the San Diego Padres and an overwhelming one against the San Francisco Giants.
Ohtani took batting practice on the field during workouts Tuesday and Wednesday, a rarity for him, and Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates said those sessions were “as good as we’ve seen it this year as far as the way the ball was coming off and the way he was getting his move off.”
Bates provided some proof of that.
“He did hit a couple balls up off the scoreboard,” he said.
Ohtani also had three plate appearances against Yoshinobu Yamamoto in a prolonged simulated game Wednesday, worked out inside Thursday and came onto the field for three rounds of outdoor batting practice around 6 p.m. PT Friday. Moments later, he had two at-bats against right-hander Emmet Sheehan, striking out before hitting a line drive to right field.
“Shohei’s not 100%, but he’s going to be in the lineup,” Roberts said, adding that veteran first baseman Freddie Freeman also isn’t fully healthy, among others. “I think that most players that are performing now are not 100%. Obviously with Shohei, it’s a bigger deal because of the player, but there’s a lot of players that are not 100%, and they’ve just got to manage it.”
Despite being compromised for much of the past three months, Ohtani finished the year batting .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs and 11 stolen bases and is likely to finish second to Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong in NL MVP voting. Ohtani also went 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA in 14 starts, but he didn’t pitch after July 3 and had essentially been ruled out of pitching by Labor Day. Ohtani went on the IL thereafter.
“During the IL, I pretty much knew I wasn’t going to pitch the rest of the season,” Ohtani said. “So I did focus on just the hitting aspect of the game and coming to understanding and wanting to execute and try new things when I came back. So those were the things that I really took the IL time to think through what I wanted to try when I was back in action.”
Ohtani had several hard-hit balls upon returning from the injured list, notably an opposite-field double off a 103 mph fastball from star Padres closer Mason Miller. But Ohtani ultimately went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts in his last five regular-season games, and by the end, Roberts noticed him being overanxious, trying too hard to get acclimated to major league pitching with limited time.
The 32-year-old Ohtani said he still has to make “little tweaks here and there” with his swing before feeling ready for Game 1.
He downplayed having limited playing time before then.
“Whether I have a lot of at-bats or not, I can figure out how I feel, especially in my setup,” Ohtani said. “So that’s something I was able to kind of see. But I do want to get into the postseason, feel the atmosphere and again kind of recalibrate what I have to.”

item.title: [MLB.com] Forever connected by Braves, Olson and Freeman welcome first postseason faceoff
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. It was an awkward and initially painful separation for the man who had been the Braves’ everyday first baseman from 2011-2021. Needless to say, the pain has faded as Freeman has spent the past five years establishing himself as a legend in another organization. He’ll always cherish his days with the Braves. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. It was an awkward and initially painful separation for the man who had been the Braves’ everyday first baseman from 2011-2021.
Needless to say, the pain has faded as Freeman has spent the past five years establishing himself as a legend in another organization. He’ll always cherish his days with the Braves. But over this next week, they will stand as the enemy.
Freeman’s Dodgers will face the Braves in the National League Division Series that begins on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The 2020 NL MVP has played 29 games against Atlanta over the past five seasons. But this marks the first time he will face his original organization in the postseason.
“I understand it will be a storyline,” Freeman said. “I get it. But it is five years later. I'm not going to try and look at it any differently. It's another team that I'm trying to get through to win another championship.”
The NLDS will create another opportunity to highlight the link that will forever exist between Freeman and Olson, the two players who have combined to provide the Braves excellence at first base over the past two decades.
Freeman certainly didn’t like seeing his job given to somebody else. As for Olson, it wasn’t easy for him to come to Atlanta to replace a franchise icon. But never once has there been any sort of animosity or awkwardness between the two first basemen.
In fact, the two have attended events together, including a Morgan Wallen concert at Truist Park last year. There is a genuine mutual respect.
“Matt is a great guy and an unbelievable baseball player,” Freeman said. “He's one of the best power hitters in our game right now. So it's fun. And he's from [Atlanta]. That massive home run he hit yesterday was just cool.”
Olson’s 416-foot home run in the seventh inning of Thursday’s night’s 6-2 win over the Phillies reminded the baseball world of his great power. Atlanta’s first baseman ranks fifth among all MLB players with 329 homers since the start of 2018, his first full big league season.
With the 41 homers hit this season, Olson joined Hank Aaron (eight times), Eddie Mathews (four times) and Ronald Acuña Jr. (twice) as the only players to tally multiple 40-homer seasons for the Braves.
“Matt had a lot on his plate when he first got here,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “He was replacing an icon. I think we got the only guy that could do it, the only guy that could step in in that role at that time. Matt's been a superstar for us.”
The Braves’ final written offer to Freeman was a five-year, $135 million deal ($27 million average annual value). The 10-time All-Star was 32 at the time.
The Braves knew Freeman might have a few more MVP-caliber seasons in him. But they also were confident Olson would provide similar production through those first few years and then continue to provide elite production while Freeman moved north of 35.
Of course, Freeman holds the edge in batting average (.306 to .259), OPS (.885 to .852) and most importantly World Series titles (2 to 0) over these past five seasons. He highlighted this run by becoming the only player in MLB history to hit a walk-off homer in a World Series game multiple times.
Olson is still bidding for that big postseason moment. But more importantly, he’s vying to lead the Braves to a World Series title, just like Freeman did in 2021.
“I’d say he’s our captain,” Braves catcher Sean Murphy said. “He goes out there every single day and hit 40 home runs. I’d say we’re happy to have Matt Olson on our team."

item.title: [Yardbarker] Dodgers Make Freddie Freeman Decision With Braves Looming

The seat sits in Section 306, Row K, Seat 5. “To commemorate Freddie’s walk-off home run in Game 1 of the 202
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers marked a lasting piece of franchise history Friday by painting one seat in the right-field pavilion blue, a tribute to Freddie Freeman timed for the start of their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
The club announced the change on social media, identifying the exact location where Freeman’s drive landed in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. The seat sits in Section 306, Row K, Seat 5.
“To commemorate Freddie’s walk-off home run in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series, we painted the seat blue where the ball landed in the Right Field Pavillion in Section 306, Row K, Seat 5,” the Dodgers wrote.
That blast came on Oct. 25, 2024, against the New York Yankees. Freeman, playing through a badly sprained right ankle, swung at the first pitch he saw from Nestor Cortes with two outs and the bases loaded in the 10th inning. The grand slam gave Los Angeles a 6-3 victory and became the first game-ending grand slam in World Series history.
A sellout crowd of 52,394 watched the ball clear the wall and settle in the pavilion seats. Freeman raised his bat before circling the bases as teammates waited at home plate.
The timing of the painted seat is deliberate. Los Angeles opens the best-of-five series at home Saturday at 1 p.m. local time against Freeman’s former club. The Dodgers earned a first-round bye after finishing the regular season with 100 wins. Atlanta advanced by eliminating the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round.
Freeman spent the first 12 seasons of his career with the Braves after the club selected him in the second round of the 2007 draft out of high school. He helped Atlanta win the 2021 World Series over the Houston Astros before signing with the Dodgers.
He has since added two more championships. Los Angeles captured the title in 2024 and repeated in 2025, giving the 37-year-old first baseman three rings. He was named World Series MVP in 2024 after homering in six consecutive Fall Classic games, a stretch that began during his final postseason with Atlanta.
In the 2026 regular season, Freeman appeared in 153 games and hit .288 with 167 hits, 32 doubles, 16 home runs and 70 RBIs. He scored 74 runs, drew 66 walks and stole seven bases while posting a .362 on-base percentage and .430 slugging percentage across 579 at-bats.
Those numbers arrived while he managed right-knee tendinitis late in the year. The Dodgers rested him selectively in September but kept him off the injured list. He returned to the lineup and finished the season as an everyday presence at first base.
The painted seat joins other recognitions of the 2024 home run, including a bobblehead giveaway the following spring. Club officials described the blue seat as a permanent marker inside Dodger Stadium.
Freeman wears No. 5, the same digit that appears on the commemorated seat. He enters the series as one of the few active players with championships on both sides of a longstanding National League rivalry.
Los Angeles is chasing a third consecutive World Series title, something no club has done since the New York Yankees from 1998 through 2000. Atlanta arrives with recent October experience against its former star and a lineup that has tested the Dodgers in prior postseason meetings.
Game 1 is scheduled for Saturday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, with the series shifting to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4 if necessary. The blue seat in Section 306 will be visible from the field when Freeman takes his first at-bat of the series.
