item.title: [The Sporting Tribune] Tarik Skubal named Game 1 starter as Shohei Ohtani provides health update
item.dc:creator: Fredo Cervantes
item.description: LOS ANGELES — With less than 24 hours before the first pitch of Game 1 of the NLDS, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made his decision: Tarik Skubal will take the ball Saturday afternoon against the Braves. The choice came from a rotation that gives the Dodgers perhaps as much depth as any team could ask for. Skubal earned the assignment over reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, fellow two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow. “With the four guys, i
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With less than 24 hours before the first pitch of Game 1 of the NLDS, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made his decision: Tarik Skubal will take the ball Saturday afternoon against the Braves.
The choice came from a rotation that gives the Dodgers perhaps as much depth as any team could ask for. Skubal earned the assignment over reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, fellow two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow.
“With the four guys, it doesn't really matter who, but I think that we feel good about Tarik taking the baseball tomorrow afternoon,” Roberts said.
As it turns out, Skubal knew his assignment before the regular season was even over.
When Roberts pulled him after just 75 pitches in his final start in San Francisco, Skubal initially wondered why. He approached his manager, expecting there might be another reason for the early exit.
Instead, Roberts gave him a message that changed the rest of his week.
“He came and shook my hand. I was at kind of a low pitch count, I thought in the moment I was going to be able to finish the game. And he was like, ‘Get ready for Game 1,’” Skubal said.
Skubal said he was “obviously excited and fired up and ready to go.”
Now comes a new experience for the reigning back-to-back unanimous Cy Young winner.
For everything Skubal has accomplished, he has never had the opportunity to pitch at home in October. That changes Saturday, when he takes the mound in front of a Dodgers crowd for the opening game of the NLDS.
“I’m excited for the opportunity to throw in front of the fans,” Skubal said.
The left-hander also knows exactly what the atmosphere can feel like when he pitched for the Tigers.
“Usually when I walk out onto the field in a playoff game, it's usually received with a lot of boos,” Skubal said. “So I'm excited to get some cheers in there for us. And to pitch at home, I think it's going to be a ton of fun in front of this atmosphere.”
His approach for the biggest start of his Dodgers career?
Keep it simple.
“I have to be really good at what makes me good,” Skubal said.
The weather will provide another challenge, with triple-digit temperatures expected Saturday. Skubal, however, doesn't appear particularly concerned.
“We probably won't have to go to the bathroom. Just sweat it out,” he joked.
The extra time between starts has also been welcomed by the left-hander.
“I think for a starter, it's easiest to take time off,” Skubal said.
He also credited Dodgers fans for the reception he has received since arriving in Los Angeles and said he is looking forward to finally pitching in front of them in October.
“I’m excited to throw in front of them tomorrow.”
Ohtani Says His Swing Is Trending in the Right Direction
While Skubal prepares for his first postseason start at Dodger Stadium, Shohei Ohtani is preparing to return to October action after recently being activated from the 15-day injured list.
Ohtani said he feels really good overall and believes his swing has benefited from the extended break.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place,” Ohtani said. “Just little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow.”
The time away from games, he said, has given him an opportunity to make adjustments while managing the ailments that surfaced during the second half.
“Being on the IL has taught me a lot,” Ohtani said.
But the Dodgers' star acknowledged that his lingering biceps and knee issues remain something he will have to manage throughout the postseason.
Asked whether those injuries could require attention during the offseason, Ohtani said he has not yet identified the root cause of everything he has been dealing with.
“I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this,” Ohtani said. “I think that process is going to happen during the off-season when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it. But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage.”
That reality isn't unique to Ohtani.
Roberts said most of the players currently preparing for the postseason are dealing with some level of physical issue.
“Most players that are performing now are not at 100%,” Roberts said.
Still, Roberts expects Ohtani to perform well when the Dodgers open their series Saturday. He also expressed confidence in Freddie Freeman, whose own lingering injuries have been a storyline heading into October, particularly after seeing Freeman in Thursday's intrasquad game.
The Dodgers will enter the NLDS with a roster expected to feature 14 position players and 12 pitchers, according to Roberts. He was not yet ready to announce the starters for Games 2 and 3.
For now, the focus belongs to Skubal.
The Dodgers acquired him to pitch in moments exactly like this one. On Saturday, in front of a home crowd and with the season entering its most important stretch, he gets the opportunity to show what he can do.
And unlike his previous playoff outings in opposing ballparks, this time, the cheers will be for him.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Dodgers not talking 3-peat yet as Braves enter NLDS with confidence
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The potential road to history for the Los Angeles Dodgers begins with a reunion as the National League Division Series starts Saturday afternoon with a visit from the Atlanta Braves. Freddie Freeman has been a major postseason contributor during the Dodgers’ consecutive World Series titles, and the veteran will be in the heart of the order again in a matchup against his former team. Freeman also was invaluable in the 2021 World Series when the Braves won their most recent title. Fr
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The potential road to history for the Los Angeles Dodgers begins with a reunion as the National League Division Series starts Saturday afternoon with a visit from the Atlanta Braves.
Freddie Freeman has been a major postseason contributor during the Dodgers’ consecutive World Series titles, and the veteran will be in the heart of the order again in a matchup against his former team.
Freeman also was invaluable in the 2021 World Series when the Braves won their most recent title. Freeman joined the Dodgers as a free agent in 2022 after Atlanta moved on to Matt Olson as their first baseman.
While Freeman has won three rings in five seasons, the Dodgers are trying to become the first National League club to win championships in three consecutive years. Only two American League franchises have ever done it: the New York Yankees and Oakland Athletics.
The Yankees were the last to accomplish the feat when they won championships in 1998, 1999 and 2000.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves,” Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. “We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure on it that doesn’t need to be there. Winning a World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
After returning from a biceps injury during the final week of the regular season, Shohei Ohtani will be back atop the Los Angeles order when the club’s postseason run begins.
Left-hander Tarik Skubal was named the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter over right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Skubal arrived just before the trade deadline in a deal with the Detroit Tigers and went 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA in 10 starts for his new club.
Skubal is 0-1 with a 4.91 ERA in two career starts against Atlanta, including an outing in April when he gave up two runs over seven innings in a no-decision.
The Braves opened their postseason by getting past the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round. Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 on Thursday behind a three-run home run from Michael Harris II and a dominating day on the mound. Six pitchers kept Philadelphia in check, including staff ace Chris Sale, who recorded the final four outs.
The Braves face the Dodgers after going 5-1 against them in the regular season, including a three-game home sweep in late August.
“Everyone knows the Dodgers have a juggernaut, but we played well against them this year,” Atlanta manager Walt Weiss said. “I know that doesn’t carry a whole lot of stock. Once the playoffs begin, everybody starts at zero. The Dodgers are healthier now than they were when we saw them.”
Weiss has yet to name his Game 1 starter, with a left-handed opener a possibility to line up against early left-handed bats like Ohtani and Freeman.
The Braves will continue to be without a pair of starters in right-hander Bryce Elder (knee) and left-hander Martin Perez (back).
Like Freeman before him, Olson has emerged as a Braves leader, along with Ronald Acuna Jr. Olson hit a team-best 41 home runs in the regular season and added another in the wild-card round. Harris hit 26 home runs in the regular season and Acuna added 20 homers and 21 steals.
“I think it’s just kind of going out there and playing our game and knowing that … we can compete with them and beat them,” said Braves catcher Drake Baldwin, an All-Star and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year who contributed 25 home runs.
–Doug Padilla, Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

item.title: [clarosports.com] La gran interrogante de los Dodgers: ¿qué versión de Ohtani verán en la Serie Divisional ante Atlanta?
item.dc:creator: Julian Castillo
item.description: Ohtani busca recuperar su mejor versión ante Atlanta tras una campaña con lesiones que frenaron su impacto en los Dodgers. item.content:encoded:
Ohtani busca recuperar su mejor versión ante Atlanta tras una campaña con lesiones que frenaron su impacto en los Dodgers.
Los Angeles Dodgers ya conoce a su rival en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional. Atlanta Braves superó la ronda de comodines y visitará Dodger Stadium este sábado 3 de octubre, en una serie al mejor de cinco juegos que abrirá a la 1:00 p.m. del Pacífico. Ahora, la atención de los fanáticos angelinos apunta a Shohei Ohtani y al nivel que podrá ofrecer después de un cierre de campaña marcado por molestias físicas.
El japonés completó una temporada productiva en términos generales, con promedio de .275, OPS de .889 y 30 jonrones, la cifra más alta del roster de los Dodgers. Sin embargo, su rendimiento quedó lejos de la continuidad que mostró en otros años, sobre todo durante el tramo final del calendario. Una lesión en el bíceps derecho y problemas en la rodilla izquierda afectaron su ritmo, limitaron su trabajo como lanzador y lo llevaron a la lista de lesionados.
Ohtani volvió para los últimos cinco juegos de la campaña regular, aunque sus números dejaron dudas. Bateó de 5-21, con un extrabase, una base por bolas y ocho ponches. Ese panorama pone el foco sobre su estado físico y su capacidad para convertirse de inmediato en un bate determinante frente a Atlanta.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Dodgers inician la defensa del bicampeonato: Braves o Phillies será su primer obstáculo
¿Cómo llega Shohei Ohtani a la Serie Divisional ante Braves?
La principal incógnita no tiene que ver con el talento de Ohtani, sino con su condición física después de un año exigente. El japonés arrastró molestias desde junio, cuando la rodilla izquierda comenzó a afectar su disponibilidad. Más tarde apareció el problema en el bíceps derecho, una lesión que tuvo impacto en su ofensiva y en su preparación para abrir juegos desde la lomita.
Los Dodgers decidieron actuar con cautela. Ohtani ingresó a la lista de lesionados de 15 días en septiembre y dejó de trabajar como pitcher. Su última apertura llegó el 3 de julio ante los San Diego Padres, partido en el que lanzó seis innings, permitió tres carreras y ponchó a nueve rivales antes de salir por tensión en el bíceps derecho.
La organización ya asumió que Ohtani no lanzará durante esta postemporada. Su aporte dependerá por completo de su trabajo como bateador designado, un rol que permite concentrar su recuperación en el ajuste ofensivo y reducir el desgaste físico. El propio jugador indicó durante septiembre que su prioridad sería el bateo, mientras los Dodgers proyectan que retome su faceta de dos vías en 2027.
Ese contexto eleva la importancia de cada turno. Los Dodgers necesitan a un Ohtani capaz de impactar el juego desde el primer lugar de la alineación, sobre todo ante una serie corta donde un mal inicio puede cambiar el rumbo de la eliminatoria.
¿Qué números tuvo Ohtani contra Atlanta en 2026?
Atlanta representa un reto incómodo para el japonés. Ohtani enfrentó a los Braves en seis juegos durante la temporada regular y conectó apenas cinco hits en 26 turnos, para un promedio de .192. Esa producción contrasta con sus números globales y refleja la dificultad que tuvo el lineup de Los Ángeles frente al pitcheo rival.
El problema tampoco quedó limitado a Ohtani. Los Braves dominaron la serie particular ante los Dodgers con cinco victorias en seis enfrentamientos y una diferencia de carreras de 26-15. Atlanta llega con la confianza de haber encontrado una fórmula efectiva contra el campeón defensor, aunque los playoffs representan un escenario distinto y Dodger Stadium recibirá los dos primeros juegos.
El bajo promedio del japonés ante Atlanta no define lo que puede ocurrir en octubre, pero sí señala un punto de atención. Ohtani deberá mejorar la calidad de sus turnos, siendo más selectivo en los lanzamiento que ataca para poder hacer daño. En una ofensiva con figuras como Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts y Will Smith, su presencia en circulación puede abrir oportunidades para el resto del orden.
Los Dodgers tampoco requieren que cargue solo con el ataque. Su tarea inmediata pasa por recuperar consistencia, seleccionar mejor los pitcheos y ofrecer una amenaza constante en cada aparición al plato.
¿Cuándo juegan Dodgers vs. Atlanta Braves en la Serie Divisional?
Los Angeles Dodgers abrirá la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional ante los Atlanta Braves este sábado 3 de octubre en Dodger Stadium. El Juego 1 comenzará a las 4:00 p.m., hora del Este, con los angelinos como locales tras asegurar la ventaja de localía.
- Juego 2: domingo 4 de octubre, Braves vs. Dodgers, 8:00 p.m. hora del Este, Dodger Stadium
- Juego 3: martes 6 de octubre, Dodgers vs. Braves, 6:00 p.m. hora del Este, Truist Park
- Juego 4: miércoles 7 de octubre, Dodgers vs. Braves, 6:00 p.m. hora del Este, Truist Park, si es necesario
- Juego 5: viernes 9 de octubre, Braves vs. Dodgers, 8:00 p.m. hora del Este, Dodger Stadium, si es necesario
¿El descanso puede ayudar a Ohtani con Dodgers?
La mejor noticia para Los Ángeles llegó con el calendario. El equipo aseguró el primer sembrado de la Liga Nacional y obtuvo cinco días de descanso antes del inicio de la Serie Divisional. Ese margen le permitió a Ohtani descansar después de volver de la lista de lesionados y trabajar en su swing sin la presión diaria de la temporada regular.
Dave Roberts espera una versión más saludable de su estrella para el sábado. La pausa no elimina por completo las dudas sobre el bíceps y la rodilla, aunque sí ofrece una ventana útil para que el japonés llegue con mayor frescura. El club también tiene margen para administrar su carga física durante una serie que contempla días de descanso entre los primeros compromisos.
La serie comienza el sábado en Los Ángeles con un duelo que marcará el tono de la eliminatoria. Ohtani no tendrá responsabilidad desde el montículo, pero su presencia en el primer turno de la alineación será una de las claves ofensivas del equipo. El descanso abre una oportunidad para que el japonés deje atrás un cierre irregular y responda en el momento que más importa para los Dodgers.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers se lo toman con calma: van por el histórico “three-peat” en la MLB
Los Ángeles busca convertirse en el primer equipo desde los Yankees de 1998-2000 en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas.
PUBLICIDAD
Los Ángeles. Freddie Freeman y Emmet Sheehan bostezaron. El mánager Dave Roberts usó pantalones cortos para la práctica de bateo.
Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles se lo toman con calma mientras se encaminan a una postemporada potencialmente histórica.
Intentan convertirse en el primer equipo desde los Yankees de Nueva York de 1998-2000 en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas. Serían el primer club de la Liga Nacional en lograrlo.
Y dejarían las expectativas altísimas para todos los demás.
“No es algo en lo que realmente estemos enfocados. Cuando hablas de ganar tres seguidas, le estás poniendo esa presión extra que no tiene por qué estar ahí“, comentó el antesalista Max Muncy. ”Ganar una Serie Mundial ya es lo suficientemente difícil”.
Los Dodgers disputaron un juego simulado el jueves, mientras se proyectaba el duelo decisivo de la serie de comodines de la Liga Nacional entre Filadelfia y Atlanta en las pantallas de video del estadio. Los Bravos vencieron a los Filis por 6-2 y jugarán en Los Ángeles el primer duelo de la serie divisional de la Liga Nacional, al mejor en un máximo de cinco encuentros, el sábado, cuando se pronostica que la temperatura alcance los 100 grados Fahrenheit (38 Celsius) para el juego diurno.
“Te enfrentas a un equipo que ya pasó por el fuego y ya vivió la emoción”, comentó Muncy.
Los Dodgers han pasado la semana de descanso recuperándose, mientras alternaban práctica de bateo en vivo y en la jaula con juegos simulados en un estadio mayormente silencioso. Aparte de las canciones de entrada al plato, los únicos sonidos eran el chasquido del bate, los gritos de los jugadores desde las bancas y los jardineros avisando a sus compañeros que ellos se encargarían de un elevado.
Freeman aprovechó el tiempo para concentrarse en ajustar la mecánica de su swing mientras lidiaba una molestia en la rodilla derecha. El plan del primera base de 37 años incluía hacer 400 swings “con la esperanza de quitarme los malos hábitos”, explicó.
En el inicio del juego simulado del jueves, conectó un doble ante Tyler Glasnow.
“De verdad me siento bien físicamente ahora mismo y depende de mí resolver la mecánica del swing”, comentó. ”No tengo dolor en la rodilla en este momento”.
Shohei Ohtani, cuatro veces nombrado el Jugador Más Valioso, ha lidiado durante semanas con molestias persistentes en el bíceps derecho y la rodilla izquierda. La rodilla lo frenó para lanzar y el brazo lo llevó recientemente a la lista de lesionados por primera vez con los Dodgers.
Regresó a tiempo para jugar en cinco partidos al final de la temporada.
Aún está por verse qué versión de Ohtani tendrán los Dodgers en la serie divisional de la Liga Nacional. Sin embargo, Roberts dijo que “se siente muy bien físicamente. Sus swings, en general, están en un gran punto”.
La alineación de jugadores de posición de los Dodgers es la de mayor edad en las Grandes Ligas, encabezada por el infielder venezolano Miguel Rojas, de 37 años, Freeman y Muncy, de 35. Ohtani tiene 32. El relevista Blake Treinen tiene 38, pero se perderá la postemporada tras lesionarse el fin de semana pasado.
“Creo que la experiencia va a ser enorme. Sabemos lo que se necesita”, aseveró Freeman
Al mismo tiempo, advirtió que los Dodgers no deben adelantarse.
“Si en este momento piensas en el panorama general, vas a perder de vista las cosas”.

item.title: [heavy.com] Mookie Betts Puts Los Angeles Dodgers-Red Sox Debate to Rest with Heartfelt Admission
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts is entering the back half of his career, and while he isn’t at the MVP level that he once was from 2017-2022, Betts is still an extremely productive and successful player. He has won three World Series titles with the Dodgers since joining the team in 2020, and he has four overall championship rings. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts is entering the back half of his career, and while he isn’t at the MVP level that he once was from 2017-2022, Betts is still an extremely productive and successful player.
He has won three World Series titles with the Dodgers since joining the team in 2020, and he has four overall championship rings.
There has always been an ongoing debate on which team Mookie Betts favors between the Boston Red Sox and the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Betts came up with the Red Sox, and played six seasons in Boston, but 2026 marked Betts’ 7th season with the Dodgers, and he’s officially ready to call the Dodgers ‘his team’.
More MLB on Heavy: Freddie Freeman Makes Honest Admission About Los Angeles Dodgers World Series Aspirations
Mookie Betts Makes Heartfelt Admission to Put Red Sox-Dodgers Debate to Rest
Mookie Betts recently talked with The Athletic about which team he will state was ‘the one he played for’ when it’s all said and done:
“When I’m done playing, I’ll remember Boston, of course, But what I’ll really remember is if somebody said, ‘Oh, you played baseball, like who did you play with?’ These are the guys I’m going to say I played with,”
Betts also made a quick note about the fact that he believes he’s in the tail end of his career, which makes sense because he is 33 years old now with a growing family.
A couple of seasons ago, Mookie Betts added to his versatility as a baseball player by transitioning from right field to shortstop, which he has excelled at (all things considered).
There are still seven seasons left on Betts’ massive contract, which will expire when he’s 40, and he’s noted he plans to retire once that runs out.
More MLB on Heavy: Why Los Angeles Dodgers Fans Need to Watch Phillies-Braves Game on Thursday
Quickly Looking at Mookie Betts’ Career
Mookie Betts is an 8X MLB All-Star, AL MVP (2019), 4X World Series champion, 7X Silver Slugger winner, and 6X Gold Glover.
He’s almost certainly headed to the MLB Hall of Fame.
Betts has 314 career home runs, 982 RBI, 1237 runs scored, and a lifetime batting average of .288 over 1654 total games played.
In 2026, Mookie Betts batted .257 with 23 home runs, 25 doubles, and an OPS+ of 113.
Overall, it was a solid 2026 campaign for Betts after a very slow start at the plate.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are still awaiting their National League Division Series opponent.
They will find out on Thursday evening after the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies conclude their Wild Card series.
Regardless of the opponent, the Dodgers are poised and ready for their three-peat quest.
That includes star infielder Freddie Freeman, who did not hold back about the team's World Series aspirations.
More MLB on Heavy: Why Los Angeles Dodgers Fans Need to Watch Phillies-Braves Game on Thursday
Freddie Freeman's Latest Comments on Championship Window
Per The Athletic's Katie Woo, Freddie Freeman had this to say about LA's proverbial 'championship window':
"This window, we are going to try and keep open as long as we possibly can, but sports are sports; you never know when those windows will close."
Freeman also noted:
"I don't have that many years left of playing, so you take a step back and realize how special it is to come to the field every day for the chance to win a championship every year," Freeman said. "You look around, you've been with certain guys for those multiple titles, and you do realize that."
The Dodgers have won each of the last two World Series, and there hasn't been a team to three-peat as Champs since the turn of the century.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Mets Have 9 Free Agency Roster Decisions to Make This Offseason
Freddie Freeman Had Another Quality Offensive Season
Now that the regular season is in the books, we can take a look at how Freddie Freeman performed for the entire campaign, and to no surprise, he had another very solid offensive season.
Across 153 games played this season, Freeman batted .288 with an OPS+ of 118, 16 home runs, 32 doubles, and 167 hits.
He battled a few lingering injuries throughout the regular season, so the Dodgers hope that his health is not a factor in the upcoming NLDS against either the Braves or Phillies.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are getting a much-needed breather this week as they wait to see which team they will face in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday with Game 1 at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers will have their answer by the end of Thursday night as the Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves meet at Truist Park — the only Wild Card Series that reached a decisive Game 3.
In the meantime, the Dodgers are using the time off to rest and prepare for their next opponent. The team has been going through workouts and simulated games at Dodger Stadium to stay sharp for when they resume play later this weekend.
As part of their on-field workouts, several Dodgers players got some swings in during batting practice. In a video shared by the team on X, the group of players who participated includes Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, among others.
Locked in for October. pic.twitter.com/RT5twoW3ED
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 30, 2026
Ohtani taking swings during the bye week is an encouraging sign after he recently returned to the Dodgers following a stint on the 15-day injured list. He typically does not hit on the field, but has done it a few times throughout his tenure with the club, usually following a slump he’s trying to break out of.
For Freeman, the extra work could be pivotal in helping him get his swing back on track.
“Today is going to be a big day to see how BP goes,” Freeman said earlier this week. “Like I kind of told you guys a couple days ago, I feel like BP’s not going to go well today, just because of how my swing is right now. And then I’ll be able to start working on if I am blocking balls to left field in BP, then I can make those adjustments coming down.
“It’s hard to explain what’s going on in this head a lot of times, but it’s going to be big because I’m going to hit BP every single day on the field. I think that will help seeing balls velocity-wise, to be able to start moving it lower and lower and down toward the shortstop, and hopefully that will get my body in line with how I want it to work going into Saturday.”
The Dodgers had to manage Freeman down the stretch as he dealt with a right knee injury that affected both his offense and defense. He was kept out of the lineup for multiple games, but the Dodgers declined to place him on the injured list.
The time off did help Freeman improve, but the results didn’t follow. He closed out the season by batting just .226/.300/.278 over his final 30 games, and he hit just one home run in the final two months of the year.
The Dodgers are hopeful that the brief layoff will help Freeman reset mechanically and rediscover his rhythm at the plate just in time for the postseason.
Freddie Freeman incorporating 2024 World Series approach
Freeman has been exploring unorthodox ways to get back on track and recalled a key adjustment he made that led to his historic showing in the 2024 World Series.
“Just doing different work. I’m trying to find something that gets me results. We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here,” Freeman noted earlier this month.
“Kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. (But) I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable. I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers Injury Updates Before NLDS: Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Edgardo Henriquez

item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Dodgers prepare to embark on another October with sky-high expectations, there are a few stars who did not end the regular season at 100% health.
Superstars Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, and flame-throwing relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez, have perhaps the biggest question marks surrounding them heading into the National League Division Series.
Here's the latest updates on all three players.
Shohei Ohtani Injury Update
Ohtani has dealt with nagging knee and biceps injuries for the majority of the season. His knee eventually shut him down from pitching ahead of the All-Star break, and his biceps injury resulted in the minimum stay on the 15-day IL, returning for a lackluster (5-for-21) final five regular season games.
General manager Brandon Gomes spoke on a Tuesday Zoom call with the media and had an update on the four-time MVP, and how his swing has been looking amid a much-needed break while the wild-card round finishes up.
“Everything is feeling great physically," Gomes said of Ohtani. "The swings, once he came back, overall were in a good place. And using these five days to continue to get reps and feeling good into this series is really important. But feels like he's in a great spot."
Manager Dave Roberts appeared to feel the same about Ohtani, and even went as far as saying that the man who hit just .245 during the second half of the season will still have a stellar postseason.
"I feel confident that you're going to see the best version of Shohei of the last two months," Roberts said. "I know that's sort of a low bar given his injury, but I do think that he's as healthy as he's been in quite some time. And every day from the training staff, it keeps getting better. So yeah, No. 1, he'll be a threat being in the lineup, but I do think that the performance piece will be what we're hoping for."
Freddie Freeman Injury Update
Freeman is no stranger to playing through injury, and has recently been dealing with right knee tendinitis that manifested itself in the form of a .184 batting average in the final 20 games he played of 2026.
"My body feels good,” Freeman said Tuesday. “I think that’s the main thing. I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple months.”
Freeman was asked to compare his current pain level to past postseasons. Fans remember his heroics in the 2024 World Series —where he would later take home MVP honors — thriving through the Fall Classic despite a sprained ankle and broken rib cartilage.
“A couple of Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse, ailment-wise,” Freeman said. “I truly feel good right now, physically. So it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days, and I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Edgardo Henriquez Injury Update
Henriquez put up a 2.85 ERA across 60 innings of work this season, averaging a 100.8 mph fastball (in the 100th percentile among active pitchers), until lower back discomfort landed him on the injured list last month. He was activated off the IL this week.
“He’s trending really well at this point,” Gomes said. “His last live BP went well. He’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort. We’ve still got a few steps to go. But if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Roberts also made sure to acknowledge how pivotal the off-week was for his fireballer. Due to an excellent track record (a career 2.73 ERA in 86 regular season appearances), he could prove to be a crucial piece this October.
“I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited,” Roberts said. “He’ll throw another live or sim game to some hitters. ... Then he should be ready to go. And given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set could be huge for us, will be huge for us.”

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Notes: Glasnow's Role, Freeman's Knee & More
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA—The start of the 2026 National League Division Series is just two days away, and the Dodgers have spent the last couple of days getting their final work in before October officially begins. With Los Angeles enjoying the first-round bye, the extra time has allowed the team to rest, prepare, and get healthy while also giving us plenty to talk about from workouts. From Tyler Glasnow’s potential role and Freddie Freeman’s knee to the Dodgers patiently waiting to find out who they’ll
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—The start of the 2026 National League Division Series is just two days away, and the Dodgers have spent the last couple of days getting their final work in before October officially begins.
With Los Angeles enjoying the first-round bye, the extra time has allowed the team to rest, prepare, and get healthy while also giving us plenty to talk about from workouts. From Tyler Glasnow’s potential role and Freddie Freeman’s knee to the Dodgers patiently waiting to find out who they’ll face in the NLDS, several interesting developments have emerged around camp.
So, with the weekend quickly approaching, here’s the latest from Dodgers camp as Los Angeles gets ready to begin its three-peat chase.
Tyler Glasnow Unlikely to Repeat His Bullpen Role From Last October for NLDS
While the Dodgers await the outcome of today’s final Wild Card game between the Phillies and Braves, they have begun laying the groundwork for their pitching staff ahead of Saturday’s NLDS opener.
While Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not confirm the team’s starting rotation order for the series, he did allude to the fact that right-hander Tyler Glasnow likely won’t be used in relief, as he was during last NLDS against the Phillies.
A big reason is the scheduling of this year’s series compared to last season, with Games One and Two on back-to-back days rather than an odd day off between them.
“He’s one of four (starting pitchers),” Roberts began. “I think it’s a little different with the layout of the games in the DS, not playing in the Wild Card also. Could he factor in one of the first three games? Possibly.
“I would say most likely Game Four. I don’t see him out of the bullpen early. We’re going to talk through that in the next couple of days here.”
That makes a repeat of last year’s strategy unlikely. The Dodgers could still turn to Glasnow out of the bullpen later in the postseason if the situation calls for it, particularly in an elimination game, but for now, it appears his focus will remain on starting.
Still, Glasnow was elite in that role last season, tossing 1.2 scoreless innings between Games One and Two at Citizena Bank Park and proceeded to toss six more shutout innings in the Dodgers’ extra-inning walk-off victory in Game Four.
Freeman Says His Knee Is Feeling Good as He Looks to Reset Before the NLDS
Having the first-round bye for the Dodgers was seen as essential by many members of the organization and the media. Still, none preached for it more than Dodgers veteran first baseman Freddie Freeman, and that makes sense given his late-season struggles and apparent knee injury.
Freddie Freeman’s knee appears to be in a much better spot heading into the Dodgers’ NLDS matchup, giving him five full days during the postseason bye to focus on getting his swing back on track.
Freeman was held out of the lineup for multiple games late in the regular season, but the Dodgers never placed him on the injured list. While the extra rest helped his knee, his offensive struggles continued, as he hit just .226/.300/.278 over his final 30 games and .184 with a .513 OPS in September.
Still, Freeman isn’t using the knee as an excuse.
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing,” Freeman said Tuesday. “I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing.”
Freeman acknowledged the knee may have contributed to some bad habits at the plate, but ultimately blamed himself.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well,” Freeman said. “I just didn’t play well the last couple of months of the season.”
Now, Freeman sees the five-day break as a valuable opportunity to reset without the pressure of immediately taking his work into a game.
“My knee’s in a good spot now, that’s why the bye week is huge,” Freeman said. “Personally, it’s huge for me that I’ve got five days to really work on the mechanics of my swing.”
With live at-bats against Dodgers pitchers planned during the break, Freeman will have plenty of time to iron out those mechanical issues before the NLDS begins Saturday.
Dodgers Keeping Three-Peat Talk in the Background, Focused on One Game at a Time
All that talk around Major League Baseball and throughout Los Angeles will be whether the back-to-back champion Dodgers can become the first National League team to three-peat.
And while that will be a major storyline following the Dodgers this October for every series they’re in, that is not the focus of the players and coaches in the clubhouse.
The three-peat has been on the Dodgers’ minds since last year’s World Series parade, but with the NLDS just days away, the players aren’t interested in adding that pressure to an already difficult task.
Max Muncy acknowledged the goal is there, but said the Dodgers are focused on preparing for their next series rather than thinking about the bigger picture.
“I mean, obviously it’s there, but it’s not something that we’re really focused on,” Muncy said. “We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure that doesn’t need to be there. Winning the World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
Freddie Freeman has a similar mindset, making it clear his attention is on the NLDS and nothing beyond it.
“Personally, I’m not thinking about three-peat,” Freeman said. “I’m thinking about the NLDS and whoever we play, and getting ready for that. I think if you think big picture in this moment, you’re going to lose sight of some things.”
Dave Roberts echoed his players, saying the Dodgers understand what’s at stake without needing to discuss it constantly.
“Our guys understand what’s at stake,” Roberts said. “I think for me, it’s balancing the importance, the opportunity that we have. Versus trying to add more pressure than there already is.”
The Dodgers know they have a chance to make history, but for now, the message throughout the clubhouse is simple: focus on the next series, not the three-peat.
Dodgers’ NLDS Opponent Still Up in the Air After Phillies-Braves Split
Later today, the Dodgers will finally know who they’ll face in the best-of-five NLDS that kicks off Saturday at Dodger Stadium, whether it’s the Phillies or Braves.
The Phillies rallied for a 4-3, 10-inning win over the Braves, tying the Wild Card Series and forcing a winner-take-all Game Three Thursday. That means the Dodgers’ eventual NLDS opponent will have to play three games in three days just to reach Los Angeles.
That’s a significant advantage for the Dodgers.
While Philadelphia and Atlanta are burning through their pitching staffs, Los Angeles is resting, preparing, and lining up its rotation. Whoever survives Thursday will arrive in Los Angeles having already played three high-pressure postseason games while the Dodgers have been sitting at home.
Philadelphia, in particular, had to dig deep Wednesday. Cristopher Sánchez threw 116 pitches over 6⅔ innings, while Andrew Painter recorded the final nine outs. If the Phillies advance, Zack Wheeler would presumably start Game Three, potentially affecting his availability for the NLDS opener.
That could be especially important considering Wheeler, Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo give Philadelphia one of the more formidable rotations in the postseason.
But Atlanta won’t escape unscathed either. Chris Sale already threw six innings in Game One, while Tyler Mahle delivered seven strong innings Wednesday. Both teams have used key starters and relievers, with one more game to go.
The Dodgers don’t have to win a Wild Card game. They don’t even have to play one. Their opponent does.
So while Los Angeles waits to find out whether it will be Philadelphia or Atlanta, it’s also watching its eventual opponent spend three games, three days, and a whole lot of pitching just to earn the right to come to Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers’ NLDS opponent remains up in the air. The advantage of making that team play all three games, however, is already locked in.

item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Dodgers await the outcome of the final game between the Philadelphia Philles and Atlanta Braves to see who they will face in the NLDS, the team is busy working on keeping their bats and arms fresh and ready for the road to a three-peat that lies ahead.
As Bill Plunkett of the OC Register notes, the last two championship wins were won mainly on the backs of the pitchers – the bullpen in 2024, and key starters in 2025. Could this finally be the year that the Dodgers win it by having their offense outslug the other teams?
"It would be nice to slug our way to a World Series one of these years," third baseman Max Muncy joked on the eve of another postseason run. "We can't keep letting the pitchers take all the credit, right?"
The offense has looked better in the month of September, and they hope to continue that and have those that weren't hitting join those that are. Plunkett has more thoughts from the players on how they're looking to perform in the playoffs here.
As Bill Shakin of the L.A. Times notes, the last two World Series runs have had signature moments from Freddie Freeman, and ponders if this playoff run will have the same.
"My body feels good," Freeman said. "I think that's the main thing. I feel like it's in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that's been going on the last couple months."
Shakin goes on to cover Freeman's lackluster second half, and has more quotes from the man himself here.
As the team moves into its newest playoff era, one player is contemplating the end of his own. Miguel Rojas announced at the beginning of the season that he would be retiring at the end of this season. Now, he's not quite so sure. Maddie Chen of the L.A.Times talks about how Rojas is facing the possible end of his career.
"From this moment on, it will be kind of like a day-to-day thing," he said. "And you might get to know that I'm stepping away from the game in an Instagram post, or from me just saying goodbye on a video. I don't know. I don't know how it's going to be, but at this moment, I'm not 100% [certain]."

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Freddie Freeman Using Bye Week to Retool His Swing for October
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman knows exactly how he wants to spend the Dodgers’ five-day break before the National League Division Series.
It’s all about his swing, and getting it right for the playoffs.
Freeman spoke at length Tuesday about his late-season struggles, the work he plans to put in during the bye and why he feels confident he can get his swing where it needs to be by Saturday. He also talked about the Dodgers’ October experience, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and the example set by his father after the death of Freeman’s mother when he was a child.
Five Days to Work on the Swing
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing. I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple months.
“I have a plan I’m going in with, and hopefully that will take care of itself throughout the course of the week where I’ll be in a good spot by Saturday.”
Freeman dealt with knee trouble during the second half, but he put the responsibility for his drop in production on himself.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well. I just didn’t play well the last couple months of the season. That’s what I’m going to go with.
“Did I have some ailments with my knees? Yes, I did. I don’t know how much that attributed to it subconsciously, trying to do stuff where it didn’t hurt as much. There were times during the course of the last couple months where there would be a three- or four-day span where the knee was a problem and I couldn’t get into the front side, so maybe I created bad habits.
“But I won’t blame it on that. I just played bad.
“My knee’s in a good spot now. That’s why the bye week is huge for me personally. I’ve got five days to really work on the mechanics of my swing, and my knee’s in a good spot where I feel like I will be able to do that.”
Freeman planned to hit on the field every day, using batting practice to work through the changes before seeing live pitching later in the week.
“Today is going to be a big day to see how BP goes. I feel like BP’s probably not going to go well today just because of how my swing is right now, and then I’ll be able to start working on it.
“If I am blocking balls to left field in BP, then I can make those adjustments. There’s a lot going on in this head a lot of times, but it’s going to be big because I’m going to hit BP every single day on the field.
“I think that will help, seeing balls velocity-wise, to be able to start moving it lower and lower and down toward the shortstop. Hopefully that will get my body in line with how I want it to work going into Saturday.”
Back to Something That Worked in 2024
The physical picture is far better than it was during another recent October.
“A couple Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse ailment-wise. I truly feel good right now physically, so it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days.
“I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Freeman said he currently has no pain in the knee and expects rest after the season to be enough heading into next spring.
For now, he is going back to a swing thought that worked during the Dodgers’ 2024 championship run.
“It’s all evolved. Today I am going to kind of get more into my legs, and I’m going to try what I used in the World Series in ’24, kind of the step-out thought, so I’m not bending over and cutting off my swing.
“That’s the thought going into today. I’m very confident that’s going to help get things back in line throughout the course of the week.”
The bye also gives Freeman something he rarely gets during the season: time to work on a change without having to test it in a game a few hours later.
“I think the rest kind of takes care of itself mentally. I think that’s more of the mental rest.
“Physically, we’ll go out there and practice today, then we’ll play in some sim games the next two days and practice again. It’s baseball. You’ve got to play every day.
“But I think it’s more of the mental rest of not trying to figure out how to do something each and every day. That’s what’s going to be beneficial to me, where I can work on something today, go into tomorrow, work on something, then see how it translates into the live at-bats against real pitchers.
“It’ll be nice to work on something in BP and not have to take that into a game two hours later and see if it works. Today I can hone in on what I want to do in BP, and that’ll be it.
“Tomorrow I’ll come into BP and do that again, so I’ll have at least 400 swings going into tomorrow’s live BP of hopefully kicking out some of the bad habits.”
NLDS First, History Later
The Dodgers enter October with a chance to win their third straight World Series, but Freeman said his focus is much smaller right now.
“Personally, I’m thinking about the NLDS and whoever we play and getting ready for that.
“I think if you think big picture in this moment, you lose sight of some things. You’ve just got to take it one day at a time.
“We do understand the bigger picture, but if you’re looking at the bigger picture, you won’t be able to get to that big picture if you’re not focusing on the now.”
The Example Freeman Got From His Dad
One of Freeman’s more personal answers came when he was asked where his habit of taking responsibility and pushing through tough stretches came from.
Freeman pointed to his father, Fred, who raised three boys after Freeman’s mother, Rosemary, died when Freddie was 10.
“What I learned from my dad is someone who had his world turned upside down when my mom passed away when I was 10 years old, and he continued to take care of three boys and work and do the best he possibly could day in and day out and not be a ‘woe is me’ person.
“Obviously when I’m 10, I’m not thinking about that stuff. But as I’ve gotten older and I look back at what that man had to go through, the flip of a switch he had, he was a single dad of three and had his own business with his brother and still continued day in and day out to be the person he is and take care of us.
“As I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized there are no excuses. That man had every excuse in the book to do whatever he wanted in 2000, and he didn’t make an excuse. He went out there and did it each and every day.
“That’s my dad. Was he hard on me about my grades? Yeah, because I wasn’t that great in school. But he’s the best dad I probably could have had in that situation, with what he was going through and what we were all going through.
“What you think of him as a very down-to-earth man, that’s who my dad is. He’s a blessing.”
Plenty of Faith in Yamamoto and the Dodgers’ Staff
Freeman also had high praise for Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the right-hander heads into his third postseason with the Dodgers.
“He is special. From the first live BP that I saw when I faced him, it’s just special stuff, special command, the poise on the mound. Nothing’s too big for him.
“He’s one of those special pitchers that we get to watch day in and day out. It feels like he can put the ball wherever he wants, and we are very confident whenever he goes out there.
“Our pitching staff is pretty special, in my opinion. We’ve got four number ones rolling out there. It just goes on and on. Our pitching staff is most likely going to do it again like they did last year, and hopefully our offense can pick it up this year.”
Experience Counts in October
The Dodgers once again enter the postseason with one of baseball’s older position-player groups. Freeman sees the years this roster has spent playing deep into October as something that can help now.
“We’ve started in February overseas the last couple years and ended up winning the World Series. We know what’s going to be happening in the playoffs. We know what’s going to be thrown at us, the atmospheres.
“I think experience is huge in this. We’ve played a lot of baseball. We’ve been together a long time. We know what it takes.
“I think experience is definitely on our side going into this.”
For Freeman, though, the first order of business remains the same one he laid out at the start of the interview.
Five days. A healthy knee. Plenty of swings.
And a chance to get everything lined up before Saturday.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Freeman Uses Dodgers Break to Repair His Troubled Swing
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Solano

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman is grinding through a structured hitting routine to shed poor habits and reclaim his elite offensive mechanics.
The Dodgers are resting since the end of the regular season on Sunday and Saturday’s National League Division Series opener against the Philadelphia Phillies or Atlanta Braves, providing Freeman with valuable recovery and preparation time.
Ready for the road ahead
According to Dodger Blue, Freeman said before Tuesday’s workout that his body felt good. He downplayed any lingering knee concerns and shifted his attention toward correcting a swing that has troubled him for the past couple of months.
Freeman had not started hitting Tuesday because the Dodgers held meetings first. He planned to begin afterward, take hitting practice every day and follow a structured routine designed to prepare him for Saturday.
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing,” Freeman noted.
“I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple of months.
“So I have yet to hit today because we just had some meetings, and we’ll get going here after I get done with this. I’ll be hitting BP every day I got a plan going in, and hopefully that will take care of itself throughout the course of the week, where I’ll be in a good spot by Saturday,” Freeman continued.
The first baseman hit .288 with 16 home runs, 70 RBIs and a .792 OPS in 153 games this season. He struggled in September, hitting .184 with one home run and seven RBIs in 20 games.
No excuses for Freeman, Dodgers
Freeman refused to use his physical condition as an excuse. He acknowledged that knee problems occasionally prevented him from properly moving onto his front side during three-or-four-day stretches.
Those limitations may have subconsciously caused compensations and created poor habits, but Freeman accepted responsibility for his performance.
He believes the break is especially important because his knee feels strong enough to handle the work required to repair his mechanics.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well,” Freeman said.
“I just didn’t play well the last couple months of the season. That’s what I’m going to go with. Did I have some ailments with my knees? Yes, I did. I don’t know how much that contributed to subconsciously trying to do stuff where it didn’t hurt as much.”
Freeman also views the layoff as more beneficial mentally than physically. The Dodgers practiced Tuesday, scheduled simulated games for the following two days and planned another practice afterward.
Instead of testing an adjustment during hitting practice and immediately carrying it into a game two hours later, Freeman can repeat the change over several days before facing teammates in live situations.
He planned to concentrate on specific details Tuesday, repeat that work Wednesday and take at least 400 swings before Wednesday’s live hitting practice. The goal is to eliminate habits developed during his difficult stretch.
“I think the rest kind of takes care of itself,” Freeman noted.
“I think that’s more of the mental rest. Physically, we’ll go out there and practice today, and then we’ll play in some sim games the next two days and practice again.
“Baseball, you’ve got to play every day. I think it’s more of the mental rest than not trying to figure out how to do something each and every day,” Freeman added.
Freeman recalled dealing with physical issues approximately 100 times worse during that postseason.
“A couple of Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse,” Freeman emphasized.
“Ailment-wise, I truly feel good right now. Physically, it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days. And I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Freeman’s accountability
Freeman acknowledges the injury’s possible influence without allowing it to become an excuse.
His preparation reflects discipline and confidence. Freeman does not expect his swing to improve without concentrated work, repetition and honest evaluation.
He also understands how to use experience constructively. Rather than simply attempting to recreate past success, Freeman is identifying which previous adjustments could solve his current mechanical problems and help the Dodgers win another World Series.
That combination of resilience, responsibility and attention to detail has helped him respond to difficult stretches throughout his career. Freeman believes his body will cooperate and trusts himself to correct his swing before Saturday.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.content:encoded:
While eight teams battle it out to see who will advance to the Division Series, the Dodgers are among four teams using this time off to prepare for October baseball.
After winning an even 100 games in the regular season, the Dodgers secured a first-round bye and will await the winner of the NL Wild Card matchup between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies. While the Dodgers continue to add the finishing touches to their postseason roster, there are some lingering questions as to which players will be a part of the team's depth chart.
21-year-old outfielder Josue De Paula made his presence known while filling in for the then-injured Shohei Ohtani, slashing .323/.500/.581 across 42 plate appearances before he was sent down to Triple-A Oklahoma City. Sonja Chen of MLB.com believes that both De Paula and utility man Hyeseong Kim can make an impact on the postseason roster, with the former being relegated to pinch-hit opportunities due to his lack of big-league experience in the outfield.
Of course, De Paula is capable of playing the corner outfield, but we only saw him play six innings in left as a Dodger. And given how important defense is in the postseason, I doubt we will see him in the field unless it's an emergency.
The month of September has given Shohei Ohtani plenty of time to prepare for his third consecutive postseason run with the Dodgers. The Dodgers still have another three days to prepare for the NLDS, and Ohtani is using this time to get his swing in the right place, per Chen.
"Everything is feeling great physically," general manager Brandon Gomes said on a Zoom call with the media on Tuesday. "The swings, once he came back, overall were in a good place. And using these five days to continue to get reps and feeling good into this series is really important. But feels like he's in a great spot."
Freddie Freeman had his power zapped in the second half of the regular season, hitting just one home run while posting a slugging percentage of .339. Freeman dealt with patellar tendonitis in his right knee, but entering the NLDS, he said that he's feeling a lot better, reports Jack Harris of the California Post.
"I truly feel good right now, physically," Freeman said on Tuesday, during a video conference with reporters ahead of the Dodgers' first pre-National League Division Series bye week workout. "So it's on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days. And I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by [Game 1 on] Saturday."

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Freddie Freeman Reveals Injury Status Ahead of Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Cameron Kiszla
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been dealing with knee pain toward the end of this season, but the Boys in Blue securing a bye for the Wild Card round may be his saving grace. Freeman said Tuesday that he feels better than he had recently, with “no pain in my knee right now.” He added that he’s using this period of five days without games to get some “mental rest,” though his physical preparation for the playoffs is far from over. Freddie Freeman making changes ahead of pla
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been dealing with knee pain toward the end of this season, but the Boys in Blue securing a bye for the Wild Card round may be his saving grace.
Freeman said Tuesday that he feels better than he had recently, with “no pain in my knee right now.”
He added that he’s using this period of five days without games to get some “mental rest,” though his physical preparation for the playoffs is far from over.
Freddie Freeman making changes ahead of playoffs
Freeman, who according to ESPN hit a dreadful .184/.259/.224 in September after a roaring summer at the plate, said he’s making some changes this week.
In particular, he’s looking at his swing and how to get back on track this October.
Freeman said “I’ll be hitting BP every day” and is working a plan he has on how to make himself a dangerous hitter again when October comes around.
After all, in June, he slashed .337/.425/.548/.973, and he followed that up with a torrid July as well, hitting .348/.384/.467/.851.
Freeman said in October 2024, he felt “probably 100 times worse,” so he think he can figure it out for this postseason, too.
“I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure it out by Saturday,” he said.
Freddie Freeman sounds off on Dodgers’ mindset ahead of playoffs
Freeman also faced the inevitable questions about this team’s quest for a third straight title, something he said he’s “personally not thinking about.”
Instead, Freeman said he’s keeping his focus on this upcoming series, including who the Dodgers will play and how to beat them.
“I think if you think big picture in this moment, you’re going to lose you lose sight of some things,” he said. “You just got to take each day one at one day at a time. And we do understand the bigger picture, but if you’re looking at the bigger picture, the you won’t be able to get to that big picture if you’re not focusing on the now.”
It sounds like Freeman and the rest of the Dodgers are locked in on this weekend.
Do you think the Dodgers will three-peat this season?

item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
