item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.content:encoded:
JustPredictions
Justice editors predict the upcoming year of sports.
Ben Khayat ’28: Only one Big Ten team will make the College Football Playoffs. The sample size is small, but the Big Ten has been downright shameful to start the 2026 season. The obvious examples are the Michigan Wolverines coming back from the dead to prevent a home loss to the Western Michigan Broncos, and the Rutgers Scarlet Knights succumbing to the UMass Minutemen, a team that didn’t win a single game last season. The rest of the conference hasn’t been much better. The Oregon Ducks came into the season ranked #2 in the country, but came up limping in their one-score win over the Boise State Broncos before getting dispatched by Oklahoma State on Saturday. The Ohio State Buckeyes led 23-3 against the Texas Longhorns, only to allow 21 unanswered points and choke what would have been the first statement win the conference has had this season. Come January, I can’t imagine many of these “top” teams will have impressed anybody enough to get an at-large bid over some other power conference opponents.
Luca D. Jordan ’28: The Chicago Bears will make the Superbowl this season. After having an amazing breakout season under head coach Ben Johnson and making their first playoff appearance since 2020, the Chicago Bears have shown explosive growth with a new offensive direction. Defined by their comeback wins, the Bears almost clinched the semi-finals last season, but quarterback Caleb Williams threw a bad pass that led to an interception against the Los Angeles Rams. Despite an unfortunate play that ended his season early, Williams has shown flashes of an all time great quarterback. When it comes down to the last few seconds, Williams is known to perform herculean throws to save the game. Although their offseason wasn’t particularly exciting, expect a surprising surge in performance across the board from the entire roster. Previous champs Seattle Seahawks are dead in the water without Sam Darnold and the Rams have added some big names to their roster, but it’s just stars over substance. The Bears have a few decades of an underdog legacy behind them, and that’s too much destiny to ignore.
Bryan Wolfe ’27: The New York Knicks are running it back! I have faith. Even though the Philadelphia 76ers have the starting five of doom and despair, I believe in the king of New York Jalen Brunson to lead us back to the promised land.
Chava Thiell ’29: Alexander Zverev will finish the 2026 ATP season with an ATP finals win and the World #1 ranking. As unfortunate as it may be for diehard Sincaraz fans, Jannik Sinner isn’t healthy and Carlos Alcaraz is still adjusting to his return to tennis after a four-month hiatus. After Zverev clinched two Slams this year, his momentum cannot seem to be stopped. Conversely, I think Aryba Sabalenka will walk away with the WTA Finals trophy, inspired by a heartbreaking US Open final loss to rival Elena Rybakina and a mission to come away from the season with a big tournament win.
Eli Sandalow ’28: The New England Patriots will go 4-13. Drake Maye looks like he regressed, AJ Brown is prone to long-term injuries and Rhamondre Stevenson is one of the most overrated running backs in the NFL right now.
Alyssa Wu ‘29: The Dodgers won’t three-peat this year.The Dodgers have a stacked lineup, with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, plus a star-studded starting rotation of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Along with their veterans, new acquisitions this year include stars like Tarik Skubal, a two-time American League Cy Young winner. Despite this, the Dodgers have not dominated through the season as many expected. They went 13-14 in August, though they have found their footing again in September. Injuries raise more concerns; Ohtani only returned to the lineup on September 23 after a stint on the injured list and is not expected to pitch for the remainder of the season. Reliever Blake Treinen, who has helped bring three championships to the Dodgers in his six seasons, suffered a season-ending injury on September 26. With Kyle Tucker and Andy Pages being the only starting position players under the age of 30, the question is whether these Dodger veterans will be healthy and as productive as they used to be during the postseason. The MLB Playoff bracket itself does not always reward the ‘best’ team. The Dodgers in 2022 are one of the clearest examples of this. In 2022, they went 111-51 and won 14 of 19 regular-season games against the Padres. However, after winning Game 1 of the NLDS, they lost three straight to the San Diego Padres, ending their season. The postseason can bring plenty of surprises, and a team’s regular season does not always predict its success in the playoffs. The Dodgers had to come back from a 3-2 deficit to win last year’s World Series, and this year’s team seems to be much more vulnerable. The Dodgers are sure to make it far in the playoffs, but another championship is far from guaranteed.

item.content:encoded:
Eight Dodgers on Monday were nominated for Major League Baseball’s All-MLB teams, an honor that has existed within the sport since 2019.
Fan voting for the honor will take place beginning Monday through Friday, October 9, with that fan vote counted alongside “a decorated panel of media members, broadcasters, former players and other officials throughout the game” in determining first and second All-MLB teams.
Shohei Ohtani is one of six nominees at designated hitter, Mookie Betts is one of 11 shortstop nominees, and Freddie Freeman one of 14 nominees at first base. All five have captured All-MLB honors in five previous years, with Ohtani collecting first-team All-MLB honors at DH in each of the last three years and four of the last five, plus second-team DH in 2022, to go with his two first-team All-MLB honors (2022-23) and one second-team All-MLB honors (2021) as a starting pitcher.
Betts is a four-time first-team All-MLB outfielder plus a second-team honor in 2019. Freeman has two first-team honors at first base, the last coming in 2023, and three second-team honors.
Max Muncy is one of 11 third baseman vying for All-MLB honors, looking for his first All-MLB selection, facing an uphill battle with Rays star Junior Caminero among those nominated at the position.
Andy Pages is the only Dodger among the 24 outfield nominees, seeking his first All-MLB selection.’
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who garnered first-team All-MLB honors last year, and Tarik Skubal, a first-teamer in each of the last two years, are the two Dodgers starting pitchers nominated at starting pitcher this year.
Tanner Scott is one of 20 relief pitchers up for All-MLB honors.
All-MLB teams will be announced during the MLB awards show on November 11, which will begin at 5 p.m. PT on MLB Network.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Locked in as No. 2 seed, Dodgers turn to Tarik Skubal vs. Giants
item.description: Having seen their chances of gaining the top seed in the National League playoffs die in a two-game span, the Los Angeles Dodgers get an opportunity to coast into the postseason when they open a three-game road set against the San Francisco Giants on Friday. Left-hander Tarik Skubal (11-7, 2.85 ERA) is scheduled to get his final tune-up for the postseason in the series opener for the Dodgers. He will be opposed by Giants right-hander Yunior Marte (0-1, 4.66). While they can’t overtake the Milwau
item.content:encoded:
Having seen their chances of gaining the top seed in the National League playoffs die in a two-game span, the Los Angeles Dodgers get an opportunity to coast into the postseason when they open a three-game road set against the San Francisco Giants on Friday.
Left-hander Tarik Skubal (11-7, 2.85 ERA) is scheduled to get his final tune-up for the postseason in the series opener for the Dodgers. He will be opposed by Giants right-hander Yunior Marte (0-1, 4.66).
While they can’t overtake the Milwaukee Brewers for the best record, the Dodgers (97-62) have clinched the NL West title and the second-best record in the league. The latter will earn them a first-round bye in the playoffs, meaning after Sunday’s regular-season finale in San Francisco, they won’t play again until next Saturday.
Skubal will be making his 10th start since he was acquired from the Detroit Tigers at the trade deadline. Los Angeles has won seven of his nine outings, including the last six.
Skubal wasn’t particularly effective in a five-inning start against the Giants last Saturday in which he allowed four runs, two on a home run by Victor Bericoto. The Dodgers supported him with seven runs in those five innings, allowing him to walk away with a win.
He has faced the Giants just three times in his career, going 2-1 with a 4.30 ERA.
Skubal should have additional firepower supporting him in the rematch as the Dodgers have brought Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages back from injuries over the last three days.
Each got extensive playing time in the just-completed home series against the Padres, with Pages playing in all three games and Ohtani the last two, each going 3-for-9.
Both are expected to play significantly against the Giants, with the team getting five days off to start next week.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman said about the importance of the first-round bye. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here. It’s good to get those guys (Ohtani and Pages) back on the field, get some ABs in them and then rest up.”
Skubal will be matched up once again with Marte, who allowed six runs in 4 2/3 innings in the meeting in Los Angeles last week. A rookie facing the Dodgers for the first time, he served up a home run to Will Smith in taking the loss in his fourth major league appearance.
The Dodgers could see a familiar face late in the game with the Giants on Thursday having claimed their former closer, Camilo Doval, on waivers from the Pirates.
After 4 1/2 seasons in San Francisco in which he recorded 107 saves and was an All-Star in 2023, the Giants sent Doval to the New York Yankees last July for four prospects. One year and one day later, the Yankees flipped the right-hander to Pittsburgh, which in turn saw him pitch just 20 times before cutting him loose, allowing the Giants to snatch him back.
Interestingly, should Doval or another newcomer — catcher Zach Morgan — get into a game during the Dodgers series, the Giants (65-94) would tie the major-league record for number of players used in a season with 71. Should they both play, they would break the record.
Giants manager Tony Vitello joked to reporters Wednesday about the possibility of setting the record.
“I guess, you know, being the first year in the organization, you’d like to get to meet everybody,” he said. “So this is one way to do it.”
–Field Level Media

item.title: [DodgersBeat] With Another 100 Win Season, Dave Roberts Joins Elite Company
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has accomplished quite a bit during his tenure as Dodgers manager, but Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants added another impressive achievement to his résumé. With the Dodgers reaching 100 victories, Roberts tied the all-time managerial record for most 100-win seasons, joining some of the most successful skippers in baseball history. Speaking with reporters following the regular-season finale, Roberts acknowledged the significance of the accomplishment while emp
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has accomplished quite a bit during his tenure as Dodgers manager, but Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants added another impressive achievement to his résumé.
With the Dodgers reaching 100 victories, Roberts tied the all-time managerial record for most 100-win seasons, joining some of the most successful skippers in baseball history.
Speaking with reporters following the regular-season finale, Roberts acknowledged the significance of the accomplishment while emphasizing the contributions of the players and organization that helped make it possible.
A Milestone Worth Celebrating
Asked whether reaching 100 wins carried significance even though the Dodgers had already secured their postseason position, Roberts made it clear that the milestone mattered.
“It does. It doesn’t change anything as far as our standing going forward in the postseason, but it’s still a nice feather in our cap to win 100 games.”
When informed that the victory tied him for the most 100-win seasons by any manager in major league history, Roberts reflected on the company he now keeps.
“Yeah, I guess I’m in some rare air, some good company. A lot of good players, a great organization, and it’s not easy, 100 games.
“There’s a lot of things that we had to go through this year, and we just continued to remain steadfast and play on. And so, yeah, that’s something to be proud of.”
Sunday’s victory provided a fitting conclusion to another successful regular season. Roberts particularly appreciated the pitching staff’s performance, with seven pitchers combining to hold San Francisco to one run while striking out 16.
“Obviously, we had a few guys that we wanted to stay away from. I thought the pitching did a remarkable job today. Bobby did a nice job picking up a couple innings, getting out of some stress there in the seventh, I think it was.
“And timely hitting. It didn’t look great early, but we hung in there as far as on the pitching side, and Alex with a big two-out hit, and then Andy finished up the season the right way.”
Preparing for Philadelphia or Atlanta
The Dodgers will now await the winner of the Phillies-Braves Wild Card Series, with Game 1 of the NLDS scheduled for Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
Roberts expects a competitive series between two familiar division rivals.
“When you start the season, those two teams were probably picked to be one-two in the East, and they’re very, very familiar with one another. So it’s going to be a good series.
“Obviously, the Phillies had to play to the end, but like I said, there’s a lot of familiarity, and all bets are off when you play within the division.
“So we’ll just sit back and take tomorrow off and have the workout on Tuesday. We’ll get to watch those guys, and then we’ll get to watch that other series during our workout.”
Getting the Big Bats Ready
Roberts also discussed the importance of the upcoming break for Freddie Freeman and Shohei Ohtani, both of whom have been working to find their offensive rhythm.
Regarding Ohtani, Roberts was encouraged by what he saw Sunday and believes the additional preparation will be valuable.
“I thought he looked fine. He looked better today. I do think that just getting some at-bats, however many he got since he came back, and then really just this week is going to be really crucial, I think, for Freddie. I think it’s going to be crucial for Sho.”
Roberts also emphasized that Ohtani emerged from his recent return to action healthy, which was the most important consideration.
“The process early was great. I thought in the middle of that he was kind of getting a little more anxious. I thought today the process was much better.
“But I think the main thing is that we feel that he came out of it healthy, and so you just expect the ensuing days he feels even better. When you look out to Saturday, I think he’ll be in a good spot.”
The Dodgers will make intrasquad games available during their preparation period, although Roberts said individual players will decide whether to participate.
For Roberts, the regular season concludes with another historic accomplishment and a chance to add to an already remarkable managerial legacy.
But the ultimate objective remains the same: 11 more wins and another World Series championship.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Miguel Rojas Reflects on (potentially) Final Regular Season Game
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants was particularly meaningful for Miguel Rojas, who may have played the final regular-season game of his career. The veteran shortstop was visibly emotional during the broadcast, but after the Dodgers completed their sweep of San Francisco and reached 100 victories, his attention was already turning toward October. Speaking with reporters after the game, Rojas emphasized the importance of finishing the regular season strong and maintaining t
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants was particularly meaningful for Miguel Rojas, who may have played the final regular-season game of his career. The veteran shortstop was visibly emotional during the broadcast, but after the Dodgers completed their sweep of San Francisco and reached 100 victories, his attention was already turning toward October.
Speaking with reporters after the game, Rojas emphasized the importance of finishing the regular season strong and maintaining the team’s momentum heading into the postseason.
“Yeah, it feels good. Finishing the season strong is something that we as a team put as a goal, not to take that foot off the gas pedal and play until the last out.
“I think it’s really important for us to continue to get momentum into the postseason, and winning is always contagious, and that’s what we’re looking for.
“We’re looking to win another 11 games for us to make history and do something really cool about our legacies and the city of LA.”
Five Days to Prepare Together
The Dodgers now have five days before Saturday’s NLDS opener, and Rojas believes the time together will provide opportunities that go beyond simply resting and recovering.
For the veteran infielder, some of the most valuable preparation comes from teammates sharing their knowledge and helping one another improve.
“Yeah, I mean, it’s going to be important because there’s so many things that we can actually take advantage of on workout days where you get feedback from your teammates more than anything.
“Not just the coaches or the game itself. You get together with your teammates and kind of swing in the cage with them and get together at the same time on the field and talk about pitches.
“You get to face your own pitchers and tell them about the movement of the pitches and ways that they can attack right-handed hitters, left-handed hitters, whatever it is.”
Rojas expressed confidence in the team’s preparation and its collective commitment to another championship run.
“I feel like we got a pretty good plan. We’re looking forward to spending three or four weeks together to finish the season, and we’re all going to make the sacrifice to be 100% in on this one.”
Bringing October Baseball Home to Los Angeles
With more than four million fans attending Dodgers games during the regular season, Rojas was also asked about the significance of securing home-field advantage for the NLDS.
For him, the opportunity to play more postseason games at Dodger Stadium is as much about rewarding the fans as it is about giving the team a competitive advantage.
“Yeah, they deserve it. It’s not just about us,” Rojas said, reflecting on the importance of giving fans the opportunity to experience the biggest postseason moments at home.
“It feels like we’re all really excited about being at home for more games and hopefully get to win at home.”
And while Sunday may have marked the conclusion of his regular-season career, Rojas was quick to point out that his Dodgers journey isn’t finished quite yet.
“We got some more games to play, so I’m really excited about that.”
For a player who has become such an important part of the Dodgers’ clubhouse, there’s still one more chapter to write. And as Freddie Freeman said after Sunday’s game, the team’s goal is to send Miggy out as a champion.
Eleven more wins.

The Dodgers' 5-1 victory over the Giants in 10 innings on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park -- keyed by Alex Call's go-ahead double and a three-run blast from Andy Pages -- secured a 100-win campaign, their fifth in the past seven full-length seasons and their sixth with Roberts at the helm. Roberts joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only ma
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- With another 162 regular-season games in the books, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has again found himself in rarefied air.
The Dodgers' 5-1 victory over the Giants in 10 innings on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park -- keyed by Alex Call's go-ahead double and a three-run blast from Andy Pages -- secured a 100-win campaign, their fifth in the past seven full-length seasons and their sixth with Roberts at the helm.
Roberts joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only managers with six 100-win seasons.
"I guess I'm in some rare air, some good company," said Roberts, who in June reached 1,000 career managerial wins faster than any other manager. "A lot of good players, a great organization, and it's not easy to win 100 games. And so there's a lot of things that we had to go through this year, and we just continue to remain steadfast and play on. And so, yeah, that's something to be proud of."
The last three seasons in which the Dodgers did not win 100 games -- 2025, '24 and the pandemic-shortened '20 campaign -- they won the World Series. In their 11 previous 100-win seasons, they failed to win a championship.
"That just means we’re due as an organization," Freddie Freeman said. "I don’t think any of us are going to be upset with winning 100 games."
The 2026 Dodgers are not just looking to win it all. They are defending their World Series title for the second year in a row, seeking to complete the Majors' first three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees.
After the bye week, in which they'll await the outcome of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and Phillies, the Dodgers' title defense begins in earnest in the NL Division Series, starting on Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers may have 100 wins in the books, but everything resets in the postseason. Moving forward, they're focused on getting the 11 wins they need to hoist the Commissioner's Trophy for a third straight year.

item.title: [MLB.com] Dodgers end season with 100th win, questions about Ohtani
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO -- Five games do not tell the story of Shohei Ohtani's year, but that season-ending sample holds a fair amount of weight as the Dodgers evaluate which version of their superstar they will get in the postseason. Ohtani knocked a base hit in three at-bats as the Dodgers closed the book on their regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings over the Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park. L.A. has won 100 games for the sixth time under manager Dave Roberts, who joins Hall of Famers B
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Five games do not tell the story of Shohei Ohtani's year, but that season-ending sample holds a fair amount of weight as the Dodgers evaluate which version of their superstar they will get in the postseason.
Ohtani knocked a base hit in three at-bats as the Dodgers closed the book on their regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings over the Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park. L.A. has won 100 games for the sixth time under manager Dave Roberts, who joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only managers to accomplish the feat.
The most meaningful games of the year are just around the corner for the back-to-back World Series champions, whose title defense picks up when the NL Division Series begins next Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
"It doesn't change anything as far as our standing going forward in the postseason," Roberts said, "but it's still a nice feather in our cap to win 100 games."
The Dodgers finished strong by going 18-7 in September, and they'll look to maintain that momentum through the upcoming bye week.
"I just think as a group we played better baseball again, and that’s what you want going into the postseason," Freddie Freeman said. "Our pitching staff is amazing. Guys started to swing the bat better. Some of us still need to use these five days to figure it out. But a lot of good things happened over the course of the end of the season."
As the Dodgers bid for a three-peat, which would be the first in the Majors since the 1998-2000 Yankees, they are counting on Ohtani to set the tone for their offense as he has consistently done in his three seasons in L.A. But in the five games after his 15-day injured list stint due to lingering right biceps and left knee injuries -- after more than two weeks without seeing live pitching -- Ohtani did not show much at the plate, hitting 5-for-21 (.238) with eight strikeouts against one walk.
Overall, Ohtani finished the regular season hitting .275 with an .889 OPS and 30 homers -- which all came before he went on the IL. His run of consecutive MVP seasons is set to end after three years, as the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong has seemingly run away with the award.
Before Sunday's finale, Roberts described Ohtani's recent performance as showing rust rather than being a legitimate concern heading into the postseason. The Dodgers believe Ohtani feels as good physically as he has in some time, and they don't think his swing looks compromised, as it did before he went on the IL.
While better results from Ohtani would have been encouraging, the Dodgers were looking for more than just the surface numbers. They wanted to see him conduct quality at-bats, which he did in his first two games back and on Sunday, with a lapse in between. But ultimately, these games were more about health and process rather than pure performance, much like a rehab assignment.
"I thought today the process was much better," Roberts said. "But I think the main thing is that we feel that he came out of it healthy, and so you just expect the ensuing days he feels even better. So, when you look out to Saturday, I think he'll be in a good spot."
Ohtani's performance began to drop off most notably when he attempted to ramp back up as a pitcher starting on Aug. 8. In the 24 games between then and his IL stint, Ohtani hit .198 and struck out 34 times in 109 plate appearances. His average bat speed (72.5 mph) and exit velocity (92.2 mph) in that span were down compared with his first 106 games (72.9 mph bat speed and 93.4 mph exit velocity).
In Ohtani's five games back from the IL, he gained a tick of average bat speed (72.6 mph) and hit the ball notably harder (96.8 mph). Even though that did not translate to immediate results, it would seem to be a positive sign for both Ohtani's health and his swing.
The postseason is a new beginning. Ohtani will have the bye week to rest up and take live at-bats, and starting on Saturday, the Dodgers are hopeful that he will swing the bat more like his usual self. But they won't know exactly what they have in their superstar until they see him under the lights.

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need. Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants Befo
item.content:encoded:
For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need.
Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants
Before getting to that point of being tied in extras, Jack Dreyer did a reasonable job of keeping the Giants at bay as an opener, but a stolen base allowed the opportunity for just a pair of singles to open the scoring in the second. Shay Whitcomb singled and stole second, later driven in by Scott Bandura—his first RBI of the season, playing in just his 13th big league game. Bandura also tried to steal a base, but this time Dreyer was alert to the danger and picked him off.
Facing a traditional bullpen game with Carson Seymour completing just one inning to open this one, the Dodgers first threatened to score in the third, the inning marked by Tony Vitello’s ejection. With two on and a 2-2 count to Mookie Betts, a check swing in which he probably went around was called a no-swing. Vitello came out to argue what had already been a topic of frustration earlier in the game and was thrown out for the seventh time in his 2026. The Giants, however, got out of the jam, as Betts struck out on the next pitch, and Sam Hentges also punched out Freddie Freeman.
What the Dodgers offense couldn’t do in the third, it did in the following frame. Kyle Tucker got on to leadoff the inning thanks to a defensive error by the second baseman and moved to third on a Max Muncy double—his 27th of the season, setting a new career high in a single season. With two on and one out, Andy Pages evened the score with a sacrifice fly.
Through the following innings, the Dodgers kept threatening but never coming through, first with a Freddie Freeman hit with a man on being taken away by a great defensive play from Jonah Cox—somewhat redeeming himself for the error that contributed to the Dodgers’ first run. That, by the way, would be Freeman’s last action in the game, replaced after five by Kiké Hernández as Dave Roberts rotated key pieces.
In the sixth, Muncy nearly wrote another chapter in his book as a giant killer. But the deepest part of the park was just deep enough to keep him from a solo shot in a ball that would’ve gone out in 23 of 30 stadiums. Perhaps the biggest squandered chance, though, came in the seventh and eighth when the Dodgers first stranded a leadoff double by Tommy Edman with three straight groundouts—an inning later, after Muncy secured his third hit of the day, Andy Pages hit into an inning-ending double play with two on and one out.
The Dodgers’ pitching was the reason the offense kept getting these opportunities to take the lead. Justin Wrobleski was the first pitcher out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, but looking for an even distribution of workload, he only completed two scoreless innings in under 30 pitches. Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz combined to strike out three, each with a scoreless frame.
Although Wrobleski had a couple of scares, the Giants truly came back to threaten again in the seventh when Bobby Miller took the mound, but also without actually breaking through. With runners at the corners and no outs, Miller secured a strikeout, then lucked into Marcelo Mayer staying at third on a wild pitch quickly recovered by Hunter Feduccia, recorded another punchout, and finished off the inning with a groundout.
With both teams exhausting new ways of threatening without actually scoring, the Giants looked like they’d take the lead with a leadoff bomb in the eighth by Christian Koss. However, the call on the field of a home run was overturned when replay made it clear it was a foul ball, and the score remained 1-1 through nine innings.
Even in the tenth, it looked like the Dodgers were going to strand the ghost runner after their first two hitters were retired without him advancing to third, but Call came through, and an intentional walk later, Pages had the big hit of the game. With the four RBI he recorded in this game, Pages left Ohtani behind and isolated himself as the Dodgers’ RBI leader this season, with 85.
Sunday particulars
Home run: Andy Pages (23)
WP —Alex Vesia (3-1): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 strikeout
LP —Duncan Davitt (0-1):1 IP, 2 hits, 4 runs, 3 earned runs, 1 walk
Up next
The Dodgers get a little under a week off before they get back on the field on Saturday at home. They’ll be playing host to the winner of the Wild Card round between the Braves and Phillies in game 1 of the NLDS. No starters have been announced for that series.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Dodgers Make Sudden Freddie Freeman Announcement
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: Freddie Freeman is back where the Los Angeles Dodgers like him: in the middle of a loaded order, on the last afternoon of the regular season. After sitting Saturday against the San Francisco Giants, the Dodgers first baseman is in Sunday’s Game 162 lineup at Oracle Park and batting third. The card posted by Underdog MLB puts Shohei Ohtani at designated hitter, Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freeman at first, Kyle Tucker in right, Teoscar Hernández in left, Max Muncy at third, Andy Pages in center, H
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman is back where the Los Angeles Dodgers like him: in the middle of a loaded order, on the last afternoon of the regular season.
After sitting Saturday against the San Francisco Giants, the Dodgers first baseman is in Sunday’s Game 162 lineup at Oracle Park and batting third.
The card posted by Underdog MLB puts Shohei Ohtani at designated hitter, Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freeman at first, Kyle Tucker in right, Teoscar Hernández in left, Max Muncy at third, Andy Pages in center, Hunter Feduccia behind the plate and Tommy Edman at second. Jack Dreyer is listed as the starter in what figures to be a bullpen game.
The off day was not a surprise. Freeman had started each of the previous 10 games and was dragging a .522 OPS over 45 plate appearances in that stretch.
Enrique Hernández filled in at first on Saturday while the club gave its 37-year-old cornerstone a breather.
That is how Dave Roberts has handled September: keep Freeman available, not exhausted, with the postseason a few days away.
Sunday’s assignment is the one Freeman has occupied for most of his career.
He has started more than 1,300 games in the three-hole across Atlanta and Los Angeles, and even after spring talk about a cleanup role behind Tucker, the Dodgers keep sliding him back between Betts and the middle of the order when they want their most reliable left-handed bat seeing traffic.
He entered the weekend hitting .290 with 167 hits, 16 homers and 70 RBIs. The power has been quieter lately — he has gone without an extra-base hit for more than two weeks — but the bat-to-ball skill is still the reason Los Angeles trusts him with runners on.
The context around the lineup is October-minded. Los Angeles is 99-62 and chasing a 100-win season in the finale. Will Smith is the only everyday starter sitting.
Blake Treinen is headed to the injured list with a shoulder issue, so the bullpen will be asked to work. First pitch is 12:05 p.m. PT / 3:05 p.m. ET on SportsNet LA.
For Freeman, the message is simple. One rest day. Then back in the three-hole, glove at first, with Ohtani and Betts in front of him and Tucker behind him.
If the Dodgers are going to finish 100-62 and carry momentum into the NLDS, they want their veteran first baseman in the middle of it — not on the bench, and not buried in the order.
Sunday is a tune-up with meaning: one more look at the group that has to win in October.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers loom large over upcoming CBA negotiations, with owners gunning for a salary cap while players battle to maintain maximum earning potential. The Dodgers, in active pursuit of their third-straight World Series title, own MLB's highest payroll at $380.5 million. That includes $30 million-plus allocated to Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Tarik Skubal and Mookie Betts on an annual basis.
The Dodgers' ability — and willingness — to outspend opponents, sometimes almost four-to-one, has frustrated fans and given cheaper owners an excuse to cry foul. While the Dodgers experienced their share of turbulence this season, this team clearly isn't going anywhere. Their profits more than make up for their expenses. Look no further than jersey sales:
MLB's top 10 jersey sellers in 2026
The Dodgers have four of the top-10 jersey sellers in MLB this season. That does not include marquee names like Kyle Tucker (acquired last offseason), Tarik Skubal (acquired at the trade deadline) or their other two-time Cy Young winner, Blake Snell.
| Player | Team |
|---|---|
| 1. Shohei Ohtani | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 2. Aaron Judge | New York Yankees |
| 3. Pete Crow-Armstrong | Chicago Cubs |
| 4. Ronald Acuña Jr. | Atlanta Braves |
| 5. Fernando Tatis Jr. | San Diego Padres |
| 6. Freddie Freeman | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 7. Bryce Harper | Philadelphia Phillies |
| 8. Mookie Betts | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 9. Yoshinobu Yamamoto | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 10. Juan Soto | New York Mets |
In 2025, the Dodgers became the first team in baseball history to generate over $1 billion in gross revenue. While owner Mark Walter's financial troubles made headlines in recent weeks, his troubles are concentrated in the business world, not the baseball world. The Dodgers are an unequivocally profitable venture; not the sort Walter is likely to relinquish any time soon.
There's a reason the Dodgers are willing to spend on premium free agents every winter. It's not because Walter loves baseball and wants to win. Perhaps that is a part of the equation, but baseball, now more than ever, is a business. And the vast majority of ownership groups view it through that cold, inflexible lens. The Dodgers spend money to make money. They fill out the stadium, sell jerseys and rake in merchandise money from all across the globe. Their roster's strong international presence, spearheaded by Shohei Ohtani and his fellow countrymen, plays no small part in that.
Also helpful: so much of L.A.'s salaries are deferred. Ohtani is making $2 million per season through the duration of his contract. He's making the same money as an unproven third-year player still under arbitration.
The Dodgers' dominance will press on — with or without a salary cap
The Dodgers are not going anywhere. Even with a salary cap. It's a sobering truth, but one all 29 opposing fanbases must accept, lest their dreams be shattered further on down the line.
That's not to say the Dodgers are unbeatable. They will eventually fall in the postseason, perhaps as soon as next month. Plenty of great organizations find ways to build competitive rosters without approaching $400 million in spending. Conversely, a high payroll does not guarantee success. Ask the last-place New York Mets, whose $349 million payroll ranks second in MLB, behind only L.A.
Los Angeles is certainly a unique case study, however. Not only are the Dodgers willing to spend, but stars clearly want to play for them. There's the allure of Hollywood. The desire to play for a world-class organization, with top-notch facilities and a great support staff. There is also, more plainly, the desire to win championships. No team in recent history is more consistently in the World Series mix than Los Angeles.
Moreover, the Dodgers just know how to run a successful organization. That is overly broad and simplistic, but it's the truth. Beyond their high-paid stars, L.A. has the best farm system in baseball, with six prospects in MLB Pipeline's Top 100. And that's after trading two top-100 prospects for Tarik Skubal. L.A. has the depth of talent behind their stars to consistently trade for upgrades at positions of need — or to develop cheaper stars to backfill "holes" in their expensive lineup.
While a salary cap would limit L.A.'s ability to sign the Shohei Ohtani, almost their entire core is locked up for the foreseeable future. Those who aren't (see: Skubal) would no doubt love to re-sign. If MLB puts a cap on deferred money, sure, that'll impact their future plans. But Los Angeles would gladly spend more money upfront. Only $30 million of Kyle Tucker's $240 million contract last winter was deferred. The Dodgers managed to sign the offseason's most prized free agent despite longer-term offers from the Mets and Blue Jays, two big-market clubs with competitive aspirations of their own. The Blue Jays had just taken L.A. seven games in the World Series.
Los Angeles has the talent and the flexibility to navigate whatever comes next. If the players win out and no salary cap is implemented, it will be business as usual. If MLB owners get their way, L.A. can maneuver around forthcoming changes — even shed major salaries — without falling far in the standings. The Dodgers have the prospect depth and development staff of a well-run, small-market club, paired with the outsized expenses of the glitzy team from L.A. That is how you build sustainably.
The Dodgers are designed to survive just about anything at this point.

Tanner Scott closed out a second straight game, earning his 25th save. Betts homered with two outs in the third inning for hi
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- - Kiké Hernández hit a tiebreaking home run leading off the ninth inning, Mookie Betts also homered and the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 4-3 on Saturday.
Bo Davidson hit a tying sacrifice fly off Evan Phillips (3-2) with two outs in the eighth for San Francisco before Hernández answered against Trent Harris (0-1) for his fourth homer.
Tanner Scott closed out a second straight game, earning his 25th save.
Betts homered with two outs in the third inning for his team's first hit before Miguel Rojas and Tommy Edman added RBI singles the next two innings.
Betts' blast to the bleachers in left-center sent the large contingent of Dodgers fans in the sellout crowd of 40,124 at Oracle Park into a frenzy on a beautiful sunny afternoon in the Bay Area.
Shohei Ohtani, playing for a fourth straight day following a 13-game absence with right biceps discomfort, went 1 for 5 with two strikeouts after an 0-for-4 showing with three Ks on Friday night.
When Camilo Doval pitched the seventh for San Francisco, he became the 71st player used by the club this season - matching Atlanta's MLB record set last year.
Los Angeles left-hander Blake Snell struck out three and didn't walk a batter, allowing one run on five hits over four innings in his final playoff tune-up.
The Giants lost their fourth straight, seventh of eight and seventh in a row to the rival Dodgers after taking four of five in the series to start the year.
Los Angeles earned its 14th shutout of the season in a 2-0 win Friday, then manager Dave Roberts rested first baseman Freddie Freeman and gave Hernández a start. The Dodgers improved their majors-best road record to 48-32.
Up next
Neither team had announced its starter for Sunday's regular-season finale, when beloved Giants broadcaster Mike Krukow will be celebrated before he retires from the booth after nearly four decades.
------

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers face the San Francisco Giants in the second game of the regular season’s final series.
The Dodgers will rotate in veterans with something to provide heading into the postseason, with Freddie Freeman notably absent for Saturday’s game.
Dodgers Lineup
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Shohei Ohtani, DH
3. Will Smith, C
4. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Miguel Rojas, 3B
7. Andy Pages, CF
8. Kike Hernandez, 1B
9. Tommy Edman, 2B
The Dodgers are facing lefty Matt Wilkinson, which lets Rojas and Kike Hernandez enter the mix in a favorable matchup with a righty-heavy lineup.
The biggest note of the game is that once again, Mookie Betts is batting leadoff, while Shohei Ohtani is hitting second.
Manager Dave Roberts has made it clear that Ohtani wasn’t guaranteed to hit leadoff against lefties, and with Betts continuing to deliver quality plate appearances, the Dodgers skipper is willing to start the order with Betts.
At-bats from Andy Pages, Kike Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, and Tommy Edman are all worth monitoring. Pages is still somewhat fresh off the injured list, while Tommy Edman has been in a slump.
Rojas and Hernandez feature so inconsistently that they are always worth following whenever they play.
Who is pitching for the Dodgers?
Blake Snell starts against the Giants after being pulled early in his last outing. Snell, who has a history of groin injuries, had some groin soreness surface against the Cincinnati Reds last week.
Initial concern about his postseason viability grew, and as a key member of the rotation, the Dodgers could ill-afford to lose him.
The injury doesn’t seem major, and Snell has a chance to get some pitching work before October kicks into high gear.
In terms of actual pitching production, Snell sits at the top, with elite stuff and sharp command.
If he is fully sharp, Snell can carry a team in the postseason, and while the Dodgers don’t need that this week, next week will be a different story.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Praises Tarik Skubal after Dodgers' Shutout Win
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has seen plenty of outstanding pitching performances this season, but Friday night’s masterpiece from Tarik Skubal was something special. The Dodgers manager had little hesitation when asked whether Skubal’s seven shutout innings against the Giants represented his finest outing since joining the club. “That was the best we’ve seen,” Roberts said following the Dodgers’ 2-0 victory at Oracle Park. “He was on a mission tonight. You could see it. Everything was worki
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has seen plenty of outstanding pitching performances this season, but Friday night’s masterpiece from Tarik Skubal was something special. The Dodgers manager had little hesitation when asked whether Skubal’s seven shutout innings against the Giants represented his finest outing since joining the club.
“That was the best we’ve seen,” Roberts said following the Dodgers’ 2-0 victory at Oracle Park. “He was on a mission tonight. You could see it. Everything was working, and he just went after those guys and did a fantastic job.”
“Pounded the zone. Everything was working tonight. Efficient. I think he went through seven innings, 75 pitches, something like that. Incredibly good.”
Skubal Had Something to Prove
Skubal had been less than pleased with his previous outing against the Giants, when he surrendered 10 hits and struggled with his fastball command. Roberts believes that disappointment helped fuel Friday’s extraordinary performance.
“I think so, yeah. He wasn’t pleased with his outing the last time, and so to come back and face the same team and do what he did less than a week later is pretty impressive.”
Asked what makes Skubal’s fastball so difficult for hitters, particularly when he’s attacking the strike zone as aggressively as he did Friday, Roberts pointed to the combination of velocity, deception and secondary pitches.
“When it’s right, it’s an explosive fastball. He stays behind it well. He hides it well, and then he’s got the secondaries to go with it.”
“Tonight certainly was really dominant with the fastball and essentially could do whatever he wanted tonight.”
Roberts Sees an Improved, More Confident Roki Sasaki
Skubal’s departure after seven innings provided another opportunity for Roki Sasaki to demonstrate what he can contribute to the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen. The young right-hander struck out two in a scoreless eighth inning, and Roberts believes he’s considerably further along than he was at this point last season.
“Yeah, he is. I think the fastball’s better. I think the split’s better, and it’s also nice that he’s already done it.”
“So just in total, he’s just a better pitcher than he was last year and a lot more confident. Certainly, the stuff was really good the last couple outings.”
Sasaki was followed by Tanner Scott, who struck out two in a perfect ninth inning to record his 24th save. Roberts liked the combination, although he was careful to avoid committing himself to specific bullpen roles for October.
“I liked it tonight. They both did a fantastic job.”
“It’s just better to have as many guys that you have confidence in in leverage. It allows us to deploy guys whenever we need to.”
“I feel comfortable with a lot of guys at the back end, for sure.”
The Offense Needs Contributions Beyond Its Superstars
The Dodgers managed just two runs Friday, both coming on solo home runs in the second inning. Although the offense has struggled to string together hits over the past several games, Roberts remains encouraged by the quality of the team’s at-bats.
“I thought obviously we had two homers tonight. Will had a really good night. I thought Mookie still looks fine.”
“We’re not putting a bunch of hits together, but it doesn’t seem like the results are there. I still like our intent in the batter’s box.”
“Try not to overthink it as far as the production the last few games, because honestly, I like where our offense is at mentally. But I do think, like I said before, this week for our group is going to be a very good thing.”
The manager also emphasized the importance of getting production from the middle and bottom of the batting order. With opposing teams likely to focus their attention on Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts and Freddie Freeman, players like Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages will have opportunities to make a considerable difference.
“It certainly adds length. As we all know, when you get to the postseason, they’re going to try to eliminate Sho and try to make other guys beat you.”
“It always sort of comes to the middle to the bottom of the order, where you’ve either got to get guys on base or get hits, get big hits.”
“The way Teo’s been swinging, Andy’s swinging, we’ve got to get Tommy on track. It’ll certainly be helpful.”
Pages Is Entering October in a Much Different Place
Roberts admitted that he’s been somewhat surprised by how quickly Pages has regained his form after missing approximately five weeks with an injury. Playing in just his fourth game since returning from the injured list, Pages collected two hits Friday, including his 22nd home run.
“I am a little bit, but in the other sense, I’m not surprised because he put in a lot of work before he was active to really hit the ground running.”
“Even the jumps defensively, covering so much ground out there, the at-bat quality. You think that when you take five weeks off, your timing is going to be off a little bit, but he put in a lot of time.”
Asked about Pages’ struggles during last year’s postseason and what might be different this time around, Roberts pointed to the young outfielder’s confidence.
“I think the one thing is the confidence. He went into last October really scuffling, and it sort of bled into October.”
“Right now, he feels really confident, swinging the bat well, and the hope is that this one bleeds into October as well.”
“His headspace is just a lot more confident this year.”
Roberts Still Likes What He Sees From Ohtani
Ohtani went hitless with three strikeouts Friday, but Roberts indicated that he’s continuing to see encouraging signs from the slugger following his return from the injured list.
“Loved them. I liked them. He’s fine.”
“I really think that, just for me, the swing decisions, the bat speed, that’s kind of all that. If that’s in place, then the results will be there.”
With the first-round bye already secured, the Dodgers have the opportunity to use their final regular-season games to sharpen their approach and prepare for the NLDS.
Friday’s performance offered plenty of encouragement on the pitching side, particularly from Skubal and Sasaki. And with Teoscar and Pages continuing to swing the bats well, Roberts has reason to believe his club is moving in the right direction as October approaches.

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers' three-peat hopes rest on their four aces — and bottom-of-order production
item.dc:creator: Bill Shaikin
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers’ path to a third straight World Series title will depend on four frontline starters, but manager Dave Roberts hopes his offense won’t leave them carrying the load. - In a 2-0 win over San Francisco, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages offered a timely reminder that the Dodgers will need consistent production from the bottom half of the lineup in the playoffs. - Hernández is a proven October hitter, while Pages is finding his swing after c
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers’ path to a third straight World Series title will depend on four frontline starters, but manager Dave Roberts hopes his offense won’t leave them carrying the load.
- In a 2-0 win over San Francisco, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages offered a timely reminder that the Dodgers will need consistent production from the bottom half of the lineup in the playoffs.
- Hernández is a proven October hitter, while Pages is finding his swing after coming back from a broken hand.
SAN FRANCISCO — This is the 60th anniversary of the 1966 World Series, in which the losing team did not score for the final 33 innings of the series.
That losing team was the Dodgers. Over the final three games of the series, Jim Palmer, Wally Bunker and Dave McNally of the Baltimore Orioles each pitched a complete-game shutout.
That art of pitching is not in style today. Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched two complete games last October, but he cannot pitch every game, even if he left that impression upon the Toronto Blue Jays.
The Dodgers’ clearest and cleanest route to a three-peat nonetheless rests upon the four shoulders of Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. If the four aces can do to October opponents what the 1966 Orioles did to the Dodgers, or some reasonable 21st century facsimile, we’ll see you at the parade.
Does Dodgers manager Dave Roberts believe his starting pitchers will have to carry the load in October?
“I hope not,” Roberts said.
Tarik Skubal gives up just three hits and strikes out 10 in his final start before the postseason to help carry the Dodgers to a 2-0 win over the Giants.
Friday’s 2-0 victory over the San Francisco Giants offered two encouraging swings. Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages each hit home runs, a reminder that a properly tuned Dodgers offense runs on more than Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Will Smith.
Skubal scattered three hits and struck out 10 in seven scoreless innings, which would have gone for naught without the Hernández and Pages home runs. Given that the Dodgers were playing the Giants and the remains of their depleted roster, it was something of a warning sign: this could happen against a postseason team.
No team can plan to score a lot of runs against the Dodgers’ starters. The opposing game plan would be to neutralize them and keep the game close enough to where one or two big swings can make the difference. The Giants, who have the National League’s second-worst record, almost pulled it off.
“When you get to the postseason, they’re going to try to eliminate Shohei and try to make other guys beat you,” Roberts said. “So it always sort of comes to the middle to the bottom of the order, where you’ve either got to get guys on base or get hits, get big hits.”
In October, Hernández is who you want at bat. He has homered in six of the seven postseason series he has played for the Dodgers, including each of the last five. In 33 postseason games for the Dodgers, he has driven in 25 runs.
For most players, offensive production drops in October, when batters face the best pitchers from the best teams. For Hernández, his career OPS is .796 in the regular season and .792 in the postseason.
And, for all his summer struggles, he is batting .354 this month, with an OPS just shy of 1.000. He’ll be, as the league-issued hoodies used to say, October ready.
For Pages, however, last October was cruel.
This October was not looking particularly promising, either. Pages missed 27 games because of a broken hand, leaving him the final six games of the regular season to get his swing back into rhythm.
“You think that you take five weeks off,” Roberts said, “that your timing is going to be off a little bit.”
So far, so good: five hits in 12 at-bats, including the home run Friday.
Pages ended the regular season last year with four hits in his final 28 at-bats. That, Roberts said, tells him this October will be different for Pages.
“I think the one thing is the confidence, how he went into last October really scuffling, and it sort of bled into October,” Roberts said, “where I think right now he feels really confident, swinging the bat well, and the hope is that this one bleeds into October as well.
“So, I think it’s definitely a different result going into October, and then also his headspace. There’s a lot more confidence this year.”
In 2025, when the Dodgers won the World Series, they ranked second among the 30 major league clubs in runs scored, and in home runs. In 2024, when they won the World Series, they ranked third in runs scored, and in home runs.
The Dodgers rank fourth in runs scored this year, and seventh in home runs. The offense is down some, if not much. In all the national postseason hype, the Dodgers projections will boil down to one sentence: Can anyone stop those starters?
“I think at first glance that’s what you see in our ballclub,” Roberts said. “But we have a lot of talented, really good hitters and I hope they work hand in hand and not just our pitching and defense carry us.”
For the Dodgers, the postseason opens one week from Saturday. If the Dodgers roll out the 1966 playbook, their October stay will be short.

item.content:encoded:
El campocorto de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, Mookie Betts, está teniendo un septiembre demente en el plato y parece alguno que puede sobrellevar la ataque en la postemporada.
El demente septiembre de Betts
Betts está bateando .367 en septiembre hasta el viernes, con 21 carreras impulsadas, seis jonrones y nueve dobles.
Tiene un OPS de 1.117 y un wRC+ de 219, ambas métricas resaltan cuán elitista ha sido. Ha sido, con diferencia, su mejor mes de la temporada y es similar a sus mejores marcas como MVP.
Anuncio
Da boletos el 16% de sus apariciones en el plato y se poncha sólo el 8,5% de las veces.
Su enfoque en el plato luce excelente, con buenas decisiones de swing y un esforzado dominio de la zona de strike que empuja a los lanzadores a realizar lanzamientos más desafiantes de los que desearían.
Cuando hace swing, tiene 32 bolas aceptablemente golpeadas este mes y la velocidad de salida promedio es de 92.6 mph, la más entrada del año hasta el momento.
Por qué los Dodgers necesitaban esta producción de Betts
Para sorpresa de nadie, Betts fue el mejor bateador del equipo en septiembre. Su wRC+ solo rivaliza con Josue De Paula, aunque el tamaño de su muestra fue mucho más pequeño que el de Betts.
Anuncio
Shohei Ohtani se perdió la viejo parte del mes por una ultraje en el padrino derecho, mientras que Andy Pages asimismo se perdió la viejo parte del mes y regresó solo en los últimos días.
Por otra parte, Freddie Freeman y Tommy Edman se han vuelto prácticamente fríos, lo que solo aumenta aún más la escazes de que alguno dé un paso al frente.
Betts ha sido el hombre que ha llevado la ataque, con 25 carreras ponderadas creadas, según FanGraphs, la viejo cantidad en el equipo, superado por Teoscar Hernández, quien tiene 19.
Con su surgimiento y la caída de Edman, Betts asumió el puesto de primer bate hasta que Ohtani regresó, y su maniobra ha sido tan bueno que incluso luego del regreso de la superestrella japonesa, el manager Dave Roberts todavía mantiene a Betts como líder contra los zurdos.
Anuncio
¿Podrá Betts sustentar esto en la postemporada?
Betts tiene un historial de mejorar durante los playoffs. En su primera temporada con los Dodgers, bateó .296/.378/.493 con OPS+ de 135 hasta octubre, cuando los Dodgers ganaron la Serie Mundial.
2021 fue más de lo mismo, bateando .319/.377/.404 con 116 wRC+. 2022 y 2023 terminaron temprano para los Dodgers y Betts tuvo problemas entreambos primaveras.
En 2024, cuando los Dodgers ganaron uno de sus primeros títulos consecutivos, Betts estuvo mágico, bateando .290/.387/.585 con 151 wRC+.
Durante la viejo parte de la temporada, Betts no fue lo que los fanáticos de Mookie esperaban, con un bautizo promedio de la muérdago y una gran defensa en el campocorto.
Anuncio
A partir de mediados de agosto y hasta septiembre, cambió el estandarte y dejó al manager Dave Roberts impresionado y sorprendido.
“No podría decirte que vi esto [coming]”, dijo Roberts. “Pero se ha vuelto más esforzado. Ha trabajado duro en eso… Y el hecho de que todo salga aceptablemente ha sido increíble. Simplemente no importa dónde lo golpees, a quién se enfrenta, [what’s] la situación… está tomando buenos turnos al bate”.
Betts, mientras tanto, sabía que su antigua producción a nivel de Tahúr Más Valioso todavía estaba en él.
“Sé que todavía soy capaz de hacerlo”, dijo Betts. “Sé que estaba ahí en alguna parte”.
De cara a octubre, pocos bateadores deberían hacer apreciar mejor a los fanáticos.
Su experiencia, anejo con su nueva producción, deberían ayudarlo a encajar en la fórmula, anejo con el pitcheo abridor de calidad, que lo colocará a él y a los Dodgers de 2026 en la inmortalidad de la MLB.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts is having a crazy September at the plate, and he looks like someone who can carry the offense in the postseason.
Betts’ Crazy September
Betts is hitting .367 in September entering Friday, with 21 RBIs, six home runs, and nine doubles.
He has a 1.117 OPS and a 219 wRC+, both metrics highlighting just how elite he has been. It has been his best month of the season by far, and it is akin to his MVP bests.
He is walking 16% of plate appearances and striking out on just 8.5% of the time.
His approach at the plate looks great, with good swing decisions and a strong command of the strike zone that pushes pitchers to throw more challenging pitches than they would want.
When he does swing, he has 32 hard-hit balls this month, and the average exit velocity is 92.6 mph, the highest of the year thus far.
Why the Dodgers needed this production from Betts
To no one’s surprise, Betts was the team’s best hitter in September. His wRC+ is only rivaled by Josue De Paula, though his sample size was much smaller than Betts’.
Shohei Ohtani missed most of the month with a right-arm injury, while Andy Pages also missed the majority of the month, returning only in the last few days.
Additionally, Freddie Freeman and Tommy Edman have gone mostly cold, only further increasing the need for someone to step up.
Betts has been the guy to carry the offense, with 25 weighted runs created, according to FanGraphs, the most on the team, second to Teoscar Hernandez, who has 19.
With his emergence and Edman’s slump, Betts took over the leadoff spot until Ohtani returned, and his play has been so good that even after the Japanese superstar returned, manager Dave Roberts still has Betts lead off against lefties.
Can Betts keep this up in the postseason?
Betts has a track record of stepping up during the playoffs. In his first season with the Dodgers, he hit .296/.378/.493 with a 135 OPS+ through October, when the Dodgers won the World Series.
2021 was more of the same, hitting .319/.377/.404 with a 116 wRC+. 2022 and 2023 ended early for the Dodgers, and Betts struggled both years.
In 2024, when the Dodgers won one of their first consecutive titles, Betts was magical, hitting .290/.387/.585 with a 151 wRC+.
For most of the season, Betts wasn’t the Mookie fans expected, with league-average hitting and great defense at shortstop.
Starting in mid-August and into September, he flipped the script and left manager Dave Roberts impressed and surprised.
“I couldn’t tell you that I saw this [coming],” Roberts said. “But he’s got stronger. He’s worked hard on that … And just for it to come together has been great. It just doesn’t matter where you hit him, who he’s facing, [what’s] the situation –– he’s taking good at-bats.”
Betts, meanwhile, knew his former MVP-level production was still in him.
“I know I’m still capable of it,” Betts said. “I know it was in there somewhere.”
Heading into October, few hitters should make fans feel better.
His experience, along with his newfound production, should help him fit into the formula, alongside the quality starting pitching, that puts him and the 2026 Dodgers into MLB immortality.
