item.content:encoded:
Redacción Deportes, 25 sep (EFE).- El japonés Shohei Ohtani, estrella de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, volvió a ser el jugador con la camiseta más vendida de las Grandes Ligas, una posición que ocupa por cuarto año consecutivo, según la lista publicada este viernes por MLB y MLB Players, Inc. (Mlbpi).
Ohtani se convirtió así en el primer jugador desde que MLB comenzó a registrar las ventas en 2010, que encadena cuatro temporadas como líder en comercialización de camisetas.
PUBLICIDAD
Desde 2023, los aficionados han comprado la camiseta Nike de Ohtani más que cualquier otra en Estados Unidos, Japón y el resto del mundo, consolidando al jugador japonés como la figura con mayor demanda comercial entre los peloteros de las Grandes Ligas.
El listado, elaborado a partir de las ventas de camisetas Nike realizadas a través de Fanatics, incluido MLBShop.com, desde el Día Inaugural de la temporada 2026, sitúa al capitán de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Judge, en el segundo puesto y al jardinero de los Cachorros de Chicago Pete Crow-Armstrong en el tercero.
PUBLICIDAD
Crow-Armstrong, quien esta temporada se convirtió en el séptimo jugador en la historia de las Mayores y el primero de los Cachorros en conectar al menos 40 jonrones y robar 40 bases, alcanzó el mejor puesto para un jugador de Chicago desde que el puertorriqueño Javier Báez fue tercero en 2018.
El listado también refleja la presencia de otras figuras de alcance internacional. El venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr., de los Bravos de Atlanta, ocupa el cuarto lugar, seguido por el dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., de los Padres de San Diego.
Los Dodgers colocaron a tres jugadores entre los diez primeros, con Ohtani al frente, Freddie Freeman en el sexto puesto y Mookie Betts en el octavo. El japonés Yoshinobu Yamamoto, también de Los Ángeles, aparece noveno.
La temporada 2026 marcó además un registro inédito para los jugadores japoneses, con tres de ellos entre los 20 primeros de la clasificación, después de que el toletero Munetaka Murakami, de los Medias Blancas de Chicago, debutara en el vigésimo puesto.
PUBLICIDAD
Yamamoto, por su parte, ocupa el noveno lugar, mientras que Ohtani mantiene el liderazgo de una clasificación que vuelve a poner de manifiesto su dimensión dentro y fuera del terreno de juego.
La lista se conoce antes del inicio de las Series de Comodines de ambas ligas, que comenzarán el próximo martes 29 de septiembre, con Ohtani, Judge y Crow-Armstrong entre las principales figuras de unos equipos que ya tienen asegurado su boleto a la Postemporada. EFE
PUBLICIDAD

New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge was second for the second straight season, MLB and the players' association affiliate MLB Players, Inc. said Friday. Judge finished third in 2023 and '24. item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Shohei Ohtani has become the first player to lead Major League Baseball jersey sales at the end of four straight seasons since the sport started tracking figures in 2010, among four players in the top 20 on the two-time World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers.
New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge was second for the second straight season, MLB and the players' association affiliate MLB Players, Inc. said Friday. Judge finished third in 2023 and '24.
Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs was third, up from 16th at the end of last season, and Atlanta's Ronald Acuña Jr. was fourth, an increase from 11th last year.
San Diego's Fernando Tatis Jr. was fifth, followed by the Dodgers' Freddie Freeman, Philadelphia's Bryce Harper, the Dodgers' Mookie Betts and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and the New York Mets' Juan Soto.
Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox was 20th, and he joined with Ohtani and Yamamoto to become the first trio of Japanese players in the top 20.
Texas' Corey Seager was 11th, followed by Toronto's Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Boston's Adley Rutschman, the Phillies' Kyle Schwarber, Pittsburgh's Paul Skenes, Seattle's Cal Raleigh, Cincinnati's Elly De La Cruz, San Diego's Jackson Merrill and Arizona's Nolan Arenado.
MLB's list tracked sales on Fanatics' sites, including MLBShop.com, since opening day.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Freddie Freeman on Finding his Swing in the Nick of Time
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman believes he’s finally beginning to rediscover his swing, and with the Dodgers having secured a first-round bye into the NLDS, the veteran first baseman is encouraged by what he’s seeing from his teammates as October approaches. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman believes he’s finally beginning to rediscover his swing, and with the Dodgers having secured a first-round bye into the NLDS, the veteran first baseman is encouraged by what he’s seeing from his teammates as October approaches.
Freeman collected two hits in Thursday night’s 4-1 loss to the Padres, both coming after he made an adjustment during his third plate appearance. He explained afterward that he’s starting to feel more comfortable using his lower half, something that had been missing from his swing during his recent struggles.
“I know the last couple of at-bats, a little better. Got more in my legs,” Freeman said. “So, trying to make adjustments pitch to pitch. Just trying to get a feel, and felt something on a foul ball in my third at-bat.”
“Took it into the next couple pitches, got a hit. Took it into the next at-bat, got a hit. So I’ll take it into tomorrow.”
Getting Hot at the Right Time
Although the Dodgers dropped the final two games of their series against San Diego, Freeman is encouraged by the individual performances he’s seeing throughout the lineup, particularly from Shohei Ohtani and Mookie Betts.
“I’m just encouraged with Shohei getting a couple of hits, Mookie staying hot,” Freeman said. “That’s really what it’s all about. Guys getting hot right now.”
“We got the first-round bye, so play some good baseball this weekend and take it into next week.”
Freeman also praised Ohtani’s return to the lineup, including the hard contact he made against Padres closer Mason Miller during Wednesday’s game.
“It’s nice for Shohei to come out there and get some hits. That ball off Mason Miller was special, so I know that would feel good for him,” Freeman said.
“Mookie’s been hot. Teo’s been swinging the bat great. Will’s been really good lately, too. So a couple of us can add on to it, and Kyle, obviously, he’s been really good the last month, too. So we’ve got a good stretch going.”
The first baseman also provided a reassuring update about his own health. Asked about the condition of his knee, Freeman offered a simple response.
“Knee’s good. I feel nothing.”
When asked whether the issue was now yesterday’s news, he confirmed that it was.
“Yeah. Yeah. All good.”
Freeman Isn’t Concerned About the Dodgers’ Record Against Playoff Teams
One of the more interesting exchanges came when Freeman was asked about the Dodgers’ struggles against quality opponents during the second half of the season.
Since their series victories over the Yankees and Phillies, the Dodgers have struggled to win series against teams with winning records, including the Padres, who took two of three at Dodger Stadium this week.
Freeman, however, isn’t particularly interested in revisiting those results.
“I wouldn’t have even known unless you guys asked,” he said. “All we care about is playing good this weekend, these three games, and take that in.”
“It doesn’t matter who we’re playing on Saturday or what we’ve done against those teams. It’s all out the window from Saturday. It’s game on there, but playing good baseball is a good option. Positive things going into the off week.”
It’s an understandable perspective from a veteran who knows that regular-season results offer little comfort once the postseason begins. The Dodgers will certainly have to start producing more runs against elite pitching staffs, but Freeman’s focus is on getting the entire lineup clicking when the games matter most.
A Well-Earned Opportunity to Rest
Freeman also emphasized the importance of the first-round bye, particularly for a team that has endured the physical demands of another long season.
“I think rest for all of us is always nice,” he said. “We’ve been grinding since February, getting ready for the season. Then you go through a 162-game schedule. It’s a lot.”
“So we played really good baseball for six or eight months, and we get rewarded for that. So we’ll take it in and rest up and get ourselves ready to go for Saturday.”
With several key players having returned from injuries in recent weeks, the opportunity to rest and prepare rather than immediately enter a Wild Card series could be especially valuable.
Four Number One Starters
Perhaps Freeman’s most emphatic response came when a reporter referred to another member of the Dodgers’ rotation as the team’s number four starter.
Freeman wasn’t having any of that.
“We have four number one starters. That’s what we have,” he said. “I don’t think anybody is going to be one, two, three or four. They’re all ready to go, and whatever role they’re going to be deployed in the NLDS, we got four starters.”
“So I think our guys, we got four number ones. If you want to call him a number four, you can call him a number four, but they’re all number ones.”
It’s a sentiment that should resonate with Dodger fans after watching the recent performances of Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow. The starting rotation appears to be coming together at an ideal time, and Freeman clearly has confidence in the arms that will be taking the mound in October.
For now, Freeman’s priorities are straightforward: carry his recent improvements into the final weekend, get the rest he’s earned, and prepare for the NLDS.
And if a few more Dodgers can find their swings along the way, all the better.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
The AL and NL Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie begins Tuesday, Sept. 29 with many of MLB’s most popular players preparing to take center stage. Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Aaron Judge of the New York Yankees and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs are leading the league in most popular player jerseys as their respective Clubs enter the final weekend of the regular season with Postseason berths secured.
Ohtani’s popularity reached new heights as he became the first player to finish four straight seasons with the most popular player jersey in the Majors since tracking began in 2010. Since 2023, fans have purchased Ohtani’s Nike jersey more than any other in the U.S., Japan and worldwide. With Dodgers teammate and reigning Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s jersey ranking no. 9 and Chicago White Sox All-Star slugger Munetaka Murakami debuting on the list at no. 20, this is also the first season that three MLB Players from Japan have their jerseys in the top 20.
After becoming only the seventh player in MLB history and first Cubs player to hit at least 40 home runs and steal at least 40 bases in a single season, Crow-Armstrong’s jersey finished as the third most popular of the season – the highest ranking for a Cubs star since Javier Báez finished third in 2018.
This list, released jointly today by MLB and MLB Players, Inc. (MLBPI), accounts for sales of Nike jerseys from the Fanatics network of sites, including MLBShop.com, since Opening Day of the 2026 Championship Season.

item.title: [FanSided] Why MLB fans should root for Roki Sasaki in the playoffs, not revel in Dodgers downfall
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Crossing the Pacific Ocean and signing with the Los Angeles Dodgers meant cultural and personal transitions for prized Japanese import Roki Sasaki. But when Sasaki officially met the U.S. media in early 2025, he made it clear he and his newest fanbase had two things in common: baseball and grief. At the time, California was still recovering from the January 2025
item.content:encoded:
Crossing the Pacific Ocean and signing with the Los Angeles Dodgers meant cultural and personal transitions for prized Japanese import Roki Sasaki.
But when Sasaki officially met the U.S. media in early 2025, he made it clear he and his newest fanbase had two things in common: baseball and grief.
Sasaki returned from the injured list this week just as a March 2025 story by the Dodgers’ official website resurfaced on social media. At the time, California was still recovering from the January 2025 wildfires that ravaged the Los Angeles area, an unfortunately familiar sight for their newest pitcher.
Nearly 15 years earlier, Sasaki lost his father, grandparents, and his family’s home in the March 2011 tsunami. He turned to baseball as an escape, just as so many others affected by tragedy often do.
"Los Angeles is facing challenging and difficult times right now,” Sasaki said in January 2025, “and as a member of the Dodgers, starting today, I am dedicated to give my best and strive forward together with the people of the city."
Baseball fans can support Roki Sasaki without rooting for the Los Angeles Dodgers
This might sound contradictory, but hear us out.
We just saw Mets fans overwhelmingly cheer for Pete Alonso, even after he smashed a game-tying home run. Citi Field cared far more about Alonso the player than it did the Orioles as a team. Had the Orioles somehow snuck into the postseason, we imagine there’d be plenty of Mets fans with even the slightest rooting interest.
The same principle — or, at least, an extremely similar one — easily applies to Sasaki. Forget the fact he signed with the reigning World Series champions and played a pivotal role during last year’s title run. He’s still a human being with emotions who went through a horrifically traumatic experience; nearly 20,000 people are believed to have died in the Great East Japan Earthquake, and over 2,550 people remained missing as of 2021.
And above all else, Sasaki hasn’t done anything wrong beyond struggling to hit the strike zone. But compare that to some of the other notable names we’ll see this postseason. San Diego’s Fernando Tatis Jr. and Ramón Laureano each served PED-related suspensions. Boston’s Jarren Duran has feuded with fans and media in a way Red Sox Nation eventually stopped defending.
We’ve long been critical of both Sasaki and how the Dodgers have refused to make him a full-time reliever. Dave Roberts confirmed earlier this week the 24-year-old will pitch out of the bullpen during the postseason, just as he did last October, and the first impressions were positive; Sasaki threw a scoreless inning and didn’t allow a walk against the Padres on Tuesday night.
We wouldn’t blame you for hoping the Dodgers lose in the NLDS. They’re a superteam seeking their third consecutive championship and fourth in six years. At least three players on the active roster — Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, and Mookie Betts — are widely considered locks for the Hall of Fame, and Tarik Skubal is well on his way.
But when Sasaki comes in from the bullpen, try not to be overly hard on him. Save your vitriol for the umpires and broadcasters.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers clinch No. 2 seed and important playoff bye despite loss to Padres
item.dc:creator: Kevin Baxter
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener. - The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning. - The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener.
- The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning.
- The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more than 4 million fans to Dodger Stadium this season.
The Dodgers didn’t win Thursday. But they got something far more valuable before they even took the field for their 4-2 loss to the San Diego Padres.
With the Atlanta Braves’ loss to the Cincinnati Reds earlier in the day, the Dodgers clinched the second seed in the National League playoffs and the first-round bye that goes with it. That means the Dodgers will get five days off next week to prepare for their playoff opener, a godsend for a bruised and bloodied team that has stumbled to the finish of the regular season.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said of the break. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here, a lot of aches and pains this year.”
For the Padres (89-70), the victory was important because it clinched a wild-card berth and a franchise-record third consecutive trip to the postseason.
In addition to Freeman, who has been hobbled all month by a sore right knee, the Dodgers are rushing to get designated hitter Shohei Ohtani and closer Edwin Díaz healthy. Both had big games Thursday with Ohtani going two for five with a run batted in, the first time he’s had multiple hits or an RBI in more than a month. Díaz, meanwhile, pitched a perfect ninth, striking out two.
Other players also are getting healthy. Center fielder Andy Pages, who missed a month with a broken hand, returned to the lineup three days ago. Dalton Rushing, who is competing for a bench spot on the postseason roster, is expected to be activated off the injured list Friday. Left-hander Blake Snell, who came out of his last start nine days ago after just an inning, will make his final postseason tuneup Saturday.
All of them will benefit from some additional rest before their playoff opener, at Dodger Stadium, on Oct. 3.
And speaking of Dodger Stadium, the No. 2 playoff seed carries another important perk: the home-field advantage for the Division Series — and possibly the World Series, if the Dodgers make it that far. Home has certainly been an advantage for the Dodgers, who drew a sellout crowd of 53,027 Thursday, pushing the team’s total home attendance over 4 million for the second straight year.
“It’s more turning of the turnstiles than any venue in the world,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The amazing thing is that it’s not just localized. It’s international. Everyone looks different at Dodger Stadium.
“It’s spectacular and our players certainly feed off of it.”
The Dodgers are one of five franchises in big-league history to draw more than 4 million fans in a season but just two others — the Toronto Blue Jays, from 1991-93, and the New York Yankees, in the final four years at old Yankee Stadium — did it in consecutive seasons.
And the Dodgers are the only team to do it since 2008. They also lead the majors in road attendance this season, having drawn 2.82 million, or 36,159 a game. For some fans, it’s hard to separate their support from the team’s success.
“A synergy exists between we the fans and the players,” said Charles Flores, an associate professor at Cal State L.A. and lifelong Dodgers fan who attended more than a dozen games this season. “One inspires the other.”
Russ Hoffman of Santa Clarita, a season-ticket holder for 40 years, agrees.
“The atmosphere created by drawing so many fans definitely contributes to their success,” he said. “Winning continuously drives the attendance and the current ownership has committed the assets to do that.”
That edge can be even bigger in the playoffs. The Dodgers lost just five of 16 postseason games at home — a .688 winning percentage — en route to World Series titles the last two years.
“During the playoffs, Dodger Stadium is a tough place to play because it’s 56,000 crazed fans yelling on every play,” said Stan Brooks, an award-winning film producer and longtime season-ticket holder. “The fans are so loud and the environment is so intense every night.”
The Dodgers (97-62) will finish the regular season with three games this weekend in San Francisco, where they will continue their preparation for the postseason.
In the final home game of the regular season Mookie Betts, dropped to second in the lineup with Ohtani’s return, went three for four with a walk, raising his average for September to .367, while Freeman had two hits for the third time in four games.
“I’m just encouraged with Shohei getting a couple hits, Mookie staying hot. That’s what it’s all about,” Freeman said. “Getting hot right now.
“That’s all we were looking forward to this last week is getting our guys back on the field.”
That didn’t add up to much offense Thursday, with the Dodgers stranding eight runners and going 0 for 8 with men in scoring position through eight innings. They avoided their first shutout of the season at home on Adrian Morejon’s balk in the eighth before Ohtani doubled in the second run with two outs in the ninth.
For the past 17 years, Chaz Perea and his four-person crew have been responsible for every bit of stadium landscaping that isn’t the field itself.
On the mound, Tyler Glasnow, who will be the Dodgers’ fourth starter in the postseason, was perfect through three innings. He walked Fernando Tatis Jr. on four pitches to start the fourth but didn’t allow another Padres batter to reach base until Ethan Salas singled with one out in the sixth.
That proved costly when Tatis singled on the next pitch, sending Salas to third, from where he scored on Dustin Harris’ sacrifice fly, putting the Padres ahead to stay.
Glasnow (5-2) got out of the inning by striking out Manny Machado, giving him a season-high 11 strikeouts and 21 in his last two starts. But San Diego then blew the game open in the seventh, chasing Glasnow and scoring three times off reliever Justin Wrobleski on run-scoring singles by Austin Hayes, Salas and Tatis.
Staff writer Maddie Lee contributed to this report.

item.title: [sandiegouniontribune.com] Padres beat Dodgers to clinch third straight postseason berth
item.dc:creator: Kevin Acee
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Finally, they are in. The Padres spent sizable portions of this season seemingly on the edge of collapse every few weeks before surging back into contention. So being no-hit for five innings and then suddenly building a sizable lead and then holding on in a frenzied finish to the game that clinched their playoff berth seemed about right. The Padres got their first hit and their first run in the sixth inning and scored three more times in the seventh before turning the game over to
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Finally, they are in.
The Padres spent sizable portions of this season seemingly on the edge of collapse every few weeks before surging back into contention.
So being no-hit for five innings and then suddenly building a sizable lead and then holding on in a frenzied finish to the game that clinched their playoff berth seemed about right.
The Padres got their first hit and their first run in the sixth inning and scored three more times in the seventh before turning the game over to the back end of their bullpen to preserve a 4-2 victory.
Their high-leverage relievers were the strength and the most consistent part of their team all season, so it was also fitting that Jason Adam, Adrian Morejón and Mason Miller strung together the final three innings to get the Padres into the playoffs for a third consecutive season.
It is the first time in team history the Padres have qualified for three consecutive postseasons and just the 10th time they will head to the playoffs in their 58 years of existence.
This was the second time in this three-year span that the Padres were spraying champagne in the visitors’ clubhouse at Dodger Stadium, the site of so many glum postgames over the years.
The Padres had reached base just once, on a walk, in five innings against Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow.
Then, suddenly, they took a lead with the major contributions being a single by a rookie who joined them on Sept. 1 and a sacrifice fly by a journeyman who was called up on Aug. 24.
The Padres’ first hit of the night was Ethan Salas’ flare the other way and just over the left side of the infield with one out in the sixth inning.
Fernando Tatis Jr. followed with a single grounded through the right side that sent Salas to third base, and Dustin Harris then hit a fly ball to center field that put the Padres up 1-0.
Yuki Matsui, who had gotten the final out in the fifth inning, got the first two outs in the sixth before Jason Adam threw one pitch to get the third out.
A one-out double in the seventh inning by Jackson Merrill off Glasnow and a pinch-hit single by Austin Hays after lefty Justin Wrobleski entered the game extended the Padres’ lead, and two-out singles by Salas and Tatis extended it further.
Adam retired the first two batters in the seventh. Morejón got the final out that inning and allowed a run in the eighth. Miller’s 38th save was earned with a four-out ninth inning in which the Dodgers scored again.
After Tommy Edman reached base when he swung through a slider that bounced past Salas, Shohei Ohtani doubled Edman home before Mookie Betts grounded out.
Padres starter Nick Pivetta matched Glasnow where it mattered most — on the scoreboard — for as long as he could.
He was pulled after yielding a two-out single in the fifth inning, and Matsui surrendered a single to Freddie Freeman before striking out Teoscar Hernández.
The Dodgers found out before the game that they had clinched a first-round bye in the playoffs, so they are essentially playing out the season to stay in shape.
Exactly three years after the Padres clinched a playoff berth with a victory at Dodger Stadium, they were playing on Thursday for the right to continue playing.
They are now striving over the next three days for the right to host their best-of-three National League Wild Card Series.
They are in position to do so, a game ahead of the Cubs, who also clinched a playoff berth Thursday. Because the Cubs won the series between the teams, the Padres have to finish a game ahead of the Cubs in the standings in order to remain the No.4 seed.

item.title: [aol.com] Alex Bregman's wild MLB playoff streak has star in rare air – injured face willing - AOL

item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball’s playoffs are coming soon and Alex Bregman will be a part of it.
Of course he is.
Bregman made baseball history Thursday, Sept. 24 when the Chicago Cubs clinched a National League wild-card berth with a victory over the Miami Marlins. And for the 10th consecutive year, injured eye willing, Bregman will take part in the postseason, this time with a twist.
Bregman, the Cubs’ 32-year-old third baseman, will become the first position player to play postseason baseball 10 consecutive seasons with multiple teams. In fact, he’s done it with three ballclubs – eight straight years with the Houston Astros and then the past two with the Boston Red Sox and Cubs, as he settled for good in Chicago by signing a five-year, $175 million contract in January.
And it seems like wherever Bregman goes, October baseball follows.
Texas loves him anyway
Bregman was a two-time All-Star and two-time champion in Houston, the brash young slugger in his first full season when they won the 2017 World Series, the MVP runner-up when they lost the 2019 Series in seven games.
After bearing much of the scorn for the club’s 2017 sign-stealing scandal, he was the chastened veteran on the 2022 squad that won a second World Series, this time without a cloud of controversy to follow.
Yet Bregman’s chops as a club cornerstone gained greater veracity a year ago, when he left the Astros and, combining his production with his baseball smarts and clubhouse gravitas, lifted the Red Sox to the postseason for the first time in three years as the Astros missed the playoffs for the first time since 2016.
Those vibes were as attractive to the Cubs as Bregman’s career .846 OPS when they pursued him after he opted out of his contract with Boston. And it’s all come together in Wrigleyville: Thanks to a second-half surge, Bregman has hit 26 home runs, posted an .804 OPS and produced 5.4 WAR, second only to presumed MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong on the Cubs.
“Anytime Alex Bregman is playing an Alex Bregman brand of baseball, it’s just good for the program,” Crow-Armstrong told USA TODAY Sports last month.
And if he manages to play just days after suffering a gruesome eye injury, the legend will only grow.
Heroes of the fall
Bregman’s postseason constancy has put himself among some legendary and curious October stalwarts.
Advertisement
Unsurprisingly, the consecutive postseasons list is littered with alumni from the three dominant playoff groups of the wild-card era: The 1990s Atlanta Braves, the late-century New York Yankees and the current batch of Los Angeles Dodgers.
Yankees closer Mariano Rivera tops the list, appearing in 13 consecutive postseasons from 1995-2007, followed by Derek Jeter, whose 12-year streak began a year after Rivera’s playoff debut.
Catcher Jorge Posada and Braves Hall of Famers Chipper Jones and Tom Glavine all played in 11 consecutive postseasons. As did lefty reliever Mike Stanton, who did it with four teams – the Braves, Red Sox, Yankees and Texas Rangers – between 1991-2002.
Who let him in?
Bregman, longtime Dodgers closer Kenley Jansen and Hall of Famer Greg Maddux all reached 10 consecutive postseasons. Current Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman and longtime third baseman Justin Turner are at the nine-year mark, Freddie winning a World Series championship with Atlanta in 2021 and two more in L.A. the past two seasons.
Retired Dodgers lefty Clayton Kershaw leads the “but for” category: He pitched in eight consecutive postseasons from 2013-2020, and would have made it 13 in a row if not for injuries in 2021 and 2024. Same with Braves Hall of Famer John Smoltz – he was present for all of Atlanta’s 14 consecutive division titles yet underwent Tommy John surgery in 2000.
And several likely 2026 participants had streaks broken thanks to one unlucky season – such as slugger Kyle Schwarber, who’d be working on a 12-year streak with the Cubs, Red Sox and Phillies if not for the 2019 Cubs missing the playoffs. Same with Mookie Betts, ticketed for his 10th postseason in 11 years with the Dodgers and Boston, missing only in ’19 with the Red Sox.
The wild-card format – which began in 1995 and expanded in 2012 and 2022 – makes this list unavoidably modern due to the expanded access it affords. Still, some players from past eras were near-constants in the playoffs.
Mr. October himself, Reggie Jackson, reached the postseason 10 times in 12 years from 1971 to 1982, winning four World Series with the Oakland Athletics and New York Yankees, and then, just for kicks, reaching the 1982 ALCS with the California Angels.
The great Yogi Berra was a 10-time World Series champion, but his longest consecutive streak of playoff runs was five years. Yet reaching the World Series 14 times in 17 years, when only two teams reached the playoffs, remains a stunning feat.
So perhaps Bregman - even with 102 career postseason games, 19 homers, 91 hits and a .791 OPS - has a little more work to do to match some of the legends of October. Yet from Houston to Boston to Chicago, he’s leaving little doubt that wherever he goes, winning follows.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Alex Bregman's wild MLB playoff streak has star in rare air – injured face willing

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers already step closer to World Series three-peat, even before playoffs begin
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: The Dodgers are already another step closer to a third straight World Series. Thanks to the Braves’ loss to the Reds on Thursday night, the Dodgers were assured of finishing the season with a top-two record in the National League, clinching a first-round bye that ensures they will not be subjected to a best-of-three wild-card series next week. Instead, the Dodgers will begin their postseason quest in the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 3, holding home-field ad
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are already another step closer to a third straight World Series.
Thanks to the Braves’ loss to the Reds on Thursday night, the Dodgers were assured of finishing the season with a top-two record in the National League, clinching a first-round bye that ensures they will not be subjected to a best-of-three wild-card series next week.
Instead, the Dodgers will begin their postseason quest in the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 3, holding home-field advantage for that best-of-five series as they go for the first three-peat by an NL team in MLB history.
First-round byes have not always been kind to the Dodgers.
After MLB expanded its postseason field five years ago — creating a five-day layoff for the top-two seeds in each league between the end of the regular season and the start of their playoff schedules — the Dodgers were knocked out in the NLDS as a bye team in 2022 and 2023. Both years, questions about the negative side effects of the weeklong break loomed large in the wake of their elimination.
Thus, after receiving a bye again in 2024, the team altered its off-week schedule, incorporating more simulated game activities and making a concerted effort to spend more time at the ballpark together on workout days.
It paid off in that year’s division series, when the Dodgers overcame a two-games-to-one deficit to the Padres en route to the first of their back-to-back titles.
Last year, the team failed to earn a top-two seed but swept the Reds in two games in the wild-card series to begin their World Series defense.
This season, securing a bye became a critical objective for the club down the stretch. The last thing their aging roster needed was two extra playoff games. Ongoing injuries to Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman also amplified the importance of getting extra time off ahead of another October gauntlet.
“It’s always helpful in the sense of giving your guys a break to reset,” manager Dave Roberts said earlier this month. “But given all the tax and where our guys are healthwise, to get that week would be huge.”
The Dodgers, who entered Thursday with a 97-61 record, still have an outside shot at the NL’s No. 1 seed, as well, but would need to run the table over the season’s final weekend and have the Brewers — who currently hold MLB’s best record at 100-59 — get swept in their final series against the already-eliminated Cardinals.
“I think it’s more about just playing good baseball,” Roberts said this week when asked how much of a priority the top seed would be. “The last couple weeks, we’ve just played good baseball, and the fallout is this or that. We want to get the bye, and then if it happens that we keep playing well and we gain a couple games on the Brewers, great.”
Indeed, the club’s primary postseason seeding objectives have already been met. They’ve won their 13th NL West division title in the last 14 years. They’ve given themselves the shortest possible route through the playoffs. And now, they’ll have ample time next week to prepare for an unprecedented three-peat bid.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres are facing off in the rubber match of their three-game series on Thursday night with plenty at stake for both teams.
The Dodgers, who have already won the National League West division, can clinch a first-round bye with a win or Atlanta Braves loss over the season's final four games.
They're also still chasing the Milwaukee Brewers for the No. 1 seed, but will need some help to secure home-field advantage throughout the postseason.
As for the Padres, they're looking to clinch a postseason spot, with their magic number currently sitting at 1.
Thus, the winner of Thursday's game will be celebrating in some capacity. If it's the Padres, they'll be making a champagne and beer mess in the visitor's clubhouse at Dodger Stadium. If it's the Dodgers, they'll be shaking hands and looking forward to their five-day layoff beginning next week.
Dodgers vs Padres Pitching Matchup on Thursday
Right-handed pitcher Tyler Glasnow is taking the mound for the Dodgers in his final tune-up before the postseason.
Glasnow has been shaky since coming off the injured list at the end of August, sporting a 4.50 ERA over 28 innings with 38 strikeouts to 10 walks. Overall this season, he's 5-1 with a 3.46 ERA and 87 strikeouts across 67.2 innings (12 starts).
Glasnow is expected to be the team's No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
Opposite Glasnow will be Padres right-hander Nick Pivetta, who missed nearly five months this season with an elbow injury but has been incredibly sharp since returning.
In his three starts since coming off the IL, Pivetta has allowed just three runs over 14 innings for a 1.93 ERA. He has 11 strikeouts to one walk in that time.

The game will be broadcast on the radio on AM570 (in English) and KTNQ 1020 AM (in Spanish).

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] How Can Dodgers Legally Get Josue De Paula On Postseason Roster?
item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed
item.description: In an unprecedented move in the Andrew Friedman era, the Los Angeles Dodgers called up a position player directly from Double-A earlier this month: Josue De Paula. item.content:encoded:
In an unprecedented move in the Andrew Friedman era, the Los Angeles Dodgers called up a position player directly from Double-A earlier this month: Josue De Paula.
De Paula is not a good defender, but his bat is off the charts. He has a great eye at the plate and dominated in Double-A. Still, the big leagues are a whole different thing. That has not seemed to bother De Paula, who has a 1.081 OPS in 11 games with 11 walks and just five strikeouts.
De Paula has gotten to serve as the designated hitter with Shohei Ohtani out, but that's about to change. His defense is not good enough to start in left field, and the Dodgers are not going to start him over Andy Pages, Teoscar Hernández or Kyle Tucker right now. However, he would still be a very valuable bat for the postseason, with the ability to get on base at a high clip.
There's one big problem, however. He was not on the 40-man roster on Sept. 1, which is the eligibility cutoff for the postseason. The Dodgers can still legally get De Paula on a postseason roster, but will need to petition the commissioner's office.
"A player who doesn't meet said criteria for postseason eligibility can still be added to a team's roster in the postseason via petition to the Commissioner's Office if the player was in the organization on Aug. 31 and is replacing someone who is on the injured list and has served the minimum amount of time required for activation," read Major League Baseball's rules for postseason eligibility. "(For example, a player on the 10-day injured list who has been on it for at least 10 days, or a player who has been on the 60-day injured list for at least 60 days.) Players who are acquired in September or after are ineligible."
De Paula is good on the first need, but the Dodgers would have to say he's replacing Dalton Rushing, who is the only current Dodger who has exceeded a minimum stay on the injured list. This would make sense, as Rushing may not be able to catch anyway and would be used as a pinch hitter. De Paula can fill that role.
More MLB: Dodgers' Freddie Freeman Explains Why Dodgers Need Bye This Year

I’m just happy I got hits w
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman delivered three RBI in the Dodgers’ 7-0 win over the Padres on Tuesday night, continuing his recent rebound at the plate. After struggling through much of September, the veteran first baseman appears to be finding his stroke just as the postseason approaches. Following the game, Freeman talked about his recent improvement, the Dodgers’ increasingly healthy lineup and the importance of securing a first-round bye.
“It’s a little better. I’m just happy I got hits when I needed to get hits. Today and the last couple of games have been a lot better, so hopefully we’re trending in the right direction when we need to.”
Freeman is also encouraged by what he’s seeing from the rest of the lineup, particularly with Andy Pages back from his hand injury and Shohei Ohtani expected to return Wednesday.
“It’s been really good. You’ve got guys swinging the bat who got off to tough starts. Kyle’s been great. Teo’s been hot. Guys are starting to come back that we’ve been missing over the last couple of weeks, too. It’s good to see Andy back, and Sho coming back tomorrow. A lot of good things happening for the offense lately.”
With the Dodgers’ magic number for clinching the National League’s second seed down to one, Freeman has his sights set on getting that job done.
“I feel like we’ve just been playing really good baseball as a group lately as well. We had to step up when guys went down, and that’s a credit to the guys that have been going. You want to be playing well going into the playoffs. We need one more win for that bye. That’s what we need. We need that, get some rest, and then have a great week of practicing going into the playoffs. Guys are swinging the bats at the right time, and hopefully we can carry that.”
Asked why the first-round bye is particularly important for this year’s club, Freeman laughed.
“I think we all know why it’s important. There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here. A lot of aches and pains this year. It’s good to get those guys back on the field and get some at-bats in them, then rest up and get some more at-bats during the live sessions and whatever we do during that week to get us ready for Saturday.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers won the World Series in 2024 with a first-round bye, and won it last year as the Nol. 3 seed, having to play in a Wild Card Series. They've shown they can win both ways, but a bye this year is a little more important. The Dodgers stars are only getting older, and with age comes wear and tear. The team has been pretty banged up, and it's no secret that they want the extra rest. "I think we all know why it's important," first baseman Freddie Freeman said, per Sporting Tribu
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers won the World Series in 2024 with a first-round bye, and won it last year as the Nol. 3 seed, having to play in a Wild Card Series.
They've shown they can win both ways, but a bye this year is a little more important. The Dodgers stars are only getting older, and with age comes wear and tear. The team has been pretty banged up, and it's no secret that they want the extra rest.
"I think we all know why it's important," first baseman Freddie Freeman said, per Sporting Tribune's Fredo Cervantes. "There's a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here. A lot of aches and pains this year."
Freeman is not kidding when he talks about the Dodgers "limping" to the finish line, even though he said it while chuckling. Shohei Ohtani is currently on the injured list, Freeman is playing through some knee issues, Andy Pages just got back in the lineup after a fractured hand and Blake Snell exited his last start after just one inning.
Not to mention the normal wear and tear a 162-game season takes on players. The Dodgers have the oldest lineup in baseball, and they could use a bye more than anyone. Not getting the bye would mean a date with either San Diego, Chicago, Philadelphia or Arizona in a best-of-three series.
Any of those matchups would be much tougher than the matchup the Dodgers had against the Cincinnati Reds in the Wild Card last year. Any one of those teams could upset the Dodgers in a Wild Card Series. However, it's hard to imagine a team coming out of a tough Wild Card Series and beating a rested Dodgers squad with its pitching lined up.

item.title: [heavy.com] Dodgers’ Freddie Freeman Makes Honest Admission Before Postseason
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dismantled the San Diego Padres 7-0 on Tuesday night at Dodger Stadium. Freddie Freeman led the charge, going 2-for-4 with three RBIs in an offense that produced nine hits and four walks against one of the best pitching staffs in the National League.
The Dodgers are 97-60. Their magic number to clinch a first-round playoff bye is one. A win over the Padres on Wednesday or an Atlanta Braves loss to the Reds gets them there.
For most teams, a bye is a nice bonus. For these Dodgers, Freeman made clear it is something far more necessary than that.
Freeman’s Candid Assessment
Freeman was asked after Tuesday’s win why securing the bye matters so much to this team.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” Freeman said. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here. A lot of aches and pains this year.”
The Dodgers have dealt with injuries at nearly every position this season. Shohei Ohtani just spent two weeks on the injured list with knee, biceps, and neck issues. Andy Pages missed a month with a fractured hand. Blake Snell has been building back from his own absence. Tyler Glasnow has never made it through a full regular season without an injury since joining the organization.
What the Bye Provides
The Dodgers have won the World Series in each of the last two seasons. They know how October works. They also know what happens when a team enters the postseason at less than full strength.
A first-round bye would give the Dodgers nearly a week off before the Division Series. It allows pitchers to reset their arms. It allows hitters coming off the injured list, Ohtani and Pages, to get additional at-bats in intrasquad games rather than jumping straight into a high-leverage series.
Freeman’s three-RBI performance on Tuesday was a reminder that the lineup is dangerous when everyone is healthy and clicking. Will Smith and Tommy Edman each homered. Mookie Betts added an RBI double. Kyle Tucker picked up a hit. The pieces are there. The question is whether they can stay on the field long enough to use them.
“We’re playing good baseball,” Freeman said. “We need to carry it on for the next five games.”
Final Word for the Dodgers
The Dodgers are built to win another championship. The talent is there. The pitching is there. The experience is there. What they need now is time. Time to heal. Time to reset. And time to arrive at the postseason as close to full strength as possible.
One more win and the bye is theirs. Freeman made the case for why nothing matters more right now.

item.title: [sandiegosun.com] MLB roundup: Drew Rasmussen helps Rays smother Yankees for AL East title
item.description:
Field Level Media
23 Sep 2026, 12:25 GMT+10
(Photo credit: Brad Penner) Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader. The Rays won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games. Yandy
item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 12:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader.
The Rays won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games. Yandy Diaz drove in four runs on a pair of singles.
Rasmussen (16-5) took a no-hitter into the seventh until Heliot Ramos opened the inning with a double to left for New York. Ramos eventually scored on an RBI single by rookie George Lombard Jr. off Kevin Kelly.
Rasmussen finished with 11 strikeouts for his fourth career double-digit strikeout performance. He finished two shy of his career-high set June 10 against the Boston Red Sox and the Rays won his 12th consecutive start.
Yankees 2, Rays 0 (Game 1)
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning as host New York recorded a shutout over Tampa Bay in the opener of a day-night doubleheader.
With the victory, the Yankees temporarily prevented the Rays from clinching the AL East and moved six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the American League's top wild-card spot.
New York's Carlos Rodon (7-3) scattered three singles over eight innings as the Yankees finished off the victory in a brisk 2 hours, 2 minutes. Rodon struck out eight in his 100th career win and also reached 1,500 strikeouts for his career. Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-5) allowed two runs on five hits over six innings with seven strikeouts to take his first loss since July 9.
Dodgers 7, Padres 0
Freddie Freeman drove in three runs, Will Smith and Tommy Edman hit home runs, and Los Angeles inched closer to the best record in the National League with a shutout of visiting San Diego.
Eight Dodgers pitchers held down the red-hot Padres offense in a bullpen game, with Justin Wrobleski (12-5) earning the win. Roki Sasaki struck out two in one inning in his return from a blister issue. The Dodgers extended their home winning streak to 11 games.
Los Angeles moved to within one game of the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers and reduced its magic number for a top-two NL spot and a bye into the National League Division Series to one. Luis Campusano had two hits for the Padres, whose magic number to clinch a playoff spot remained at two.
Phillies 6, Brewers 4
Bryson Stott delivered the tiebreaking hit in the eighth inning to guide Philadelphia to a victory over visiting Milwaukee. Brandon Marsh homered and knocked in three runs as the Phillies lowered their magic number to two to clinch a postseason berth.
Zack Wheeler ended up with a no-decision after striking out 11 while giving up three runs and five hits in 5 2/3 innings. Wheeler struck out the first seven batters he faced, setting a Phillies record for consecutive strikeouts to begin a game. His first-inning strikeout of Brice Turang was the 2,000th of his career.
The Brewers saw their lead over the Dodgers for the top record in the majors shrink to one as they lost just the third time in their last 13 games. William Contreras knocked in three runs.
Marlins 8, Cubs 2 (12 innings)
Griffin Conine plated the go-ahead run that ignited a six-run 12th inning for visiting Miami, which snapped a three-game losing by beating Chicago and postponing the Cubs' playoff celebration for at least a day.
On a night when runs were scarce until the final inning, both teams endured a pair of scoreless extra frames before Conine broke the drought with a leadoff, golf-shot single off Caleb Thielbar that fell just inside the left field line. Esteury Ruiz, the automatic runner, scored from second to make it 3-2 as the Marlins sent 10 batters to the plate in the inning.
The Cubs could have clinched a wild-card playoff spot with a win or Arizona loss, but neither of those happened keeping the Diamondbacks mathematically alive. Josh Ekness (3-4) struck out a pair in the 11th inning to get the win while Thielbar (3-4) gave up three runs -- two earned -- in his inning of work.
Guardians 3, Red Sox 2
Nathaniel Lowe drove in Chase DeLauter with a sacrifice fly in the ninth inning and Cleveland held on to beat host Boston in the first game of a three-game series.
Cleveland not only extended its winning streak to six but maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for first place in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings, his 14th straight start allowing three runs or fewer. Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings as the Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
White Sox 14, Royals 11
Chase Meidroth smacked a three-run home run among his three hits and drove in five, and Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk and Munetaka Murakami also homered to power Chicago past host Kansas City.
Chicago won for the fourth time in five games to remain one game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox, who hold the third and final AL wild-card spot, reduced their magic number to earn a playoff berth to three.
Vinnie Pasquantino hit a ninth-inning grand slam for the Royals, who lost their fifth straight. He went 3-for-5 with a double and also drove in five.
Nationals 3, Tigers 1
CJ Abrams hit a pair of home runs and drove in all three runs as visiting Washington topped Detroit. Abrams reached 100 RBIs for the season with his solo shot in the second inning, then broke a 1-1 tie in the seventh with his 33rd long ball of the season, a two-run blast.
Dylan Crews had two hits and scored the other run for the Nationals. Rookie Jackson Kent (2-4) earned the win in long relief. He allowed one run on six hits over four innings and struck out three. Opener Riley Cornelio lasted 2 2/3 innings, striking out four and walking three.
Ben Malgeri scored the Tigers' only run. Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark each had two hits.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 0
Jared Jones and two relievers combined on a one-hitter as Pittsburgh beat visiting St. Louis for a fifth straight win. Jones (5-6) lowered his ERA to 1.08 in four September starts and struck out nine with zero walks over seven innings while throwing 63 of his 86 pitches for strikes.
Pittsburgh broke a scoreless tie with two outs in the sixth inning on Ryan O'Hearn's RBI single against Andre Pallante (12-8). Pallante allowed one run on three hits with two walks and two strikeouts over six innings.
St. Louis struck out 14 times and lost for the fifth time in its last six games.
Astros 7, Mariners 0
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as Houston slugged and pitched its way past host Seattle.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros, who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the West. Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings of relief.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle. The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Reds 4, Braves 0
Brandon Williamson fired six scoreless innings and Cincinnati supported him with three solo homers to defeat host Atlanta in the opener of a three-game series.
Cincinnati ended a two-game losing streak and evened the season series with Atlanta at 2-2. Williamson (5-4) worked six scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two strikeouts. Elly De La Cruz (29), Dane Myers (8) and Eugenio Suarez (25) each hit a home run for the Reds. It was Suarez's 350th career homer, making him the 10th active player to reach that mark.
Atlanta starter JR Ritchie (1-4) pitched five innings and allowed one run on four hits and three walks. The rookie struck out a career-high eight batters.
Mets 6, Rangers 3
Francisco Alvarez laced a go-ahead two-run double in the sixth, then scored an insurance run on an unusual sacrifice fly for visiting New York, who damaged Texas' playoff hopes with a win in the opener of a three-game interleague series in Arlington.
Juan Soto had an RBI single in the third, and Carson Benge capped the scoring with a run-scoring double in the seventh for the Mets. The club won hours after removing the interim tag from manager Andy Green and signing him to a three-year extension.
Josh Jung had an RBI double in the third, and Elias Diaz and Wyatt Langford lofted sacrifice flies in the fourth for the Rangers, who entered Tuesday with a one-game lead over the Houston Astros in the AL West.
Diamondbacks 7, Rockies 2
Nolan Arenado homered and doubled among his three hits, Michael Soroka tossed seven strong innings, and Arizona kept its slim postseason hopes alive with a win over host Colorado in Denver.
Geraldo Perdomo also had three hits and Ildemaro Vargas finished with two hits for Arizona, which remains alive in the NL wild-card race, sitting four games behind Philadelphia, San Diego and the Chicago Cubs for the third and final spot with five games to go.
Mickey Moniak homered for Colorado, which finished with just three hits and just one after the third inning. The Rockies (57-100) are the first team to lose 100 or more games in four straight seasons since the 1962-65 New York Mets.
Twins 3, Giants 2
Walker Jenkins homered, Luke Keaschall contributed both offensively and defensively, and Minnesota evened its road interleague series against San Francisco.
Taj Bradley (12-6) combined with four relievers on a six-hitter for the Twins, who used two late diving catches by Keaschall in right field to prevent the Giants from taking the first two of the series.
Bradley allowed just one other hit -- a fifth-inning single by Drew Gilbert -- in his six innings. He walked three and struck out six. Keaschall's one-out triple scored Ryan Kreidler, then Brooks Lee gave Minnesota the lead for good with a run-scoring single to plate Keaschall.
A's 9, Angels 7
Carlos Cortes hit a go-ahead two-run homer in the bottom of the eighth inning and the Athletics overcame a six-run deficit to beat Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
In addition to the homer off Sam Bachman, Cortes also delivered a pinch-hit RBI triple in the seventh, helping the Athletics end a six-game losing streak. Zack Gelof hit a two-run homer later in the eighth for the A's. Shea Langeliers and Lawrence Butler each had three hits and an RBI for the Athletics.
Denzer Guzman homered and drove in four RBIs for the Angels, who have lost four of their last six games. Mike Trout added three hits and two runs for Los Angeles (60-97), which has never lost 100 games in a season.
Blue Jays at Orioles, ppd.
The scheduled game between Toronto and host Baltimore was postponed due to ongoing inclement weather. The game will be made up as part of a split doubleheader on Wednesday, with games starting at 1:35 p.m. and 6:35 p.m. ET.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers extend home winning streak to 11 with shutout of Padres
(Photo credit: William Liang)
Freddie Freeman drove in three runs, Will Smith and Tommy Edman hit home runs and the Los Angeles Dodgers inched closer to the best record in the National League with a 7-0 victory over the visiting San Diego Padres in the opener of a three-game series Tuesday.
Eight Dodgers pitchers held down the red-hot Padres offense in a bullpen game, with Justin Wrobleski (12-5) earning the win. Roki Sasaki struck out two in one inning in his return from a blister issue. The Dodgers extended their home winning streak to 11 games.
Los Angeles fell one game behind the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers and reduced its magic number for a top-two NL spot and a bye into the NL Division Series to one.
Rookie designated hitter Josue De Paula had two hits with a run scored for the Dodgers, with Shohei Ohtani expected to return from a biceps injury as a hitter Wednesday.
Luis Campusano had two hits for the Padres, whose magic number to clinch a playoff spot remained at two. Right-hander Michael King (12-10) gave up five runs on six hits over four innings, his most runs allowed in a start since May 30.
It was just the second loss in 15 games for San Diego, which is close to locking up a third consecutive playoff berth for the first time in franchise history.
The Dodgers took advantage of King's loss of command to start a four-run outburst in the second inning, all with two outs. The Dodgers loaded the bases on two singles and a hit batter, while Edman and Mookie Betts both walked to force in runs.
Freeman followed Betts with a two-run single for a 4-0 lead.
Freeman added a run-scoring single in the fourth inning, while Edman hit a home run in the sixth and Smith hit his in the seventh. Edman homered for the second straight game, while Smith went deep in his third consecutive start.
'The Dodgers welcomed back Andy Pages from a broken left hand, and he was hit by a pitch and drew a walk in four plate appearances.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers score 5 two-out runs off Padres starter Michael King in 7-0 victory
Tommy Edman and Will Smith homered as the Los Angeles Dodgers scored six runs with two outs to beat the San Diego Padres 7-0 in a series opener between rivals with the two best records in the majors this month
LOS ANGELES -- Tommy Edman and Will Smith homered as the Los Angeles Dodgers scored six runs with two outs to beat the San Diego Padres 7-0 on Tuesday night in a series opener between rivals with the two best records in the majors this month.
The Dodgers (97-60) moved within one game of NL Central champion Milwaukee (98-59) for the top mark in the big leagues and home-field advantage throughout the postseason. However, the Brewers own the head-to-head tiebreaker.
Los Angeles needs one win or an Atlanta loss to clinch a first-round bye into a National League Division Series.
The NL West champion Dodgers improved to 15-5 in September with their fifth straight victory; the Padres fell to 14-5 and had their five-game winning streak snapped.
San Diego is tied with Chicago and Philadelphia at 87-70 for the three NL wild cards — four games ahead of Arizona with five to play.
Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado were a combined 1 for 7 with five strikeouts for the Padres.
The Dodgers chased Michael King (12-10) after four innings in his career-high 32nd start of the season. The right-hander gave up five runs on six hits and struck out five as his four-game winning streak ended.
Los Angeles broke out with four runs in the second. King got the first two outs on six pitches before loading the bases. Teoscar Hernández and rookie Josue De Paula hit consecutive singles before King plunked Andy Pages, who just came off the injured list.
King then issued back-to-back walks to Edman and Mookie Betts, forcing in two runs. Freddie Freeman's two-run single made it 4-0.
Betts had a ground-rule double and scored on Freeman's two-out single for a 5-0 lead in the fourth.
Edman's solo shot came with two outs in the sixth and Smith added a 396-foot drive with one out in the seventh for a 7-0 lead.
Brock Stewart started a bullpen game and Justin Wrobleski (12-5) got the win for the Dodgers, who used eight pitchers to earn the fifth shutout in franchise history when deploying at least that many.
Among them was reliever Edwin Díaz, who struck out two in one inning. Roki Sasaki's four-seam fastball touched 100 mph while he pitched one inning. The Japanese right-hander came off the injured list earlier Tuesday after missing nearly a month with a blister on his right middle finger.
Padres LHP Robbie Ray (13-8, 3.60 ERA) starts Wednesday against Dodgers RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-8, 2.51).
___
This story has been corrected to show the Dodgers scored six runs with two outs, not five.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers shutout of Padres reveals potential (and unexpected) playoff strength
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Last year, the Dodgers hardly used their bullpen in the playoffs. This year, they would like that to once again be the blueprint. item.content:encoded:
Last year, the Dodgers hardly used their bullpen in the playoffs.
This year, they would like that to once again be the blueprint.
In their bid to three-peat as World Series champions, of course, the Dodgers are expected to be led by their star-studded rotation. Shohei Ohtani isn’t pitching, but Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are.
And if all goes according to plan, they will handle the bulk of the innings.
However, replicating the starting pitching excellence of last October won’t be easy. A season ago, the Dodgers’ four-man rotation of Ohtani, Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow accounted for 113 of the team’s 165 postseason innings (including relief appearances from Glasnow and Yamamoto). Together, they posted a 2.55 ERA.
It was historic production.
Which also means, it’s fair to assume some regression will be possible –– both in workload and effectiveness.
Thus, having more reliable bullpen options this time around could be equally important for the Dodgers. And while that might have felt like a daunting reality earlier this year, when the unit was banged up and struggling through the middle portion of the campaign, Tuesday night was a reminder that the relief corps could be a strength in this fall’s title pursuit.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.”
In a 7-0 win over the San Diego Padres, the Dodgers were not supposed to have the pitching matchup –– countering Padres ace Michael King with a makeshift bullpen game in a rivalry series opener at Dodger Stadium.
Instead, eight different Dodgers relievers held the previous red-hot Padres to a five-hit shutout. Along the way, several arms who once seemed like question marks continued to round into increasingly promising form.
“It was fantastic,” Roberts said. “This is as good as our bullpen has been, has thrown.”
It started with opener Brock Stewart, a key right-handed weapon in the Dodgers’ bullpen who began the game with a scoreless first inning, continuing his late-season resurgence after another injury-plagued year.
From there, the baton was passed on down.
Justin Wrobleski, who is in the midst of a late-season conversion to the bullpen for the second-straight year, escaped a jam in the second. Blake Treinen, who might be on the postseason roster bubble given the Dodgers’ relief depth, offered one of his best outings of late by issuing only a two-out walk in a scoreless third.
Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters
California Post News: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube, WhatsApp, LinkedIn
California Post Sports Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X
California Post Opinion
California Post Newsletters: Sign up here!
California Post App: Download here!
Home delivery: Sign up here!
Page Six Hollywood: Sign up here!
The highlight of the night came in the fourth and fifth, when Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz hung a couple more zeroes in what were important appearances from each.
For Sasaki, the outing marked his first since returning from the injured list and making his own late-season move back to the bullpen, where he could reprise his role as closer from last year’s playoffs. He worked around a pair of singles with two strikeouts and a fastball that, even after being sidelined for the last month by a blister, sat at 99-100 mph.
For Díaz, Tuesday was not only a third-consecutive scoreless outing since his own return from the IL, but his most impressive yet as he makes a bid for the playoff roster. He retired the top of the Padres lineup in order with a pair of strikeouts, and has now retired 9 of 11 batters he has faced since rejoining the active roster.
Asked postgame if Díaz –– the $69 million offseason signing who lost the closer’s job amid a previously dismal debut Dodgers season –– could still pitch his way back into ninth-inning duties, Roberts said it’s “certainly possible.”
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” Roberts added.
By that point, the Dodgers had already pulled away from the Padres. They mounted a four-run rally with two outs in the second against King, who issued back-to-back bases-loaded walks to Tommy Edman and Mookie Betts before Freddie Freeman slashed a two-run single through the infield. The offense tacked on more runs in the fourth (on another Freeman RBI single), the sixth (on a solo home run from Tommy Edman), and the seventh (a Will Smith solo blast).
In what was the lineup’s toughest test in a while, they passed with flying colors.
Still, the night’s most encouraging developments came from the ‘pen, which capped off the game with two scoreless innings from Kyle Hurt, then stress-free appearances in the eighth and ninth from Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer.
The unit’s most trusted arms at the moment, Tanner Scott (who figures to be vying with Sasaki for the postseason closer role) and Evan Phillips, weren’t even required. Nor was Edgardo Henriquez, who remains sidelined by a back injury but still could return in time for the playoffs.
“We know we have a good group, and anytime we get to carry the load and everybody has success and throws up zeros, it’s special,” Stewart said. “That’s really hard to do, for all eight guys or whatever it was today. So yeah, it’s cool.”
With a smirk, he added: “Write stories about it.”
Come October, of course, the Dodgers will be hoping their relievers are the main story.
But if the rotation falters, the club seems significantly better-suited to handle it than it did a year ago.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know,” Roberts said. “But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”

With the win, the Dodgers are up five games on the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League playoffs, with five games remaining in the regular seaso
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — On a night the Los Angeles Queens won a championship in the inaugural season of the Women’s Pro Baseball League, the Los Angeles Dodgers beat a King. Four runs with two outs in the second inning off Michael King paced a 7-0 win for the Dodgers over the San Diego Padres in Tuesday night’s series opener at Dodger Stadium.
With the win, the Dodgers are up five games on the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League playoffs, with five games remaining in the regular season. The Dodgers’ magic number to clinch a bye into the NLDS is down to just one.
King hadn’t allowed more than three runs in any of his previous nine starts, with a 2.26 ERA during that span, and he retired his first five batters faced on Tuesday. Then with two outs in the second inning, the next six batters reached, breaking open the scoring.
Teoscar Hernández singles for the Dodgers’ first hit, then Josue De Paula singled on an 0-2 pitch before Andy Pages was hit by a pitch in his very first plate appearance back since getting hit by a pitch one month prior, to load the bases. Tommy Edman walked on four pitches for the game’s first run, Mookie Betts only needed five pitches to walk home another run, then Freddie Freeman grounded a single through the infield, and under the legs of a leaping Edman, to score two more.
Betts hit a ground-rule double in the fourth, followed by another RBI single by Freeman for a fifth run against King.
Solo home runs by Edman in the sixth and Will Smith in the seventh off the Padres bullpen padded the scoring.
With Emmet Sheehan optioned on Tuesday and Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list, the Dodgers have only three active pitchers they plan to use as starting pitchers in the postseason at the moment. That means they have 11 relievers, and on a day following an off day and the day before a start by the MLB leader in innings per start, the Dodgers used .. pitchers to cover the nine innings.
Starters Justin Wrobleski and Roki Sasaki — the latter just activated on Tuesday — each pitched only one inning, both scoreless. Sasaki was hitting 100 mph in his first game action in four weeks.
Kyle Hurt was the only Dodgers pitcher to toss more than one inning, taking care of the sixth and seventh.
Jack Dreyer was the first pitcher of Sunday’s game, and the last pitcher on Tuesday.
It’s only the third time in franchise history the Dodgers used eight pitchers in a shutout of no more than nine innings, done also on September 29, 2019 in San Francisco and May 15 this year in Anaheim. For some perspective, when the Dodgers beat the Expos 1-0 Montreal in 22 innings on August 23, 1989 — Rick Dempsey homered, Tommy Lasorda got Expos mascot Youppi ejected — the Dodgers only used five pitchers that day.
Tuesday particulars
Home runs: Tommy Edman (8), Will Smith (10)
WP — Justin Wrobleski (12-5): 1 IP, 1 hit
LP — Michael King (12-10): 4 IP, 6 hits, 5 runs, 2 walks, 5 strikeouts

item.title: [MLB.com] Miguel Rojas Wins 2026 Roy Campanella Awards
